Q607
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What pathologic finding characterizes sympathetic ophthalmia (SO) and can distinguish SO from Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) syndrome?
Correct answer: D. diffuse granulomatous inflammation sparing the choriocapillaris
Rationale
Sympathetic ophthalmia (SO) is a granulomatous panuveitis that occurs after accidental or surgical trauma to 1 eye, followed by later inflammatory reaction of the fellow eye. Whereas the choriocapillaris is classically uninvolved in early SO, VKH typically involves the entire choroid/choriocapillaris.

Q608
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
Medulloepitheliomas of the ciliary body develop from what tissue?
Correct answer: A. medullary epithelium
Rationale
Medulloepithelioma is a rare tumor of the ciliary body, and rarely retina or optic nerve, that is composed of neuroepithelial cells derived from primitive medullary epithelium (the inner layer of the optic cup) (figures). This congenital tumor is usually seen in children 4-12 years old. There are rare reports of medulloepithelioma in adults. The tumor appears as a cystic ciliary body mass that may erode into the iris root and anterior chamber. Rarely secondary glaucoma, hyphema, and ectopia lentis may occur. Pathologically, the tumor shows ribbons and cords of primitive round and oval cells, forming multiple layers of neuroepithelial tubules lined by a thin basement membrane. A primitive vitreous-like material composed of hyaluronic acid is secreted on one surface. The neuroblastic cells are similar in appearance to the cells of retinoblastoma. Mucinous cysts and Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes may be seen. Medulloepitheliomas may demonstrate heteroplastic tissue from several germ layers, such as cartilage or smooth muscle, and are termed teratoid medulloepitheliomas. Rarely medulloepitheliomas have large numbers of undifferentiated cells, mitotic figures, and evidence of tissue invasion, and are termed "malignant," although the course is usually benign if enucleation is performed before orbital invasion.

Q609
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What cell type does retinoblastoma originate from?
Correct answer: D. neuroblastic
Rationale
Retinoblastoma was once thought to be of glial origin, and tumors simulating retinoblastoma were referred to as "pseudogliomas," but the neuroblastic origin of retinoblastoma from nucleated layers of the retina is now well established.
Retinoblastoma does not originate from epithelial or mesenchymal cells.

Q610
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What histologic finding is associated with Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) syndrome?
Correct answer: A. Dalen-Fuchs nodules
Rationale
Dalen-Fuchs nodules are collections of epithelioid histiocytes and lymphocytes between Bruch membrane and the RPE. They can be seen in sympathetic ophthalmia and ­Vogt-­Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) syndrome. In VKH syndrome, the entire choroid, including the choriocapillaris, is typically involved by the inflammatory process; relative sparing of the choriocapillaris is characteristic of sympathetic ophthalmia. Fundus autofluorescence and optic nerve head atrophy are not usually associated with VKH syndrome.

Q611
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the order in which the 3 phases of wound repair occur?
Correct answer: A. inflammation, repair, contraction
Rationale
The purpose of wound healing is to restore the anatomical and functional integrity of an organ or tissue. There are 3 stages to wound healing:
  • The acute inflammatory phase, which may last from minutes to hours. Blood clots quickly in adjacent vessels in response to tissue activators. Neutrophils and fluid enter the extravascular space. Macrophages remove debris from the damaged tissues, new vessels form, and fibroblasts begin to produce collagen.
  • Regeneration, the replacement of lost cells, occurs only in tissues composed of cells capable of undergoing mitosis throughout life (eg, epithelial cells, fibroblasts). Repair is the process of restructuring of tissues that leads to a fibrous scar.
  • Contraction is the final phase; the reparative tissues start to shrink so that the scar is smaller than the surrounding uninjured tissues.
Infection is a complication of wound healing. Scarification is a confounding term that means scratching. Although ""retraction" means "the act of withdrawing" and could be used as a substitute for "contraction," it is not regularly used in wound-healing terminology.

Q612
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
An Asian patient presents with a recent history of bilateral uveitis with hearing disturbance complaining of poor vision. She has been told nothing can be done to improve her vision and comes for a second opinion. There are yellow-white subretinal scars in her fundus. What was the most likely diagnosis at the time of her active disease?
Correct answer: A. Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome
Rationale
Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome occurs most commonly in people with Asian, Asian Indian, Hispanic, Native American, and Middle Eastern ancestry. There are 4 stages: prodromal, acute uveitic, convalescent, and chronic recurrent. This patient likely described having the prodromal and acute uveitic phases in her past. The prodromal stage is marked by flulike symptoms. Auditory problems are observed in 75% of patients and frequently coincide with the onset of ocular disease. Central dysacusia, generally involving higher frequencies or tinnitus, affects 30% of patients early in the disease course, typically improving within 2-3 months; however, persistent deficits may remain. The acute uveitic stage is characterized by sequential blurring of vision in both eyes, 1-2 days after the onset of neurological symptoms, with bilateral granulomatous anterior uveitis, varying degrees of vitritis, thickening of the posterior choroid, optic nerve edema and multiple serous retinal detachments. Several weeks later, the exudative retinal detachments resolve and gradual depigmentation of the choroid occurs, leading to the classic sunset-glow fundus. Integumentary changes (perilimbal vitiligo [Sugiura sign], vitiligo, alopecia, poliosis) occur during the convalescent stage. The chronic recurrent stage is characterized by recurrent bouts of granulomatous anterior uveitis, which may occur concomitantly with subclinical choroidal inflammation requiring systemic therapy. Visually debilitating sequelae of chronic inflammation develop during this last stage; they include posterior subcapsular cataract, glaucoma, CNV, and subretinal fibrosis. The fundus exam in this patient most likely revealed subretinal fibrosis. These changes have not been described in sympathetic ophthalmia. Susac syndrome is associated with hearing loss but does not have the retinal findings described. Instead, fundus exam reveals diffuse or localized narrowing of retinal arteries with a “boxcar” segmentation. Subretinal fibrosis and uveitis is an uncommon panuveitis syndrome of unknown etiology with bilateral white-yellow lesions in the posterior pole that either fade without retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) alterations, become atrophic, or enlarge and coalesce into large, white, stellate zones of subretinal fibrosis. It is not associated with auditory disturbances.
The figures show various findings associated with different phases of VKH. Note also, the diagnosis of VKH requires bilateral involvement and the absence of penetrating ocular injury and other ocular or systemic disease. Cerebrospinal fluid shows lymphocytic pleocytosis initially. Topical and systemic steroids are the first line of therapy, with immunosuppressants for recurrent or resistant cases.
Figure 1: Color fundus photographs (A, B) and late fluorescein angiograms (C, D) showing bilateral exudative retinal detachments with early peripapillary and extrafoveal subretinal fibrosis. Late fluorescein angiograms demonstrate numerous punctate hyperfluorescent leaks at the level of the retinal pigment epithelium, late filling of serous retinal detachment spaces, and variable blockage and staining of areas of subretinal fibrosis. Vision was hand motion in the right eye and 20/400 in the left eye.
Figure 2: Color fundus photographs (A, B) and late fluorescein angiograms (C, D) of same patient, 1 year after referral showing resolved exudative retinal detachments, widespread retinal pigment epithelium alterations, and residual peripapillary and extrafoveal subretinal fibrosis in each eye (arrows). Late fluorescein angiograms demonstrate central blockage corresponding to areas of subretinal fibrosis and faint staining of the borders of the fibrosis. Vision was 20/400 in each eye.

Q613
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A 5-year-old male patient presents with a complaint of light sensitivity that his parents say has been present since he was an infant. The family reports intermittent hematuria, as well. On examination, the patient has a small rim of rudimentary iris tissue present bilaterally, and foveal hypoplasia OU. What is the most important next step in diagnosis and management?
Correct answer: A. renal ultrasonogram
Rationale
This patient's presentation is concerning for aniridia and Wilms tumor. An association between sporadic aniridia and Wilms tumor has been associated with 11p13 chromosomal deletions and mutations in the PAX6 gene (in the same location). An autosomal dominant pattern of heredity is also associated with aniridia, but not Wilms tumor. Foveal hypoplasia can be seen in association with aniridia, but a fluorescein angiogram would not be the most likely next step in diagnosis and management. Because of the possibility of Wilms tumor, particularly with a history of hematuria, this patient must get imaging of the kidneys, initially with ultrasonography and often magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) after the ultrasonography is done. An x-ray for renal calculi would not show the Wilms tumor unless calcification were present (it is not normally associated with this tumor). Genetic counseling may be indicated in some cases of aniridia, but if the patient has a Wilms tumor, then the patient likely has a sporadic mutation.

Q614
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What lacrimal gland tumor is most likely associated with bone remodeling?
Correct answer: D. benign mixed tumor
Rationale
Pleomorphic adenoma (or benign mixed tumor) of the lacrimal gland is pseudoencapsulated and slowly grows by expansion, thus indenting the bone of the lacrimal fossa, producing focal excavation of the bone.
Adenoid cystic carcinoma is malignant, aggressive, and rapidly growing, thus causing bone erosion.
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma tends to be diffuse and cause proptosis.
Fibrous histiocytoma most commonly presents in the upper nasal orbit and does not tend to cause bone remodeling.

Q615
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
In hemolytic glaucoma, what characteristic material accumulates in the trabecular meshwork?
Correct answer: D. hemosiderin-laden macrophages
Rationale
Hemolytic glaucoma is characterized by the accumulation of hemosiderin-­laden macrophages in the trabecular meshwork. Rigid hemolyzed erythrocytes are seen following intraocular hemorrhage in ghost cell glaucoma. Pigmented epithelioid melanocytes can invade the trabecular meshwork in the setting of uveal melanomas. In phacolytic glaucoma, eosinophilic ­protein-­laden macrophages are seen within the trabecular meshwork.

Q616
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
Histopathologic examination of an excised orbital tumor reveals keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, keratin debris, sebaceous glands, and hair follicles. What lesion was excised?
Correct answer: B. dermoid cyst
Rationale
Dermoid cysts (figures) are most commonly found near the fronto-zygomatic or naso-frontal sutures. Dermoid cysts are choristomas (normal tissue in an abnormal location) and are similar to epidermoid cysts in that both are cystic structures lined by stratified squamous epithelium. However, by definition, dermoid cysts contain dermal elements such as sebaceous glands, hair follicles, and sweat glands. The cyst cavity fills with keratin debris. Dermoid cysts of the orbit are congenital, but they may not become symptomatic until adult life. They may cause proptosis with bony remodeling of the orbit and can erode into the cranial cavity. Trauma to the orbit can cause rupture with a foreign-body granulomatous inflammatory response.

Q617
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A 35-year-old patient with cognitive impairment, adenoma sebaceum, and sharply delineated hypopigmented lesions on the skin, has the retinal lesion depicted in the image. On optical coherence tomography (OCT) imaging, in what layer is the lesion present?
Correct answer: D. nerve fiber layer
Rationale
This is a retinal astrocytic hamartoma that is confined to the nerve fiber layer. A retinal astrocytic hamartoma is a benign retinal tumor composed of glial cells, predominantly astrocytes. It is believed to be congenital in most cases, but it can become clinically apparent sometime after birth. Retinal astrocytoma may present as 1 or multiple lesions occurring unilaterally or bilaterally. In children, phakomas are relatively flat, with a smooth surface, indistinct margins, and a gray-white color that makes them difficult to detect. A second type of phakoma, more often found in adults, occurs adjacent to or on the optic nerve, with calcified surface yielding a “mulberry” appearance. Retinal astrocytic hamartomas are frequently associated with tuberous sclerosis complex, a syndrome that includes various combinations of low-grade intracranial astrocytoma, cutaneous angiofibromas, cutaneous depigmented macules, cardiac rhabdomyoma, renal angiomyolipoma, and other hamartomas. The exact prevalence of retinal astrocytic hamartoma in tuberous sclerosis is not known.
Approximately one-third to one-half of patients with tuberous sclerosis have retinal or optic nerve hamartoma, and in half of these, the hamartomas occur bilaterally. The tumor can be seen in patients with neurofibromatosis as well. Clinically, the lesion can masquerade as a small retinoblastoma, but handheld OCT imaging can be used to demonstrate that the tumor is confined to the nerve fiber layer.

Q618
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
Conjunctival nevi are most commonly found in what anatomic location?
Correct answer: D. bulbar
Rationale
Conjunctival melanocytic nevi most commonly appear on the perilimbal interpalpebral bulbar conjunctiva in childhood. Nevi can also occur in the caruncle. Nevi occur only rarely in the palpebral and forniceal conjunctiva.

Q619
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
Pathologic examination of an eye reveals a loss of the inner retina (nerve fiber layer, ganglion cells, inner plexiform layer, and inner two-thirds of the inner nuclear layer) and preservation of the outer one-third of the inner nuclear layer and intact outer plexiform, outer nuclear, and photoreceptor layers. What diagnosis can you make from these pathologic findings?
Correct answer: C. retinal artery occlusion
Rationale
The retinal blood vessels supply the nerve fiber layer, ganglion cell layer, inner plexiform layer, and the inner two-thirds of the inner nuclear layer. Loss of this vascular supply leads to ischemic necrosis and eventual atrophy of these retinal layers as shown. In contrast, the outer retina (outer one-third of the inner nuclear layer, outer plexiform layer, outer nuclear layer, and photoreceptors) is supplied by the choroidal circulation. Choroidal ischemia would cause loss of these outer retinal layers.

Q620
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
How should tissue or fluid be submitted for flow cytometry?
Correct answer: D. unfixed and unfrozen (fresh)
Rationale
Flow cytometry is used to identify cell surface markers on cells moving single file in a fluid stream. In ophthalmology, it is most often used to evaluate lymphoid proliferations. Tissue must be sent fresh (without fixative and unfrozen) in a timely manner to prevent cell loss. Fluorochrome-labeled antibodies bound to specific cell surface receptors are sorted by a photodetector. The information gathered is an adjunct to morphologic and immunohistochemistry evaluation performed on additional formalin-fixed tissue. It is performed on vitreous, aqueous, or adnexal tissue, not on solid tumors.

Q621
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
By what mechanism does von Hippel–Lindau (VHL) syndrome cause angiogenesis?
Correct answer: B. increased vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) transcription
Rationale
Von Hippel–Lindau syndrome leads to angiogenesis, owing to increased VEGF transcription. Retinal capillary hemangioblastomas are a common manifestation of the syndrome (more than 60% of VHL syndrome patients have them). This is the result of mutation of the VHL gene on chromosome 3 that leads to overproduction of VEGF and other hypoxia-inducible factors. Less commonly, cerebellar and/or spinal hemangioblastomas can develop.
Reduced Wnt signaling, increased Rb protein, and VHL polymerization are not mechanisms that lead to angiogenesis in von Hippel–Lindau syndrome.

Q622
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A pathologic specimen of a corneal button is shown below, with arrows indicating subepithelial bullae. What is the most likely cause of the corneal pathology in this case?
Correct answer: D. phacoemulsification of a dense cataract
Rationale
The corneal button shows subepithelial bullae, stromal edema, and the absence of guttae or Descemet thickening. This is most likely bullous keratopathy secondary to intraocular surgery, such as phacoemulsification of a dense cataract.
Fuchs dystrophy would be expected to show guttae, or focal excrescences in Descemet membrane. Descemet is also typically irregular and thickened.
Keratoconus would result in apical thinning and steepening, and hydrops would show a rupture in Descemet membrane.
Thiel-Behnke corneal dystrophy shows subepithelial honeycomb opacities at the level of Bowman layer that are observed histologically as replacement of Bowman layer with a fibrous pannus in a sawtooth pattern.

Q623
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
In keratoconus without hydrops, what layer of the cornea demonstrates focal discontinuities?
Correct answer: A. Bowman layer
Rationale
Keratoconus is characterized by inferior or inferotemporal corneal stromal ectasia. Histologic findings in keratoconus include central stromal thinning and focal discontinuities in Bowman layer. The base of the cone may demonstrate a Fleischer ring, which is iron deposited in the basal epithelial cells and may be demonstrated with iron stains such as Prussian blue. In patients with a history of corneal hydrops, a break in Descemet membrane may be observed.

Q624
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
In what gene have mutations been found to correlate to nevi of Ota, blue nevi, and uveal melanoma?
Correct answer: C. GNAQ
Rationale
GNAQ

Mutations in the GNAQ and GNA11 genes have been found in 50%–85% of blue nevi and uveal melanomas and in a smaller percentage of nevi of Ota. They are considered founding mutations in the development of uveal melanoma. PAX6 mutations are associated with congenital eye malformations, including aniridia (WAGR syndrome = Wilms tumor, aniridia, genitourinary malformations, and mental retardation); congenital cataract; ectopia pupillae; Peters anomaly; morning glory disc anomaly; optic nerve hypoplasia; and colobomas of the optic nerve, retina, and choroid. BAP1 gene mutations have been identified in about 80% of uveal melanomas with a poor prognosis (class 2 tumors). Almost half of the tumors from patients with cutaneous melanoma have mutations in the BRAF gene. Mutations in the BRAF gene are only found in uveal melanoma in rare cases.

Q625
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
The funduscopic examination of a single patient's left (A) and right (B) eyes is shown in the figure. What is the most likely systemic diagnosis?
Correct answer: C. Sturge-Weber syndrome
Rationale
The figure shows a diffuse choroidal hemangioma affecting the left eye. The unaffected right eye also is shown. Diffuse choroidal hemangiomas typically occur in the setting of Sturge-Weber syndrome (encephalofacial angiomatosis).
Retinal capillary hemangioblastomas typically occur in von Hippel-Lindau syndrome. Retinal arteriovenous malformations typically occur in Wyburn-Mason syndrome. Retinal capillary hemangiomas may occur in neurofibromatosis type 1.

Q626
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A 75-year-old man is referred to an ophthalmologist for evaluation of an eyelid lesion (Figure 1). On examination, there is a flat, pale yellow lesion that is firm to palpation. Histology of the lesion is shown in Figure 2. What is the diagnosis?
Correct answer: C. basal cell carcinoma, morpheaform variant
Rationale
The histology shown represents the morpheaform variant of basal cell carcinoma (BCC). BCC appears clinically as a slow growing, elevated lesion with ulceration and pearly raised edges. The morpheaform or sclerosing growth pattern appears as a flat, pale yellow, indurated plaque. This variant is often infiltrative and difficult to stage. Other variants of BCC include nodular and multicentric. Basal cell carcinoma is the most common malignant eyelid lesion. The main risk factor is sunlight exposure. Lesions are just about as common in the medial canthus (48.3%) as in the lower lid (47.5%). Lesions affecting the medial canthus are more likely to be deeply invasive and involve the orbit. BCC originates from the stratum basale, or stratum germinativum and the outer root sheath of the hair follicles. Histology demonstrated islands of basaloid cells connected to overlying dermis with peripheral palisading. A clear space may surround the islands of tumor cells as a result of artifact in processing. The malignant morpheaform variant shows thin cords and strands of cells infiltrating a fibrotic stroma.
Of patients with BCC, 0.7% have nevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome, also known as Gorlin-Goltz syndrome. This autosomal dominant syndrome results in multiple BCCs in young patients, odontogenic jaw cysts, skeletal abnormalities, palmar and plantar pits, neurologic abnormalities, and endocrine disorders. Treatment of choice is complete excision with surgical margin control. This can be achieved with frozen sections or Mohs surgery. Morbidity with BCC is usually secondary to local invasion, as metastasis is extremely rare.

Q627
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
In this patient who has granular corneal dystrophy type 1 (GCD1), what type of stain is shown in Figure 1, with hyaline deposits staining red and stromal collagen staining blue?
Correct answer: B. Masson trichrome
Rationale
Special stains are used to determine the composition of the deposits in corneal stromal dystrophies. Masson trichrome is used to identify deposits in granular dystrophy in which collagen stains blue and hyaline material stains red.
Alcian blue is used to identify mucopolysaccharide deposition in macular dystrophy.
Congo red stains amyloid orange by standard light microscopy in lattice dystrophy; on examination with polarized light, the amyloid exhibits birefringence with dichroism (orange and apple green).
Periodic acid-Schiff stains glycogen and proteoglycans magenta.

Q628
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What clinical feature typically leads to phthisis bulbi?
Correct answer: C. low intraocular pressure (IOP)
Rationale
Phthisical globes demonstrate shrinkage, atrophy, and disorganization (SAD eyes). Loss of adequate IOP leads to shrinkage of the eye. A formerly hypertensive eye will often demonstrate normal or low IOP as it becomes phthisical. Phthisical eyes might demonstrate vitreous hemorrhage or hemorrhage in other ocular structures. Intraocular ossification occurs late; it is a typical histologic finding in phthisis bulbi.

Q629
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What pathologic change distinguishes squamous cell carcinoma of the conjunctiva from conjunctival intraepithelial neoplasm (CIN)?
Correct answer: D. stromal involvement
Rationale
Conjunctival and corneal intraepithelial neoplasms are uncommon tumors. The most important assessment to be made histologically in ocular surface squamous neoplasia (OSSN) is whether the neoplasia is contained by the basement membrane, as in conjunctival intraepithelial neoplasia (partial-thickness dysplasia of the epithelium), or carcinoma in situ (full-thickness dysplasia of the epithelium), or whether neoplastic cells have invaded the stroma (squamous cell carcinoma).
Altered maturation of cells (dysplasia), nuclear hyperchromatism and pleomorphism, and dyskeratosis are common in both CIN and squamous cell carcinoma.

Q630
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the most common intraocular malignant neoplasm?
Correct answer: C. choroidal metastasis
Rationale
Choroidal metastasis is the most common intraocular malignant neoplasm overall. Choroidal melanoma is the most common primary intraocular malignant neoplasm. Primary ocular lymphoma is not the most common intraocular malignant neoplasm. Retinoblastoma is the most common intraocular malignant neoplasm in children, but not the most common intraocular malignant neoplasm overall.

Q631
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
Penetrating keratoplasty is performed on a patient with suspected granular dystrophy. What histochemical stain can aid in confirming this dystrophy?
Correct answer: A. Masson-trichrome
Rationale
Masson-­trichrome highlights deposits of hyaline material that characterize granular corneal dystrophy. Congo red stains amyloid deposits in lattice and ­granular-­lattice dystrophies. Alcian blue stains nonsulfated glycosaminoglycan deposits in macular dystrophy.

Q632
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A 4-year-old boy presents with a pigmented lesion of his left eye (see figure). It has been present since birth. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: D. congenital nevocellular nevus
Rationale
A congenital nevocellular nevi is a sharply demarcated, darkly pigmented lesion of the skin that can occur anywhere on the body. Large lesions greater than 20 cm have an increased rate of malignant transformation. A nevus of Ota is a diffusely pigmented dermal lesion that frequently involves the sclera. A nevus flammeus is a congenital vascular anomaly that presents as a red skin lesion that darkens over time. A blue nevus is a small, dark blue-grey dome-shaped dermal lesion of 10 mm or less in size.

Q633
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
The corneal deposits in granular dystrophy (figure) are composed of what material?
Correct answer: B. hyaline
Rationale
Granular corneal stromal dystrophy is an autosomal dominant condition with irregular, well-circumscribed deposits of hyaline material in the corneal stroma (figure). The opacities are initially seen in the central cornea and have intervening clear spaces. The hyaline material stains bright red with Masson trichrome stain as shown and is composed of electron-dense material with rod-shaped bodies in an amorphous matrix. The noncollagenous protein may derive from the corneal epithelium or keratocytes. A mutation in the TGFBI gene on chromosome 5q31 is responsible for the formation of keratoepithelin. Three clinical forms of granular dystrophy are defined, with similar ultrastructural features and variations in the rate of progression, appearance, and depth of the deposits. Avellino corneal dystrophy is a variant of granular dystrophy and has been traced to families in Avellino, Italy. These patients have granular dystrophy but also show lattice stromal dystrophic changes. Different mutations in the TGFB1 (formerly BIGH3) gene are thought to cause granular, Avellino, lattice, and Reis-Bücklers dystrophies. Early symptoms are recurrent erosions. At later stages, superficial keratectomy, photokeratectomy, or corneal transplantation may be indicated.

Q634
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the key pathology finding that distinguishes a teratoid medulloepithelioma from a non-teratoid medulloepithelioma?
Correct answer: A. presence of heteroplastic tissue
Rationale
Heteroplastic tissue is defined as the presence of tissue arising from 2 or more different embryonic germ layers. Teratoid medulloepitheliomas contain tissue that is not of ectodermal origin, such as cartilage or skeletal muscle.
Retina, vitreous, and ciliary body epithelium are all derived from ectoderm.

Q635
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A 1-year-old child presents with a bright red lesion of the upper eyelid that has existed since birth but has recently been enlarging in size. There is mild, symmetric astigmatism in both eyes. The mother insists on treatment to remove the entire lesion. What is the best treatment option?
Correct answer: D. oral beta-blockers
Rationale
Capillary hemangiomas are common eyelid lesions in children. These may appear at or shortly after birth and clinically appear as bright red lesions that grow rapidly over weeks to months. These lesions are nonencapsulated and usually involute spontaneously. Histologic appearance depends on the stage. Early lesions show sheets of benign endothelial cells surrounding capillary channels. Involuting lesions display increased fibrosis and hyalinization of capillary walls. Although lesions eventually involute and regress, they can pose a risk for amblyopia.
β-blockers are often used as first-line treatment of capillary hemangiomas, usually with significant reduction in size. Excision of these lesions should be performed with care because it can lead to significant blood loss from the large feeder vessels that are present within the hemangiomas. Historically, treatment for vision-threatening or cosmetically unacceptable lesions has included injection of steroids. This presentation is inconsistent with amblyopia, because the refractive correction is symmetric. Injection of steroids has the potential complication of central retinal artery occlusion and should be reserved for nonresponsive, vision-threatening lesions.

Q636
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A patient presents with an eyelid mass. What is the most frequent indication for a frozen section?
Correct answer: A. to surgically control the margins of a neoplasm
Rationale
Frozen sections are appropriate to ensure complete resection of the neoplasm. Frozen sections are generally not recommended on melanocytic lesions because of the potential for artifact. A formal diagnosis should be made on permanent sections. Frozen sections should not be used as means to expedite a diagnosis.

Q637
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
From highest to lowest, what is the order of mortality rates for iris, ciliary body and choroidal melanomas?
Correct answer: B. ciliary body melanoma > choroidal melanoma > iris melanoma
Rationale
Uveal melanomas can arise in the anterior (iris) or the posterior (ciliary body or choroid) uveal tract. Iris melanomas have the best prognosis, whereas posterior melanomas have a high mortality rate. Melanomas of the ciliary body have the least favorable prognosis, possibly because they may be more frequently diagnosed at a later stage.

Q638
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What syndrome may include the lesion shown in the figures?
Correct answer: B. Goldenhar syndrome
Rationale
The photo shows an epibulbar dermoid. Dermoids are firm, dome-shaped, white-yellow choristomas typically at or straddling the limbus, most commonly in the inferotemporal quadrant. Dermoids may occur in isolation or, particularly when bilateral, as a manifestation of a developmental syndrome such as linear nevus sebaceous syndrome or Goldenhar syndrome. Goldenhar syndrome is characterized by upper eyelid coloboma, preauricular skin tags, and vertebral anomalies in addition to epibulbar dermoid.
NF1 patients develop melanocytic and neuroglial lesions. Apert syndrome is a type of craniosynostosis in which the patients also may have syndactyly. In tuberous sclerosis, patients develop benign tumor growth in multiple organs.

Q639
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the most common histopathological finding in temporal arteritis?
Correct answer: D. epithelioid histiocytes
Rationale
Temporal arteritis is a noninfectious inflammatory disorder characterized by granulomatous inflammation within the vessel wall. The most common finding is histiocytes (tissue macrophages) at the level of the internal elastic lamina. Multinucleated giant cells may also be present, but they are not a necessary finding to make the diagnosis (even though the synonym of temporal arteritis is giant cell arteritis). Plasma cells and eosinophils are found more commonly in other types of inflammation, such as allergic reactions.

Q640
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the most common cause of infectious retinitis?
Correct answer: B. Toxoplasma
Rationale
Toxoplasma

Toxoplasmic retinochoroiditis is the most common infectious retinitis. It may be caused by reactivation of a congenital infection or by a newly acquired infection in an immunocompetent or immunocompromised individual. Clinically, these patients present with a panuveitis or posterior uveitis with prominent vitritis and focal retinochoroiditis. In the setting of reactivation of a prior infection, the focal retinochoroiditis typically occurs adjacent to a pre-existing scar.
While the other organisms listed in the answer choices (Candida, cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus type 1) may all cause retinitis, they are less common causes than Toxoplasma.

Q641
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is a typical histopathologic feature of sclerocornea?
Correct answer: B. peripheral corneal stromal vascularization
Rationale
In sclerocornea, typically the peripheral, and sometimes the central, cornea is opaque with disorderly arranged, thickened collagen fibers and extension of scleral and episcleral vessels into the affected stroma. In addition, the curvature of the cornea is flattened.
Breaks in Bowman membrane and inflammation are not characteristics of sclerocornea.

Q642
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What syndrome is associated with this lesion?
Correct answer: B. tuberous sclerosis
Rationale
The photo shows astrocytic hamartomas, or retinal astrocytomas, which are associated with tuberous sclerosis. Patients with Wyburn Mason develop arteriovenous malformations (AVMs). Those with Goldenhar syndrome may develop limbal dermoids. Patients with von Hippel-Lindau syndrome develop retinal capillary hemangioblastomas.

Q643
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
An ophthalmologist performs a fine needle biopsy on a cream-colored choroidal lesion in a 56-year-old woman. Cytology reveals atypical cells suggestive of metastatic carcinoma. What systemic workup should be performed next?
Correct answer: D. breast examination and mammography
Rationale
In a woman, the most common metastatic lesion to the choroid is from breast cancer. Of patients who present to the ophthalmologist with uveal metastasis, about 30% have no known history of systemic cancer. After subsequent systemic evaluation, about 50% have no detectable primary cancer, and the primary lesion remains occult.

Q644
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
Primary optic nerve sheath meningiomas arise from what tissue?
Correct answer: D. arachnoid
Rationale
Primary optic nerve sheath meningiomas arise from the arachnoid sheath of the optic nerve. Together, the dura, arachnoid, and pia make up the meninges. The myelin sheath covers the optic nerve, starting posterior to the lamina cribrosa, but is not the tissue from which meningiomas arise.

Q645
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
When glaucoma occurs in association with angle recession, what is the cause of the glaucoma?
Correct answer: B. damage to the trabecular meshwork
Rationale
Recession of the anterior chamber angle is due to a tear in the face of the ciliary body, between the longitudinal and circular muscles, with posterior displacement of the iris root. Concurrent damage and eventual scarring of the trabecular meshwork can lead to glaucoma. Lens subluxation and iridodialysis can occur in addition to angle recession after blunt ocular trauma; however, the glaucoma that occurs in association with angle recession is most commonly caused by damage to the trabecular meshwork.

Q646
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A patient who recently relocated from another city presents to establish care for an "eye tumor" OD. Records from his previous ophthalmologist are presently unavailable, and he is unsure of the exact diagnosis, but he tells the new ophthalmologist that the lesion has been stable for years. On examination, a jet-black elevated mass originating from the prelaminar nerve extending into the peripapillary region is noted. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: A. melanocytoma
Rationale
Melanocytomas, also known as magnocellular nevi, are uncommon melanocytic uveal tumors that are deeply pigmented, and often peripapillary in location. These lesions are typically dark brown or even jet black and can be mistaken for melanomas; however, they rarely transform into melanoma. Documented growth should prompt work-up for possible melanoma. Melanocytomas may be elevated and often have feathery margins due to extension into the nerve fiber layer, and as such can cause a relative afferent pupillary defect and visual field defects.
Histologically, large polyhedral cells that are densely packed with melanin and have small nucleoli are seen. Often, there is so much pigment that it is necessary to bleach the section in order to make a diagnosis. Choroidal nevi and congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium (CHRPE) are other pigmented uveal lesions that would not be expected to change over time; however, in this case the peripapillary location is more suggestive of a melanocytoma. Choroidal melanoma would not be expected to maintain stability over time.

Q647
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the normal timeframe after a corneal abrasion for the epithelial anchoring fibrils to reform?
Correct answer: C. 4-6 weeks
Rationale
Within an hour of a corneal abrasion, the parabasilar epithelial cells begin to migrate across the denuded area until they touch other migrating cells; then contact inhibition stops further migration. Simultaneously, the surrounding basal cells undergo mitosis to supply additional cells to cover the defect. Although a large corneal abrasion is usually covered by migrating epithelial cells within 24 to 48 hours, complete healing, which includes restoration of the full thickness of epithelium (5-7 layers) and re-formation of the anchoring fibrils, takes 4 to 6 weeks.

Q648
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What stain is used to identify the elastosis of degenerated collagen in pingueculae and pterygia?
Correct answer: D. Verhoeff–van Gieson
Rationale
Histologic examination of stromal collagen in pingueculae and pterygia shows fragmentation and basophilic degeneration, referred to as elastotic degeneration or solar elastosis. Verhoeff-van Gieson stains the elastin, even after the tissue has been treated with elastase for digestion of true elastin.
Congo red is used to stain amyloid deposits, which appear red orange under standard light. Under polarized light, they exhibit birefringence, changing from red orange to apple green. This can be useful for conjunctival amyloid deposits or lattice corneal dystrophy. Alcian blue is used to stain mucopolysaccharides such as macular corneal dystrophy. Periodic acid–Schiff (PAS) is used to stain basement membrane, such as corneal epithelial basement membrane, Descemet membrane, and the lens capsule.

Q649
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A patient who was diagnosed with sebaceous carcinoma of the right lower eyelid at an outside institution has been referred for further management. What is the best next step in the management of this patient's condition?
Correct answer: C. Request pathology slides from the outside institution for review.
Rationale
It is considered within the standard of care to forward the slides from the original biopsy to the institution where where definitive treatment for malignancy will be undertaken. At most hospitals, this is written policy to insure that the diagnosis is internally confirmed prior to treatment and to provide the pathologist with an example of the histologic features of the tumor so that the tumor can be identified in subsequent biopsies or excisions. Mohs excision and frozen section margin control are not recommended for sebaceous carcinoma because of the difficulty in identifying pagetoid spread on frozen sections.

Q650
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What sign may indicate malignant transformation of a choroidal nevus?
Correct answer: A. increase in basal dimension
Rationale
An increase in the basal dimension is worrisome for malignant transformation of a choroidal nevus. Some nevi may develop choroidal neovascular membrane, drusen, or overlying retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) changes without malignant transformation. Hyperplasia of the RPE is a congenital lesion and not related to malignancy. Cotton-wool spots (nerve fiber layer infarcts) are also unrelated to choroidal nevi and may be seen in ischemic conditions like diabetic or hypertensive retinopathy.

Q651
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A 55-year-old white man presents without symptoms for evaluation. His ocular history is unremarkable. His slit-lamp examination is abnormal, as shown. What is his most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: B. primary acquired melanosis
Rationale
The figure shows tarsal pigment in a white patient. This presentation is most consistent with primary acquired melanosis. Congenital melanosis is more often seen in more darkly pigmented individuals and is typically on the bulbar conjunctivae. Ocular melanocytosis manifests as pigment on the episclera, below the conjunctivae. A nevus is typically well circumscribed and is most often located on the bulbar conjunctivae, near the limbus.

Q652
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
Corneal limbal dermoids are classified as what type of lesion?
Correct answer: C. choristoma
Rationale
Corneal limbal dermoids (figures) are choristomas, which are tumors composed of mature normal tissue that is present at an abnormal location. They are present at birth with little postnatal growth. They consist of various amounts of normal mature tissue (keratinized dermal epithelium, dermal collagen, adipose tissue, dermal appendages such as hair follicles or sebaceous or acinar sweat glands, peripheral nerves) in an abnormal location on the corneal surface, often straddling the limbus. Corneal dermoids are solid tumors, in contrast to orbital dermoid cysts. There is a frequent association with Goldenhar syndrome (preauricular appendages or aural fistulae, maxillary or mandibular hypoplasia, vertebral anomalies, eyelid cleft abnormalities, and Duane syndrome). Excision is often indicated because of irritation, cosmesis, and interference with vision. Tissue should be available for patch grafting in case the dissection is too deep, but usually superficial removal suffices.

Q653
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What optic nerve cells produce and maintain the myelin sheath?
Correct answer: C. oligodendrocytes
Rationale
Oligodendrocytes, astrocytes, and microglial cells are all types of glial cells, which support the function of the central nervous system. Oligodendrocytes produce and maintain the myelin sheath of the optic nerve; astrocytes are involved with support and nutrition; and microglial cells (central nervous system [CNS] histiocytes) have a phagocytic function. The axons of retinal ganglion cells are contained within the optic nerve.

Q654
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A child with a history of yellow-red skin lesions presents with unilateral recurrent hyphema. A few iris nodules are noted. What histologic findings would be expected on skin or iris biopsy?
Correct answer: A. large histiocytes with foamy cytoplasm and Touton giant cells
Rationale
The case described clinically resembles juvenile xanthogranuloma, which may feature yellow-red skin lesions. Intraocular features may include recurrent hyphema. A biopsy of a skin or iris nodule would be expected to feature large histiocytes with foamy cytoplasm and Touton giant cells. Necrosis with formation of pseudorosettes can be seen in retinoblastoma. Bilateral diffuse uveal melanocytic proliferation is characterized by infiltration of the uveal tract by benign nevoid or spindle-shaped cells. Caseating granulomas are a feature of tuberculous granulomas, but tuberculous uveitis does not feature recurrent hyphemas.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q655
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
Retinal astrocytic hamartomas are most associated with what systemic condition?
Correct answer: B. tuberous sclerosis
Rationale
Tuberous sclerosis complex (Bourneville-Pringle disease) is an autosomal dominant condition that may be associated with astrocytic hamartomas in the retina, optic disc, and brain. The figures show selected findings. The retinal lesions may be relatively flat, gray-white lesions with indistinct margins, or they may be sharply demarcated and elevated, containing multiple, reflective, calcific spherules. The retinal tumors are seen in approximately 40% of patients. Growth is slow, and vision is usually not affected. They may rarely cause exudative changes requiring photocoagulation. These are not pathognomonic of tuberous sclerosis. Similar hamartomas are seen occasionally in neurofibromatosis and in normal patients. Two tumor suppressor genes are associated with tuberous sclerosis: TSC1(9q34) produces tuberin, and TSC2(16p13.3) produces hamartin. Retinal lesions are more common in patients with the TSC2 mutation. These 2 proteins form a heterodimer that normally inhibits cell proliferation. The mechanisms of these gene defects that lead to the clinical findings in tuberous sclerosis are not known, but more than 400 mutations have been described.
The classic triad (Vogt triad) in tuberous sclerosis is facial sebaceous adenomas (angiofibromas), mental deficiency, and seizures. Other dermatologic features include periungual fibromas, cafe-au-lait spots, shagreen patches, and the pathognomonic "ash-leaf" spot. Many of the tumors in tuberous sclerosis are hamartomas. Visceral tumors including cardiac rhabdomyomas, renal cysts, and angiomyolipomas may occur. Brain tumors are cortical tubers and subependymal nodules, containing glial and neuronal elements that often calcify.

Correct answer: A. astrocytes

Oligodendrocytes, astrocytes, and microglial cells are all types of glial cells, which support the function of the central nervous system. Oligodendrocytes produce and maintain the myelin sheath of the optic nerve; astrocytes are involved with support and nutrition; and microglial cells (central nervous system [CNS] histiocytes) have a phagocytic function. The axons of retinal ganglion cells are contained within the optic nerve.

Q657
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What primary cellular element is observed histologically in the preretinal membranes found in proliferative vitreoretinopathy?
Correct answer: C. retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells
Rationale
Because retinal pigment epithelial cells are frequently identified in associated excised epiretinal membranes in this condition, proliferative vitreoretinopathy (PVR) membranes are thought to form as a result of proliferation of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells along with other cellular elements, including Müller cells, fibrous astrocytes, macrophages, fibroblasts, and myofibroblasts. Amacrine and bipolar cells, which are found in the inner nuclear layer of the retina, are not a major constituent of PVR membranes. Unless there is rupture of Bruch membrane, choroidal melanocytes do not have access to the subretinal space or vitreous cavity and therefore are not typically observed in PVR membranes.

Q658
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What effect on survival did the Collaborative Ocular Melanoma Study demonstrate for pre-enucleation external beam radiation in patients with large melanomas?
Correct answer: A. no effect on survival
Rationale
The Collaborative Ocular Melanoma Study compared standard enucleation against enucleation with presurgical radiation therapy and showed that there is no evidence that pre-enucleation external-beam radiotherapy on patients with large choroidal melanomas improves 5-year mortality rates. However, local recurrence in the orbit was more frequent after enucleation alone. While details of the study are not included in the BCSC, here is a brief summary of the details. There were 1003 patients enrolled in the study, and 5-year outcomes were known for nearly 80% of the study population. The 5-year survival rates were 57% for enucleation alone, and 62% for pre-enucleation radiation. No significant difference was found in survival between the 2 groups from all causes of metastatic melanoma. In the enucleation-alone group, 26% died from confirmed metastatic melanoma, compared to 28% in the preenucleation radiation group.
Other issues to be considered with the use of pre-enucleation external beam radiation include the added cost of radiation, the risk of induced secondary tumors in the radiation field, secondary ptosis, patient inconvenience, and the delay in enucleation with the risk of local extension or recurrence. In contrast, radioactive plaque application to the sclera overlying a choroidal melanoma is probably the most common form of treatment (figure). Local tumor control rates are as high as 90%, with late complications of radiation optic neuropathy and maculopathy.

Q659
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A 49-year-old woman presents with right eye pain. The slit-lamp examination reveals ciliary flush, anterior chamber cell, mutton-fat keratic precipitates, and posterior synechiae. The patient states that she has had similar episodes of this pain in the past. Further examination reveals small tan nodules in the lower conjunctival fornices. What would a conjunctival biopsy be expected to reveal?
Correct answer: B. noncaseating granulomas
Rationale
This patient has recurrent granulomatous uveitis secondary to sarcoidosis. The small tan nodules in the conjunctival fornices are indicative of granulomatous conjunctivitis. Noncaseating granulomas would be expected on conjunctival biopsy. These are round to oval aggregates of epithelioid histocytes with or without multinucleated giant cells. These pathologic findings alone are not pathognomonic for sarcoidosis but must be correlated with clinical findings after infectious causes are ruled out.
Linear deposition of immunoglobulins and complement (C3) on the basement membrane would be found in mucous membrane pemphigoid (MMP) and would not be associated with granulomatous uveitis.
Gram-positive cocci in pairs would be indicative of infection with Streptococcus spp. These infections would not be associated with granulomatous uveitis.
Elastotic degeneration is the pathologic finding in pinguecula and pterygium.

Q660
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What stain can be useful to obtain after biopsying the eyelid of an individual with a chronic, unilateral papillary conjunctivitis?
Correct answer: A. oil red O
Rationale
Sebaceous gland carcinoma can have several presentations, including a painless, slow-growing, firm nodule of the conjunctiva; chronic unilateral conjunctivitis/blepharitis; and eyelid thickening and deformity, with focal loss of eyelashes. On biopsy, it is important to pay attention to histopathologic characteristics, including presence of anaplastic cells, multiple mitoses, and lipid. Performed on frozen section slides, staining with oil red O and Sudan black demonstrates intracytoplasmic lipid in the vacuolated cells.

Q661
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
Leukemic retinopathy can cause hemorrhages in what levels of the retina?
Correct answer: A. preretinal, intraretinal, and subretinal
Rationale
Posterior segment findings in leukemia include retinal hemorrhages, white-centered hemorrhages (pseudo-Roth spots), cotton-wool spots, subhyaloid hemorrhage, vitreous hemorrhage, and subretinal or choroidal hemorrhage. Retinal vascular occlusions are common. Retinal hemorrhages are caused by vascular occlusions and concomitant anemia and thrombocytopenia. Perivascular infiltration of leukemic cells can give vessels a sheathed appearance or produce yellow-gray nodules in the retina or subretinal space.
Leukemia also frequently involves the uvea. Choroidal infiltrates can be difficult to see on examination, but can be detected as diffuse choroidal thickening on ultrasonography. The iris may be thickened by leukemic cells, and these cells can invade the anterior chamber, forming a pseudohypopyon and secondary glaucoma.
Leukemic infiltration of the optic nerve may present with disc edema and severe vision loss. This should be treated urgently with systemic and intrathecal chemotherapy plus radiation to preserve vision.
All the eye findings of leukemia can be caused by 1 or more of the following: increased viscosity from increased numbers of leukemic cells, hemorrhage due to decreased platelets and alteration in the clotting cascade, and infiltration of tissues by leukemic cells.

Q662
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A 1-week-old baby presents with red eye and mild papillary reaction. The diagnosis of Chlamydia trachomatis can be made by obtaining conjunctival scrapings that demonstrate what finding on Giemsa stain?
Correct answer: C. intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies
Rationale
Chlamydia trachomatis neonatal conjunctivitis typically occurs at around 1 week of age and is characterized by mild swelling, hyperemia, and a papillary reaction with minimal to moderate discharge. The gold standard for diagnosis is the detection of intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies.

Q663
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What ancillary test is most useful in the initial evaluation of choroidal melanoma?
Correct answer: C. A- and B-scan echography
Rationale
Ultrasonography is considered the most useful ancillary tool in evaluating choroidal melanomas. A- and B-scan ultrasonography are used to measure choroidal melanoma size, to evaluate internal tumor reflectivity, and to evaluate for the presence of extrascleral extension. Standardized A-scan typically demonstrates high initial reflectivity followed by low-amplitude internal reflections (low internal reflectivity). B-scan can inform the examiner about the thickness, basal diameter, and general shape of the mass.
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is not a widely used modality in assessing melanocytic intraocular tumors, but it has utility in assessing eyes with opaque media and can provide information regarding possible extrascleral extension. OCT may be better than ultrasonography in trending choroidal lesions <1 mm in thickness and can also provide diagnostic information regarding the architecture of the neurosensory retina and retinal pigment epithelium. Fluorescein angiography is used to detect the presence of an independent tumor circulation, a supportive but not definitively diagnostic finding in choroidal melanoma. Indocyanine green angiography may also identify local alterations in choroidal blood flow.

Q664
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
If a conjunctival biopsy is being performed for suspicion of ocular cicatricial pemphigoid (OCP), then half of the specimen should be submitted in formalin for routine histology and the other half should be submitted in what medium for immunofluorescence studies?
Correct answer: A. Michel medium
Rationale
OCP is a form of autoimmune cicatrizing conjunctivitis of autoimmune etiology. Typically, it involves not only the conjunctiva but also other mucous membranes. When this diagnosis is suspected clinically, conjunctival biopsy is performed to establish the diagnosis. Half of the specimen is submitted in formalin for routine histologic examination, and half is submitted in a special medium (eg, Michel or Zeus) or saline for direct immunofluorescence analysis. 
Glutaraldehyde is used for electron microscopy, absolute alcohol is used for cytology, and Bouin solution is used for small biopsies.

Q665
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is a common histopathologic finding in aphakic/pseudophakic bullous keratopathy?
Correct answer: C. decreased or absent endothelial cells
Rationale
Intraocular surgery, most often cataract surgery, results in loss of endothelial cells. The loss of endothelial cells may lead to bullous keratopathy, characterized by Descemet folds, stromal edema, epithelial edema, and microcystic epithelial separations or bullae. Other forms of intraocular surgery, including multiple and/or complicated glaucoma procedures, may lead to similar findings.
Epithelialization of the endothelial cells may be present in posterior polymorphous dystrophy, iridocorneal endothelial syndrome, and epithelial ingrowth.
Fibrous growth in the anterior chamber may be present in corneal graft failure, with proliferation of tissue from the graft host interface onto the posterior corneal surface and anterior chamber.
Vascular and fibrous proliferation in the subepithelial layer may be present in bullous keratopathy, but not as commonly as endothelial loss.

Q666
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What pathologic findings characterize the inflammation in phacoantigenic uveitis (also known as phacoanaphylactic endophthalmitis or lens-induced granulomatous endophthalmitiis)?
Correct answer: D. zonal granulomatous inflammation
Rationale
Phacoantigenic uveitis (phacoanaphylactic endophthalmitis) presents the classic pathologic picture of zonal granulomatous uveitis, as compared to nodular (tuberculosis) and diffuse (sympathetic ophthalmia) patterns. Phacoantigenic uveitis is usually associated with penetrating ocular injuries with rupture of the lens capsule. The exposed lens material provokes a granulomatous inflammation. Histologically, there is a central nidus of degenerating lens material, with a surrounding zonal granuloma. The zonal granuloma demonstrates multinucleated giant cells and neutrophils adjacent to the lens material, with an intermediate mantle of lymphocytes and histiocytes and surrounding fibrous connective tissue with chronic inflammation.

Q667
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
Fuchs dystrophy can be identified based on the pathologic examination of thickening of what layer?
Correct answer: A. Descemet membrane
Rationale
The defining characteristic of Fuchs dystrophy is endothelial cell loss and the presence of focal thickening or excrescences of Descemet membrane called guttae. In cases of progressive endothelial cell loss, corneal edema may develop.

Q668
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What clinical finding is a risk factor for malignant transformation of a choroidal nevus?
Correct answer: A. thickness greater than 3 mm
Rationale
Choroidal nevi rarely transform into malignant melanoma. By age 80, a patient's risk of malignant transformation of an existing choroidal nevus is about 0.8%.
The most important risk factor for malignant transformation is nevus thickness. Virtually all choroidal melanocytic tumors thinner than 1 mm are nevi, and virtually all choroidal melanocytic lesions thicker than 3 mm are melanomas. Lesions between 1 mm and 2 mm in thickness can be difficult to classify, and close observation is often recommended. Lesions between 2 mm and 3 mm in thickness may be managed based on clinical risk factors with observation or immediate treatment.
Other predictive risk factors for malignant transformation include subretinal fluid, subjective clinical symptoms (metamorphopsia, photopsia, visual field loss), presence of overlying orange pigment, lack of overlying drusen, juxtapapillary location, basal dimension 7 mm or greater, and low to medium internal reflectivity on A-scan echography.

Q669
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
Histologically, what are the most common type of cells in a choroidal melanoma?
Correct answer: B. spindle-B and/or epithelioid cells
Rationale
The correct answer is spindle-B and/or epithelioid cells. Choroidal nevi may be composed of 4 types of nevus cells: plump polyhedral nevus cells, slender spindle nevus cells, plump fusiform dendritic nevus cells, and balloon cells. Histologically, posterior uveal melanomas are commonly composed of spindle cells and/or epithelioid melanoma cells. Less commonly, balloon cells similar to those seen in choroidal nevi may be present. Spindle-cell melanoma consists primarily of spindle-B melanoma cells. It may also contain spindle-A cells; however, a tumor consisting entirely of spindle-A cells is considered a nevus. Monocytes and Touton giant cells are inflammatory cells.

Q670
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A 70-year-old patient presents with a chronic chalazion, asymmetric eyelid inflammation, and loss of normal adnexal structures. What is the preferred next step in management?
Correct answer: A. excisional biopsy
Rationale
This description is suspicious for sebaceous adenocarcinoma (figure). Full-thickness eyelid biopsy is indicated to avoid sampling only superficial inflammatory change overlying a potentially malignant lesion. Conjunctival map biopsies are helpful to define the extent of the process. A superficial biopsy can miss the underlying pathology. Radiation and cryotherapy are not indicated without a tissue diagnosis.

Q671
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the preferred management for the abnormality seen in this asymptomatic 4-year-old girl?
Correct answer: B. total excision
Rationale
The figure depicts a yellow lesion in the inferior temporal conjunctivae. This is a dermolipoma, a congenital choristoma. The lesion is typically asymptomatic but may cause astigmatism if it extends anteriorly. Given that the lesion can extend into the orbit and/or lacrimal gland, it is most often observed; indications for subtotal excision are a cosmetically unacceptable appearance, irritation, and astigmatism.

Q672
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What anterior segment finding(s) is (are) characteristic of Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome?
Correct answer: A. corectopia and polycoria
Rationale
Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome is part of the spectrum of developmental anomalies termed anterior segment dysgenesis. Ocular manifestations include corectopia and polycoria, posterior embryotoxon, iris strands adherent to Schwalbe line, iris hypoplasia, and a maldeveloped anterior chamber angle. Abnormal endothelial cells are seen in iridocorneal endothelial syndrome. Peripheral anterior synechiae are associated with other diseases such as chronic angle closure and rubeosis iridis. Fibrillar material in the anterior chamber angle is seen in pseudoexfoliation syndrome.

Q673
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What disorder typically results in Touton giant cells in histologic specimens?
Correct answer: B. juvenile xanthogranuloma
Rationale
The Touton giant cell can be distinguished by the presence of several nuclei in a distinct pattern: a ring of nuclei surrounds a central homogeneous, eosinophilic cytoplasm; and foamy cytoplasm surrounds the nuclei. Touton giant cells are seen in lesions with high lipid content, such as fat necrosis, xanthomas, and xanthogranulomas. Both bacterial keratitis and Acanthamoeba keratitis are characterized histologically by a dense infiltrate of neutrophils with variable tissue necrosis. Follicular cell lymphoma is characterized histologically by closely packed follicles that contain atypical lymphoid cells.

Q674
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A 35-year-old patient develops hypotony after blunt ocular trauma. What pathologic abnormality is demonstrated in this ultrasound biomicroscopy image?
Correct answer: A. separation of the ciliary body from the scleral spur
Rationale
Prolonged hypotony after blunt ocular trauma may be due to a cyclodialysis cleft, as found in this patient. In this condition, the ciliary body separates from the scleral spur, providing direct access of aqueous to the suprachoroidal space. Gonioscopy can be difficult to perform and interpret in these patients due to a shallow anterior chamber and soft eye (from hypotony). Anterior segment OCT and ultrasound biomicroscopy can be helpful in these cases to evaluate for the presence and extent of a cyclodialysis cleft. Disinsertion of the iris root results in iridodialysis. A tear between the circular and longitudinal fibers of the ciliary body is found in angle recession, seen as a widened ciliary body band on gonioscopy. A tear of the trabecular meshwork may be seen as a small trabecular cleft on gonioscopy. None of these conditions except a cyclodialysis cleft can cause hypotony.

Q675
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
In what gene are polymorphisms associated with pseudoexfoliation syndrome?
Correct answer: B. LOXL1
Rationale
LOXL1

Polymorphisms in the lysyl oxidase-like 1 gene (LOXL1) are associated with pseudoexfoliation syndrome. Lysyl oxidase is a pivotal enzyme in extracellular matrix formation, catalyzing covalent crosslinking of collagen and elastin. FOXC1 and PITX2 mutations are associated with Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome. PAX6 mutations are associated with developmental abnormalities, such as aniridia and Peters anomaly.

Q676
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
By what mechanism does orbital extension of choroidal melanomas most often occur?
Correct answer: A. growth through scleral emissary canals
Rationale
Choroidal melanomas can extend through scleral emissary canals into the orbit. Superficial invasion of the sclera is often seen, but extension through intact sclera into the orbit is extremely rare. Retinoblastoma can invade the lamina cribrosa, extending into the optic nerve and brain; however, uveal melanoma does not typically invade the optic nerve or brain. The irradiation (eg, brachytherapy) used to treat choroidal melanomas does not usually lead to scleromalacia.

Choroidal metastasis from what primary malignancy is most common in women?
Correct answer: C. breast
Rationale
Choroidal metastasis most commonly arises from the breast in women and second most-commonly from the lung. The lung is the most common site of primary malignancy in men.

Q678
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A 52-year-old man presents with the subconjunctival finding shown in the figure. What pathology finding would be consistent with a fibrous histiocytoma?
Correct answer: B. proliferation of spindle fibroblasts, wounded histiocytes, and occasional multinucleated giant cells
Rationale
Basophilic calcific deposits in the sclera anterior to the lateral rectus muscle are consistent with senile calcific plaque. Activated spindled fibroblasts loosely arranged in short fascicles with a prominent capillary network are consistent with scleral nodular fasciitis. A palisading arrangement of epithelioid histiocytes around a central core of necrotic collagen is consistent with episcleritis. Finally, proliferation of spindle fibroblasts, wounded histiocytes, and occasional multinucleated giant cells is consistent with fibrous histiocytoma or fibroxanthoma. (See figure).

Q679
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What histologic change corresponds to commotio retinae?
Correct answer: D. disruption in the architecture of the inner and outer segments of the photoreceptors
Rationale
The changes resulting from contusion injury to the retina manifest clinically as areas of retinal whitening. For many years, it was believed that this indicated a possible diagnosis of retinal edema or focal ischemia, both of which demonstrate retinal opacification clinically. The advent of optical coherence tomography showed that retinal whitening can also correspond to disruption in the architecture of the retinal photoreceptor inner and outer segments. The presence of subretinal fluid does not significantly change the color of the ocular fundus. Microinfarcts of the nerve fiber layer (NFL), or ­cotton-­wool spots, are located in the superficial retina. Myelin is not typically present in the retinal NFL; ganglion cell axons acquire myelin sheaths posterior to the lamina cribrosa.

Q680
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What stain best demonstrates the histological stromal deposits in macular corneal dystrophy?
Correct answer: C. alcian blue
Rationale
Macular corneal dystrophy (MCD) is an autosomal recessive condition with bilateral limbus to limbus deposition of mucopolysaccharides within the cornea (first figure). The mucopolysaccharides are positively stained by alcian blue and colloidal iron stains (second figure). Clinically there are focal gray-white stromal opacities, with hazy intervening stroma and early visual loss within the first decade of life. In contrast to the other major stromal dystrophies, the corneal endothelium is often also involved. The glycosaminoglycans accumulate in the endoplasmic reticulum of the keratocytes and endothelial cells and extracellularly within the stroma. Three subtypes of MCD have been described based on immunoreactive stains for keratan sulfate.

Q681
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
Histologically, optic nerve head melanocytoma is consistent with what melanocytic tumor?
Correct answer: C. magnocellular nevus
Rationale
Melanocytomas (magnocellular nevi) are rare tumors composed of characteristic large, polyhedron-shaped nevus cells that have small nuclei and abundant cytoplasm filled with large melanin granules. Magnocellular nevus of the ciliary body or optic nerve head typically appears as a dark brown to black lesion. It is usually located eccentrically over the optic nerve head, and it may be elevated. It often has fibrillar or feathery margins as a result of extension into the nerve fiber layer. Because a melanocytoma rarely transforms into melanoma, it is important to differentiate the two. Melanocytomas can produce an afferent pupillary defect and visual field abnormalities ranging from an enlarged blind spot to extensive nerve fiber layer defects.
Combined hamartoma of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and retina is a rare disorder that occurs most frequently near the optic nerve head margin, though it may also be observed in the peripheral fundus. Typically, the hamartoma appears as a pigmented, slightly elevated lesion with vitreoretinal traction and tortuous retinal vessels. Glial cells within this lesion may contract, producing traction lines seen clinically in the retina. Exudative complications associated with the vascular component of the lesion may be seen. These lesions have been mistaken for melanomas because of their pigmentation, slight elevation, and propensity to change in young individuals.
Hyperplasia of the pigmented ciliary epithelium or the RPE usually develops in response to trauma, inflammation, or other ocular insults.

Q682
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
In Schnabel cavernous optic atrophy, what material can be histopathologically demonstrated in the optically clear spaces within the optic nerve?
Correct answer: D. mucopolysaccharides
Rationale
Schnabel initially described cavernous optic nerve atrophy (figure) in 1892. Extremely high intraocular pressures (IOP) can lead to infarction of the optic nerve, as the vascular supply to the post-laminar nerve from the short posterior ciliary arteries is compromised. Initially, the infarction is manifested by ischemic swelling of the nerve, but this is followed by glial phagocytosis of the necrotic nerve fiber bundles, leaving large, cavernous spaces separated by the pial septae. The cavernous spaces were previously thought to contain vitreous, but are now believed to contain mucopolysaccharides. This unique form of optic nerve atrophy also is seen with vascular disease involving the proximal optic nerve, including atherosclerosis and vasculitis.
Inborn errors of metabolism can lead to ganglioside accumulation in diseases such as Tay-Sachs, not Schnabel cavernous atrophy. Cholesterol and amyloid are not found in this disease process, either.

Q683
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
An 85-year-old white man is referred for a suspicious subretinal process in the right eye. He is asymptomatic. On examination, the vision is 20/30 OU with pseudophakia on slit-lamp examination. His left fundus demonstrates small and medium-sized drusen. His right fundus demonstrates drusen and a temporal subretinal pigmented lesion measuring 10 mm in base and 4.5 mm in thickness. Ultrasonography demonstrates a subretinal lesion with medium or high internal reflectivity. There are no vascular pulsations seen. Fluorescein angiography demonstrates decreased choroidal filling in the area of the lesion. What is the most appropriate management?
Correct answer: B. observation
Rationale
The diagnosis is peripheral exudative hemorrhagic chorioretinopathy (also termed peripheral or exudative disciform lesion). Most likely this is secondary to a leaking choroidal neovascular membrane outside the macular area. This is most common in the older age group and is often seen in patients with concurrent macular degeneration. Often, these lesions will have associated surrounding subretinal hemorrhage. However, the clinical appearance may simply be a peripheral pigmented choroidal mass. They tend to be acoustically dense (though extremely acoustically hollow may also be seen). The most diagnostic sign is the absence of choroidal spontaneous vascular pulsation within the lesion, which is more indicative of a uveal melanoma.
Fluorescein angiography would reveal early hypofluorescence due to blockage by hemorrhage and late hypofluorescence or hyperfluorescence with retinal pigment epithelial atrophy or hypertrophy.  Observation of this lesion is indicated. In 1 month, it is very likely that the lesion would resolve or regress enough to indicate the diagnosis. On needle biopsy, the cytologic specimen will be mostly red blood cells. One may also see an immediate deflation of the mass when the needle passes into the lesion.

Q684
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is a feature of mild persistent fetal vasculature?
Correct answer: D. Mittendorf dot
Rationale
Persistent fetal vasculature (PFV) is a congenital sporadic condition in infants. It is unilateral in two-thirds of cases. The spectrum of PFV ranges from mild cases with prominent hyaloid vessel remnants, a large Mittendorf dot, and a Bergmeister papilla to severe cases with microphthalmia, ciliary process elongation (classic for PFV), a retrolenticular plaque, a thick, fibrous persistent hyaloid artery, and prominent radial iris vessels. Retinoblastoma may be part of the initial differential diagnosis.

Q685
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What tissue response occurs within the lens epithelium in the setting of anoxic or hypoxic injury, such as posterior synechiae or markedly elevated intraocular pressure (IOP)?
Correct answer: A. metaplasia
Rationale
In circumstances that make the lenticular epithelium anoxic or hypoxic, such as posterior synechiae or markedly elevated intraocular pressure (IOP), a metaplastic response may occur, producing fibrous plaques intermixed with basement membrane.

Q686
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A teenager undergoes evaluation of a unilateral conjunctival mass (part A of the figure below). It is slightly elevated without signs of inflammation or vascularization, and is irregularly pigmented. Biomicroscopy shows multiple small cystic structures within the pigmented mass as shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: B. conjunctival nevus
Rationale
The description is most compatible with a benign conjunctival nevus, which are common conjunctival lesions. Cystic changes within the lesions are highly suggestive of nevi. Conjunctival nevi may not acquire visible melanin pigment until puberty, or may remain amelanotic. They are usually flat near the limbus, and slightly elevated at other sites (bulbar conjunctiva, caruncle, and eyelid margin). Conjunctival nevi pathologically demonstrate typical nevus cells, with benign nuclei, nesting tendencies, and melanin pigment in approximately 70%. Conjunctival nevi proliferate in the junctional area of the epithelium and then "fall off" into the substantia propria of the conjunctiva. Many conjunctival nevi have associated small epithelium cysts lined by stratified squamous epithelium, often with goblet cells, in the substantia propria (part B of the image shown with the question). These cysts may be seen with the biomicroscope. Inflammation can cause vascular injection, and rapid growth can occur at puberty. Melanomas of the conjunctiva are rare in children. Pyogenic granulomas are granulation tissue at the site of injury, from ruptured chalazia or sutures from pterygium or strabismus surgery. Corneal limbal dermoids are opaque corneal/limbal choristomas with characteristic choristomatous elements including adipose tissue and hair follicles.

Q687
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What type of cell is shown in this specimen from a choroidal nevus?
Correct answer: C. spindle cells
Rationale
Choroidal nevi may be composed of 4 types of cells: plump polyhedral nevus cells, slender spindle nevus cells, plump fusiform dendritic nevus cells, and balloon cells. The cells pictured here are spindle cells. 
Melanocytoma is composed of large polyhedral cells. Melanomas can be composed of epithelioid melanoma cells. Choroidal osteomas are composed of compact bone, with intratrabecular spaces that are filled with loose connective tissue that contains large and small blood vessels, vacuolated mesenchymal cells, and scattered mast cells.

Q688
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
The histopathology demonstrated in this photo is most characteristic of what disorder of the uveal tract?
Correct answer: B. juvenile xanthogranuloma (JXG)
Rationale
The histopathology photo is demonstrative of Touton giant cells, which are characteristic of juvenile xanthogranuloma (JXG), a benign non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis. Touton giant cells consist of a ring or horseshoe-shaped arrangement of nuclei containing a central area of eosinophilic cytoplasm, with surrounding foamy cytoplasm around this nuclear arrangement. Behçet disease, sympathetic ophthalmia, and sarcoidosis can all affect the uveal tract but do not demonstrate this unique histopathology.
