Q689
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
Xanthelasma most commonly occur in patients with what cholesterol level?
Correct answer: D. normal high-density lipoprotein (HDL) and low-density lipoprotein (LDL)
Rationale
Xanthelasma are flat, yellowish skin lesions typically found on the upper and lower eyelids, around the inner canthus in middle-aged people. These lesions are frequently seen in patients with elevated serum cholesterol levels (in up to 50% of cases), but they are more common in patients with normal cholesterol levels. They can also be seen in young people with disorders of lipid metabolism. Presence of xanthelasma does not require workup in older patients, but appropriate workup is justified, especially in younger patients. These lesions are composed of lipid-laden or "foamy" histiocytes that aggregate in the superficial dermis around blood vessels. These lesions may be observed. For patients who request removal, options include surgical excision, CO2 or argon laser, or application of trichloroacetic acid (TCA). It is important to inform patients that these lesions may recur. Care must be taken with surgical excision, as removal of significant portions of the anterior lamella may lead to cicatricial ectropion. Laser application can also lead to significant scarring and ectropion.

Q690
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What histopathologic finding is typically seen in congenital hereditary endothelial dystrophy (CHED)?
Correct answer: A. thickened Descemet membrane
Rationale
Histopathological findings in congenital hereditary endothelial dystrophy (CHED) are very similar to those seen in pseudophakic/aphakic bullous keratopathy and include thickened Descemet membrane and focal or diffuse endothelial atrophy. The primary abnormality in CHED is thought to be degeneration of endothelial cells during or after the fifth month of gestation and not the result of surgical trauma as in pseudophakic/aphakic bullous keratopathy.
A multilaminar endothelium may be seen in CHED but is less common. Thinned corneal stroma and atrophic corneal epithelium are not usually associated with CHED.

Q691
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What component of the vitreous serves as a scaffold for vitreoretinal membrane formation?
Correct answer: C. collagen fibrils
Rationale
The collagen fibrils of the vitreous can provide a scaffold for glial and fibrovascular tissue from the retina and uveal tract to grow and extend into the vitreous to proliferate as membranes. These membranes usually have a contractile component, which can lead to retinal traction.

Q692
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A 13-year-old boy presents with redness of the right eye, constant epiphora, and umbilicated, nodular, waxy lesions on the lid margin. What kind of conjunctivitis does this patient most likely have?
Correct answer: D. follicular
Rationale
Molluscum contagiosum, which is caused by a member of the poxvirus family, is characterized by ­dome-­shaped, waxy epidermal nodules with a central umbilication. If present on the eyelid margin, these nodules can cause a secondary follicular conjunctivitis. Histologically, the epithelial nuclei are displaced peripherally by large eosinophilic (pink) viral inclusions known as molluscum or ­Henderson-­Patterson bodies. As the infected cells migrate to the surface, the viral inclusions become more basophilic (blue/dark purple). Bacterial conjunctivitis is associated with a papillary reaction and purulent discharge. In pseudomembranous conjunctivitis, the fibrin network is easily peeled off, leaving the conjunctiva intact; pseudomembranes form on the conjunctiva. Giant papillary conjunctivitis (GPC) occurs in primary and secondary forms, all of which are at least partially caused by chronic ocular allergy. Primary forms of GPC include vernal and atopic keratoconjunctivitis. Secondary GPC is caused by contact lenses, ocular prostheses, or exposed sutures.

From what material are optic nerve drusen believed to develop?
Correct answer: D. calcified mitochondria
Rationale
Drusen of the optic nerve head are calcific, usually bilateral, deposits embedded within the parenchyma of crowded discs and abnormal vasculature. Evidence suggests that abnormal axonal metabolism leads to mitochondrial calcification and drusen formation. Hard macular drusen are composed of hyaline material.

Q694
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What anterior corneal dystrophy is associated with corneal tissue that stains positively with Masson Trichrome and Congo red?
Correct answer: A. granular type 2 dystrophy (Avellino dystrophy)
Rationale
Granular type 2 dystrophy (formerly Avellino dystrophy) has features of both granular type 1 and lattice dystrophies. It stains positively with Masson trichrome as well as Congo red. Granular type 1 dystrophy stains positively with Masson trichrome but not with Congo red. Lattice dystrophy stains positively with Congo red but not Masson trichrome. Macular dystrophy stains positive with Alcian blue but negatively with trichrome and Congo red.

Q695
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A patient is a survivor of bilateral retinoblastoma. What is the chance that the patient's children will be affected by retinoblastoma?
Correct answer: A. 45%
Rationale
Retinoblastoma is caused by a mutation in the RB1 tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 13 (13q14). Both copies of the RB1 gene must be mutated in order for a tumor to form.
If a patient has bilateral retinoblastoma, there is an approximately 98% chance that they have a germline mutation. Therefore, the children of a bilateral retinoblastoma survivor have a 50% chance of inheriting one abnormal gene from the affected parent. Of those who inherit the abnormal gene, 90% develop somatic mutations in the remaining normal RB1 allele, leading to multiple tumors in one or both eyes. Thus, the chance that a bilateral retinoblastoma survivor will have a child with retinoblastoma is 45%. (50% chance of inheriting the abnormal RB1 allele and 90% chance of penetrance). About 10% of retinoblastoma patients have a family history of retinoblastoma.
Sporadic cases with no family history make up about 90% of all retinoblastomas. Of these, 60% will have unilateral disease and no germline mutations. The remaining 40% have new germline mutations and will develop multiple tumors. Of note, approximately 15% of the sporadic unilateral patients are carriers of a germline RB1 mutation. Unless there are multiple tumors in the affected eye, these patients are indistinguishable from children without a germline mutation. Genetic counseling for retinoblastoma can be very complex. A survivor of unilateral retinoblastoma has a 7% to 15% chance of having an affected child.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q696
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What diagnosis is demonstrated by the histopathology image shown?
Correct answer: A. phacoantigenic uveitis
Rationale
Phacoantigenic uveitis develops when an amount of lens cortex is retained in an eye following cataract extraction or following traumatic lens capsule disruption. Histopathology (see figure with caption) will show zonal granulomatous inflammation at the site of lenticular trauma. The inflammation can be either granulomatous or nongranulomatous, with corresponding keratic precipitates.
Phacolytic uveitis occurs when a hypermature cataract develops and high-molecular-weight lens proteins leak through the capsular bag into the anterior chamber. Macrophages ingest the lens proteins and become lipid laden, having a refractile appearance. Keratic precipitates in phacolytic uveitis are not typically seen.
The treatment for both types of uveitis is typically surgical: Removal of the lens material will often cause resolution of the uveitis. If a very small amount of cortex is left in the anterior chamber in the case of phacoantigenic uveitis, topical corticosteroids are sometimes employed to manage modest inflammation until the lens material is resorbed by macrophages.
Infectious endophthalmitis is a clinical diagnosis, and an aqueous or vitreous specimen may grow the infectious agent. IOL-associated uveitis such as uveitis-glaucoma-hyphema syndrome is generally related to chafing of intraocular tissue by an intraocular lens.

Q697
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What clinical feature of conjunctival melanomas is associated with a poor prognosis?
Correct answer: C. involvement of the eyelid margin
Rationale
Approximately 50%–70% of cases of conjunctival melanoma arise from PAM with atypia; the remainder develop from a nevus or are de novo. Melanomas are usually nodular and can involve any portion of the conjunctiva. The nodule may be pigmented or amelanotic (15%–25% of conjunctival melanomas). Conjunctival melanomas metastasize to regional lymph nodes in 25% of patients, as well as to the lungs, liver, brain, bone, and skin. The overall mortality rate in these cases ranges from 15% to 30%. Clinical features associated with a worse prognosis include:
  • nonbulbar conjunctival location (ie, plica semilunaris/caruncle, forniceal or palpebral conjunctiva)
  • increased tumor thickness
  • involvement of the eyelid margin

In these cases, calcifications are usually focal and discrete, occurring within granulomas (toxocariasis) or a retrolental membrane (persistent fetal vasculature) or at the level of the RPE (Coats disease).

What is a choristoma?
Correct answer: D. normal tissue in an abnormal location

A choristoma is a congenital anomaly in which there is normal, histiologically mature tissue in an abnormal location. Limbal dermoid is an example of this: normal, mature skin present in the abnormal location of the ocular surface. A hamartoma is an increased amount of normal tissue in a normal location. Capillary hemangioma is an example of a hamartoma: an increased number of capillary blood vessels in the normal location of the dermis.

Q702

A 65-year-old white woman with vitritis and negative treponemal antibody and interferon gamma release assay test results initially responds well to systemic corticosteroids; however, as the steroids are tapered, her vitritis becomes robust. Correct answer: B. 60%-70%
Rationale
The case described clinically is consistent with primary vitreoretinal lymphoma (PVRL). The cytopathology secures the diagnosis. In more than two-thirds of cases of PVRL, patients will have or will go on to develop intracranial disease. In fact, PVRL is a subset of primary central nervous system lymphoma (PCNSL). Approximately 20% of patients with PCNSL (who do not yet have intraocular involvement) will go on to develop PVRL.

Q703
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A 62-year-old man presents with a palpable mass causing fullness of the upper lid. It has been progressing over 3 years. He denies pain or diplopia. A computed tomography (CT) scan reveals that the mass is well circumscribed and the globe is displaced down and toward the nose. What is the best next step in the management of this patient?
Correct answer: B. excisional biopsy
Rationale
The most common epithelial tumor of the lacrimal gland is pleomorphic adenoma (benign mixed tumor). This tumor is pseudoencapsulated and grows slowly by expansion. Typically, the patient experiences no pain. Histologically, pleomorphic adenoma has a fibrous pseudocapsule and comprises a mixture of ductal-derived epithelial and stromal elements. Transformation into a malignant mixed tumor can take place in a long-standing or incompletely excised pleomorphic adenoma, with relatively rapid growth after a period of relative quiescence. Carcinomas, including adenocarcinoma (carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma) and adenoid cystic carcinoma, can also develop in recurrent pleomorphic adenomas. To avoid recurrence and potential malignant transformation, the most appropriate management for this patient is lateral orbitotomy with excisional biopsy.
When a pleomorphic adenoma is suspected, incisional biopsy should be avoided. Fine needle biopsy of orbital masses may not adequately sample all representative areas of the tumor and lack tumor morphology, because it is difficult to make several passes at different angles through an intraorbital tumor. Observation is not the best management because long-standing pleomorphic adenomas can undergo malignant transformation.

Q704
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A glistening tan tumor is found on the inner surface of the pars plicata. Histopathology reveals proliferation of the nonpigmented ciliary epithelium. What is the diagnosis?
Correct answer: C. ciliary body nevus
Rationale
A Fuchs adenoma (also called pseudoadenomatous hyperplasia) is usually an incidental finding at autopsy and rarely becomes apparent clinically. It appears as a glistening, white or tan, irregular tumor arising from the inner surface of the pars plicata. It consists of benign proliferation of the nonpigmented ciliary epithelium with accumulation of basement membrane-like material.

Melanocytomas (magnocellular nevi) are benign tumors that may be located eccentrically on the optic nerve head, or on the iris, ciliary body, or choroid. Iris melanocytoma cells may seed the anterior chamber angle, thus causing glaucoma. Melanocytomas are composed of characteristic large, polyhedron-shaped nevus cells that have small nuclei and abundant cytoplasm filled with large melanin granules.

Ciliary body melanomas are comprised of spindle cells and/or epithelioid cells, not ciliary epithelium. Ciliary body nevi , which are usually small and incidentally found on histologic examination of globes enucleated for other reasons, are comprised of nevus cells without atypia or significant mitotic activity.

Q705
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What anterior segment histological findings are characteristic of primary congenital glaucoma (PCG)?
Correct answer: C. hypoplastic scleral spur and an anomalous insertion of the ciliary muscle
Rationale
PCG is thought to be the result of arrested development of the anterior chamber elements. Histologically, the anterior chamber retains an immature conformation that is characterized by anterior insertion of the iris root, mesenchymal tissue in the anterior chamber angle, and a poorly developed scleral spur in which the ciliary muscle inserts directly into the trabecular meshwork. Hypertrophy of the ciliary muscle, trabecular meshwork, and Schlemm canal are not associated with PCG. Endothelialization of the trabecular meshwork and anterior iris surface is seen in iridocorneal endothelial syndrome. Neovascularization of the trabecular meshwork and anterior iris surface is present in many diseases associated with ischemia, including diabetes, central retinal vein occlusion, intraocular tumors, and ocular ischemic syndrome.

Q706
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
An 18-month-old boy was referred by his primary care physician for evaluation of leukocoria on the left eye. A complete eye exam showed a normal right eye. On the left, a large elevated retinal mass consistent with retinoblastoma was noted. It filled about 80% of the eye with evidence of overlying vitreous seeding. Nodules and neovascularization were noted on the iris. B-scan ultrasonography shows no extrascleral extension. What treatment is most appropriate for this boy?
Correct answer: D. enucleation
Rationale
Based on the International Classification of Retinoblastoma, this child has unilateral Group E disease. Although intra-arterial chemotherapy via neurovascular cannulization of the ophthalmic or middle meningeal artery has shown great promise and is becoming more widely used, it is usually indicated for Group A–D lesions or in patients with bilateral disease. In this child with a large unilateral tumor, vitreous and iris seeding, and iris neovascularization, the best course of action remains enucleation. Of note, a long segment of intraorbital nerve should be removed along with the globe in case optic-nerve extension has occurred. 
Observation is not a reasonable option; spontaneous involution of retinoblastoma, while reported, is a rare event. Evisceration might allow for local tumor dissemination. Exenteration is reserved for large orbital extensions of retinoblastoma, typically seen in neglected cases.

Q707
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What pathologic changes are seen in the Descemet membrane in patients with congenital hereditary endothelial dystrophy (CHED)?
Correct answer: B. thickened Descemet membrane with atrophic endothelium
Rationale
The underlying abnormality in CHED is degeneration of the corneal endothelium. The histologic appearance is that of focal or diffuse absence of endothelial cells. In addition, the Descemet membrane is thickened, and there is diffuse stromal edema with marked corneal thickening. Changes in the Bowman layer and epithelium can occur secondary to long-standing edema.

Q708
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What type of corneal degeneration produced the histologic specimen pictured?
Correct answer: B. actinic keratopathy
Rationale
Figures A and B demonstrate actinic keratopathy. Histologic examination reveals irregular, basophilic globules deep to the epithelium in the region of Bowman layer and the anterior stroma.
Bullous keratopathy will have subepithelial bullae and stromal edema. Keratoconus will have central stromal thinning and small focal discontinuities in the Bowman layer. Salzmann nodular degeneration will show focal absence of Bowman layer with nodular, sclerotic subepithelial collagenous and/or fibrotic material.

Q709
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
How does corneal stromal healing differ from stromal healing in other tissues?
Correct answer: B. avascular stromal healing
Rationale
Corneal stromal healing is avascular. Healing in the corneal stroma occurs via the process of fibrosis rather than the fibrovascular proliferation seen in other tissues. The avascular aspect of corneal wound healing is critical to the success of penetrating keratoplasty as well as the various forms of refractive surgery.
The corneal epithelial healing process begins within 1 hour of injury, including the covering of a large epithelial abrasion within 24 to 48 hours and complete healing in 4 to 6 weeks. Stromal keratocytes, fibroblast-like cells (also known as fibrocytes), are activated following a central corneal wound and eventually migrate across the wound, laying down collagen and fibronectin. In full-thickness corneal wounds, the endothelial cells adjacent to the wound slide across the posterior cornea; few cells are replaced through mitosis.

Q710
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What histopathologic finding can distinguish the conjunctival from the corneal epithelium?
Correct answer: B. presence of goblet cells
Rationale
The conjunctival epithelium is nonkeratinizing stratified, squamous, with goblet cells. The conjunctival epithelium is contiguous with the corneal epithelium, but the latter has no goblet cells. The goblet cells are a source of mucin in tears and are essential in the lubrication of the ocular surface. Both conjunctival and corneal epithelium are stratified, but the corneal epithelium usually has 5 to 7 layers of cells. The corneal endothelium consists of a single layer of cells.

Q711
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What demographic group has the highest incidence of choroidal osteoma?
Correct answer: A. young females
Rationale
Choroidal osteoma is a benign bony tumor most often seen in young female patients, but it has been reported in children, men, older adults, and different races.
Clinically, osteomas are yellow-orange, discrete geographic lesions adjacent to the optic disc. Histologically, the tumor is composed of normal-appearing compact bone located in the juxtapapillary choroid. There is loose connective tissue and blood vessels between the bony trabeculae.

Q712
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
Conjunctival intraepithelial neoplasm is a precursor to what tumor?
Correct answer: A. squamous cell carcinoma
Rationale
The term conjunctival intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) was coined by Pizzarello and Jakobiec in 1978 to describe severe epithelial dysplasia of the conjunctiva and cornea, which was recognized as a precursor to invasive squamous cell carcinoma. This is not grouped under the umbrella term ocular surface squamous neoplasia (OSSN). CIN (figures) predominantly affects older patients, especially men, and is associated with xeroderma pigmentosum, UV-B exposure, and viruses including herpes simplex, human papillomavirus, and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). The growths are usually slightly elevated, well demarcated, and often have prominent vascularization. Pathologic changes are graded according to the vertical extent of epithelial dysplasia (grade I, less than 25%; grade II, 25% to 75%; and grade III, more than 75%).
Squamous cell carcinoma is diagnosed when invasion beyond the epithelial basement membrane is identified. Immunohistochemical stains may be helpful in identifying proliferative potential and cell differentiation. Treatment is surgical, with margins of at least 2 mm to 3 mm, with deeper dissection if necessary. Cryotherapy and topical agents (mitomycin C, 5-fluorouracil, and interferon alpha-2b) have also been effective as adjuvants or as primary therapy.

Q713
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
The immunohistochemical stain of desmin might be helpful in diagnosing what neoplasm?
Correct answer: D. rhabdomyosarcoma
Rationale
Because desmin is a marker of striated muscle differentiation, it can be useful in the diagnosis of rhabdomyosarcoma. Cytokeratin is appropriate in the workup of carcinoma. S100, ­Melan-­A, and HMB45 immunohistochemical stains are useful in the diagnosis of melanocytic tumors. A panel of immunohistochemical stains, including CD20 (a marker of B-cell differentiation), is important in the workup of ocular adnexal and intraocular lymphomas.

Q714
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What sexually transmitted disease should be excluded in a 35-year-old patient with multiple conjunctival papillomas?
Correct answer: B. HIV
Rationale
The presence of multiple or extensive conjunctival papillomas in an adult should raise concern for possible systemic immunosuppression. HIV/AIDS should be considered if there is no obvious underlying etiology (eg, a history of solid organ transplantation, requiring immunosuppressive medication). Gonorrhea or chlamydia can present with acute or subacute purulent conjunctivitis, but would not be the cause of conjunctival papillomatosis. Syphilis is rarely implicated as a cause of granulomatous conjunctivitis, but not conjunctival papillomas.

Q715
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
An iris mass contains multinucleated giant cells with an annulus of nuclei surrounded by a lipid-filled clear zone. What is the diagnosis?
Correct answer: A. juvenile xanthogranuloma
Rationale
Touton giant cells have an annulus of nuclei surrounded by a clear zone filled with lipids. They are characteristic of the lesions of juvenile xanthogranuloma (JXG), where focal proliferations of foamy and epithelioid histiocytes are found. JXG is usually seen in children under 2 years of age. Small, round skin papules, which are orange or tan in color, are usually present. JXG of the eyelid, limbus, retina, choroid, and optic nerve have rarely been reported. Spontaneous hyphemas may occur from the iris lesions, which may be localized or, if infiltrative JXG, can cause heterochromia. JXG is self-limited and usually regresses by the age of 5 years, although rare cases are described in adults. Treatment is necessary with the development of secondary glaucoma, which responds to medical therapy. Excision or radiation therapy is occasionally necessary. In contrast, the granulomas in sarcoidosis are typically noncaseating with epithelioid cells, lymphocytes, and Langhans-type giant cells with nuclei on the periphery of the giant cell in an incomplete circle. Toxoplasmosis does not typically cause iris granulomas, and the acute lesions are associated with retinal necrosis and gliosis. HLA-B27 uveitis causes lymphocytic infiltration of involved tissues.

Q716
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
How should tissue be prepared to submit it for flow cytometry?
Correct answer: D. kept fresh or immersed in RPMI media
Rationale
Flow cytometry requires fresh tissue. The tissue can be submitted in gauze moistened with saline or in a special nutrient or tissue culture medium such as RPMI.

Q717
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the most important test to obtain in a patient with primary vitreoretinal lymphoma?
Correct answer: C. magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and orbits
Rationale
Most patients with primary vitreoretinal lymphoma will develop central nervous system (CNS) involvement. Conversely, of patients who present with CNS involvement, approximately 20% will have intraocular involvement. Patients with suspected primary vitreoretinal lymphoma should undergo magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain with contrast, as well as a spinal tap for cytologic studies to evaluate for CNS involvement. Since lymphomas do not usually erode or otherwise affect bony or skeletal structures, a CT of the brain and orbits may appear normal. Although choroidal melanoma often spreads to the liver and abdomen, these are uncommon locations for metastasis of ocular lymphoma. Serum chemistry profiles are unlikely to provide any suggestion of stage or metastasis.
Uveal lymphoma is usually more indolent and is associated with systemic lymphoma in up to one-third of cases. Evaluation for systemic involvement includes use of computed tomography (CT) or combined CT and positron emission tomography (PET) imaging of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis.

Q718
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
When nonocular primary neoplasms spread to the eye, what is the most common intraocular site of metastasis?
Correct answer: C. choroid
Rationale
The uvea is the most common intraocular site for metastasis of nonocular primary neoplasms. Within the uvea, 88% of metastases are to the choroid, followed by metastases to the iris (9%) and ciliary body (2%). Metastatic disease involving the optic nerve and retina is uncommon.

Q719
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A chalazion has recurred several times at the same site. An oil red O stain was requested to help rule out malignancy. How should the tissue be prepared for the stain?
Correct answer: D. frozen
Rationale
Recurrent chalazions should be biopsied and the tissue should be sent for pathologic examination to rule out sebaceous gland carcinoma. It is important to make the pathologist aware that sebaceous gland carcinoma is high on the differential diagnosis list, because oil red O stain must be done on frozen sections prior to routine processing. Sebaceous cells contain lipid that stains positively with oil red O.

Q720
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
At the time of presentation of choroidal melanoma, what percentage of patients demonstrate evidence of metastatic disease?
Correct answer: C. 2%
Rationale
At the time of diagnosis of choroidal melanoma, clinically evident metastatic melanoma is found in less than 2% of patients. This increases to 25% at 5 years and 34% at 10 years after initial diagnosis. Once metastatic disease is diagnosed, median survival is usually less than 6 months. Metastatic disease is most common to the liver (89%), lung (24%), bone (17%), and skin. Metastatic evaluation is necessary to determine if other conditions exist that may affect treatment decisions, including second independent primary malignancies, and to determine if the choroidal melanoma has metastasized. Evaluation should include comprehensive physical examination, chest x-ray, liver function, and ultrasound testing, and further imaging studies including computed tomography (CT), positron emission tomography (PET), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), as indicated. Factors associated with increased mortality from choroidal melanoma include ciliary body location, tumor size and possibly thickness, diffuse growth pattern, extraocular extension, epithelioid cell type, mitotic activity, lymphocytic infiltration, tumor vascularization, and somatic monosomy 3 or 8q addition.

Q721
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
The lacrimal gland is divided into 2 lobes (orbital and palpebral) by what structure?
Correct answer: B. levator palpebrae aponeurosis
Rationale
The lacrimal gland, situated anteriorly in the superotemporal orbit, is divided into orbital and palpebral lobes by the levator palpebrae aponeurosis.
Müller muscle, like the levator palpebrae, acts to elevate the eyelid. Whereas the levator palpebrae is innervated by the third cranial nerve, Müller muscle is innervated by the sympathetics. Therefore, the 2-3 mm of ptosis that may be seen with Horner syndrome are due to involvement of Müller muscle.
The trochlea is a fibrous structure located in the superonasal orbit, which acts as a pulley to change the direction of action of the superior oblique muscle.
Whitnall ligament is formed by a condensation of tissue surrounding the levator palpebrae and is the point at which the levator palpebrae muscle (above the ligament) transitions to the levator palpebrae aponeurosis anteriorly and Müller muscle posteriorly (below the ligament).

Q722
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A 70-year-old man presents with a soft, translucent lower-lid lesion located 2 mm away from the lateral canthus. The lesion is painless but bothers the patient. What is the likely pathology finding?
Correct answer: A. a cyst lined with a double layer of cuboidal epithelium with an empty lumen
Rationale
The clinical description is consistent with a ductal (sweat gland) eccrine cyst. These cysts are lined with a double layer of cuboidal epithelium. They differ clinically from apocrine cysts that have a brown color related to the cellular decapitation secretion containing lipofuscin pigment.
Epidermoid cysts are white and have a rubbery or firm consistency. They are lined with stratified squamous keratinizing epithelium containing keratin. Seborrheic keratosis presents clinically as a well-circumscribed oval, dome-shaped to verrucoid papule that varies from pink to brown. Pathology shows a pseudohorn cyst or cysts lined with acanthotic stratified epithelium.

Q723
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What principle of corneal wound healing is responsible for the finding shown?
Correct answer: B. anterior-posterior direction of keratocytes
Rationale
The figure depicts a corneal scar. Following a central corneal wound, neutrophils arrive at the site via the tears, and the edges of the wound swell. The corneal matrix glycosaminoglycans, keratan sulfate and chondroitin sulfate, disintegrate at the edge of the wound. The stromal keratocytes, fibroblast-like cells (also known as fibrocytes), are activated and eventually migrate across the wound, laying down collagen and fibronectin. The direction of the keratocytes and collagen is not parallel to the stromal lamellae. Hence, cells are directed anteriorly and posteriorly across a wound that will always be visible microscopically as an irregularity in the stroma and clinically as an opacity. If the wound edges are not well-apposed, the gap will not be completely filled by the proliferating keratocytes, resulting in focal stromal thinning. If a thin layer of anterior corneal stroma is lost with an abrasion, epithelium will fill the shallow crater, forming a facet. The endothelium lays down a new thin layer of Descemet membrane. If the internal aspect of the wound is not covered by Descemet membrane, stromal keratocytes may continue to proliferate into the anterior chamber as fibrous ingrowth, or the posterior wound may permanently remain open.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q724
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
An asymptomatic 37-year-old woman presents with the fundus lesion shown. What method would be most accurate in making or confirming this patient's diagnosis?
Correct answer: D. ocular ultrasonography
Rationale
The image shows a localized choroidal hemangioma with the characteristic orange-red color located posterior to the equator. Choroidal hemangiomas are typically unassociated with any systemic condition. Ocular ultrasonography is the most definitive noninvasive test. Characteristic findings include high reflectivity with large reflective "spikes" corresponding to the fluid-filled channels of the large hemangioma-associated vessels within the deeper mass. Although a characteristic "halo" may be visible on other imaging, echography is the most sensitive and specific.
CT scan is of little value, as it does not distinguish the vascular nature of choroidal hemangioma from other tissue types (such as melanoma or metastasis). Fundus fluorescein angiography demonstrates rapid choroidal vascular filling, but may be mimicked by a "collar button" melanoma or a melanoma that has extended through the Bruch membrane. Fine-needle biopsy is not indicated for choroidal hemangioma diagnosis; this technique would not be diagnostic and would risk significant choroidal hemorrhage.

Q725
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What condition may be diagnosed by finding Heinz bodies (see image below) on red blood cell membranes in an anterior chamber aspirate?
Correct answer: B. ghost cell glaucoma
Rationale
Ghost cell glaucoma may occur following an intraocular hemorrhage, wherein blood breakdown products may accumulate in the trabecular meshwork. The spherical shape and rigidity of the cell membrane make it difficult for the cells to transit through the trabecular meshwork. Heinz bodies consist of degenerating hemoglobin and appear as small globules within the red blood cells.

Pseudoexfoliation results in fibrillar material deposited on anterior chamber structures. Siderosis usually occurs following a ferrous intraocular foreign body. Lymphoma is not associated with Heinz bodies.

Q726
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What type of cells in the retina proliferate in response to trauma?
Correct answer: B. glial cells
Rationale
The retina is made of terminally differentiated cells that typically do not regenerate when injured. Because the retina is part of the central nervous system (CNS), glial cells (eg, Müller cells, fibrous astrocytes), rather than fibroblasts, proliferate in response to retinal trauma.

Q727
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A patient with severe, recurrent corneal erosions had bilateral corneal refractile branching stromal opacities and underwent penetrating keratoplasty to clear the visual axis. Now there is recurrence of opacities in the corneal graft. On histopathology of the corneal button, what staining of the stromal deposits was most likely seen?
Correct answer: B. orange-red with Congo red
Rationale
Lattice dystrophy is relatively common and is characterized by refractile branching lines in the corneal stroma. Subtle refractile lines, central and subepithelial ovoid white dots, and diffuse anterior stromal haze appear early in life and, in a corneal graft, these may be the first signs of recurrence. The typical branching refractile lines, so-called lattice lines, develop as the condition progresses and are best seen against a red reflex or with indirect illumination. These lines start centrally and superficially and spread centrifugally, becoming deeper. The stroma can take on a "ground-glass" appearance, but the peripheral cornea typically remains clear. Epithelial erosions recur often and may occur as early as the first decade of life.
Lattice corneal dystrophy more commonly recurs in corneal grafts than other stromal dystrophies. Lattice dystrophy type I is an autosomal dominant stromal dystrophy secondary to mutation in TGFBI. Keratoepithelin, the protein encoded by the TGFBI gene, is produced in the corneal epithelium. Since the epithelium in a corneal graft is host-derived, the protein will continue to deposit.
Histologically, the stromal deposits in lattice dystrophy consist of amyloid. The amyloid deposits stain orange-red with Congo red and demonstrate green birefringence with cross-polarization.
The stromal deposits in granular dystrophy type I consist of hyaline, which stains red with Masson trichrome. The stromal deposits in granular dystrophy type II (Avellino dystrophy) consist of both hyaline and amyloid. Some of the deposits will stain positively with Congo red and other deposits will stain positively with Masson trichrome.
Macular dystrophy contains stromal deposits of mucopolysaccharide, which stain blue with Alcian blue.
In Schnyder corneal dystrophy, cholesterol crystals deposit in the stroma. Lipids dissolve during normal histologic processing, and frozen sections must be obtained to demonstrate the presence of lipid with Oil-Red-O stain.

Q728
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What optic nerve tumor is frequently associated with neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1)?
Correct answer: B. optic nerve glioma
Rationale
A glioma (astrocytoma) may arise anywhere along the visual pathway, including the optic disc and optic nerve. Optic nerve gliomas are frequently associated with neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1). These tumors typically present in the first decade of life and are low-grade juvenile pilocytic astrocytomas.
Primary optic nerve sheath meningiomas arise from the arachnoid meningeal layer of the optic nerve sheath. These are less frequent than secondary orbital meningiomas, which extend into the orbit from an intracranial site, often the sphenoid wing. Meningioma may rarely be associated with neurofibromatosis in the younger age group, but it is much less frequently seen in NF1 than is optic nerve glioma.
The plexiform type of neurofibroma is associated with NF1, but occurs in the eyelid or orbit, not in the optic nerve. Neurofibromas are nerve sheath tumors, consisting of a mixture of fibroblast, Schwann cells, and axons, which form thickened, tortuous nerves. The consistency is firm and rubbery. These classically present with an S-shaped mechanical ptosis of the upper eyelid and feel like a "bag of worms" on palpation.
A melanocytoma is a deeply pigmented benign melanocytic tumor that can occur on the optic disc. This type of tumor does not have an association with neurofibromatosis.

Q729
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the most common growth behavior of magnocellular nevi?
Correct answer: D. little or no growth
Rationale
Magnocellular nevi present in the eye as melanocytomas. Melanocytomas may occur in the iris, ciliary body, choroid, or optic nerve. They have either no or slow growth, and malignant transformation to melanoma is rare.

Q730
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A conjunctival biopsy is performed in order to evaluate for cicatricial pemphigoid. Half of the biopsy should be placed in 10% neutral-buffered formalin. Into which fixative or transport medium should the other half be placed?
Correct answer: B. Zeus transport medium
Rationale
When a patient presents with cicatricial conjunctivitis, conjunctival biopsy may be performed to evaluate for autoimmune etiologies, including mucous membrane pemphigoid (MMP), also known as ocular cicatricial pemphigoid. Direct immunofluorescence is the gold standard for diagnosis and cannot be performed on formalin-fixed tissue. For this reason, at least half of the conjunctival biopsy specimen should be placed in Michel or Zeus medium for immunofluorescence studies. Saline may also be used. The other half of the biopsy is placed in formalin for routine histologic examination. 

In MMP, direct immunofluorescence demonstrates IgG, IgM, IgA, and/or C3 complement in the epithelial basement membrane zone. Histopathologic findings are non-specific but typically show a band-like infiltrate of lymphocytes and plasma cells in the superficial stroma. 

Glutaraldehyde is the appropriate fixative for electron microscopy.
Absolute ethanol or methanol is used for crystals (eg, corneal urate crystals).
Saccomanno fixative is good for liquid specimens or smears (eg, vitreous biopsies, fine needle aspirates).

Q731
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the most common secondary tumor in retinoblastoma survivors?
Correct answer: C. osteosarcoma
Rationale
Osteosarcomas represent 40% of tumors arising within the field of radiation and 36% outside the field of radiation in patients previously treated for retinoblastoma.

Q732
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
In a patient with a central nervous system (CNS) hemorrhage, what cell types would stain positive for hemosiderin?
Correct answer: A. microglial cells
Rationale
The cells of the supportive tissue of the central nervous system (CNS), oligodendrocytes, astrocytes, and microglial cells, are glial cells. Oligodendrocytes produce and maintain the myelin sheath of the optic nerve, astrocytes are involved with support and nutrition, and microglial cells (CNS histiocytes) have a phagocytic function. Thus, the macrophages of the CNS, or microglial cells, would engulf hemosiderin after a CNS or retinal hemorrhage. Bipolar cells, which are neuronal cells found in the inner nuclear layer of the retina, are not phagocytic cells.

Q733
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the major vision-threatening complication of choroidal osteoma?
Correct answer: A. choroidal neovascularization
Rationale
Choroidal osteomas are benign bony tumors that usually arise from the juxtapapillary choroid, most commonly in young adults and adolescents. Choroidal neovascularization is the most significant complication of choroidal osteoma and should be treated with anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) injections if it occurs.

Q734
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What layer of the cornea is not replaced when it is destroyed?
Correct answer: C. Bowman
Rationale
The endothelial and epithelial layers are critical to corneal wound healing. The epithelium should cover the defect within days to prevent permanent corneal weakness. Stromal keratocytes, fibroblast-like cells, migrate across the wound, laying down new collagen and fibronectin. The endothelium slides across the posterior defect and lays down a new layer of Descemet membrane. Bowman layer is not replaced once it is incised or destroyed.

Q735
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the predominant cell type found in Dalen-Fuchs nodules?
Correct answer: A. histiocytes
Rationale
A characteristic finding in sympathetic ophthalmia is the presence of Dalen-Fuchs nodules (figure). These nodules are collections of epithelioid histiocytes and lymphocytes between the retinal pigment epithelium and Bruch's membrane, usually beneath the peripheral retina. The macrophages may demonstrate pigment phagocytosis. Other characteristic pathologic findings in sympathetic ophthalmia include a diffuse granulomatous panuveitis, macrophages and giant cells in the choroid with pigment phagocytosis, preservation of the choriocapillaris, exudative retinal detachments, and retinal perivasculitis. Sympathetic ophthalmia is described after perforating ocular trauma, ocular surgery including vitrectomy, glaucoma procedures, cataract extraction, and noninvasive procedures such as cyclophotocoagulation. Ninety percent of cases occur within 1 year of injury, but the range of reported cases is 2 weeks to 50 years.

Q736
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
For an 18-year-old patient with bilateral, biopsy-proven, conjunctival intraepithelial neoplasia, what element of history should be obtained?
Correct answer: A. unprotected sex
Rationale
In a young patient with conjunctival intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN), immunosuppression, particularly when caused by HIV infection, must be excluded. As such, a history of unprotected sexual encounters can predispose the patient to HIV infection, so the clinician should obtain that history. Cigarette smoking and ultraviolet (UV) exposure (eg, tanning), although they are risk factors for CIN in older men, would not be likely to cause CIN in such a young patient. Binge drinking is not related to CIN.

Q737
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
Clinical presentations of iridocorneal endothelial syndrome share in common the proliferation of what tissue?
Correct answer: C. corneal endothelium
Rationale
Iridocorneal endothelial (ICE) syndrome is caused by a proliferation of the corneal endothelium over the trabecular meshwork and iris (first figure), eventually causing peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS) and secondary angle-closure glaucoma (second figure). ICE syndrome has 3 classical clinical presentations, which were initially described as separate clinical entities: (1) essential iris atrophy, with the abnormal endothelium and Descemet membrane growing over the iris surface creating PAS, heterochromia, corectopia and iris thinning, atrophy, and holes (third figure); (2) iris nevus syndrome (Cogan-Reese) with pseudo-nevi of the iris caused by compression of the iris stroma by the ICE membrane; and (3) Chandler syndrome, with corneal guttata and corneal edema. Most patients are young to middle age, and the involvement is usually unilateral. Glaucoma eventually develops in 50% of patients from the secondary angle closure. Corneal guttata are common in all patients. Electron microscopy shows single and multiple endothelial cell layers, with motile elements including filopodia and cytoplasmic actin. Immunocytochemistry suggests similarities to corneal surface epithelial cells.

Q738
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What cells adhere to form posterior synechiae?
Correct answer: D. epithelial cells
Rationale
Posterior synechiae form when the pigmented epithelium of the iris is stimulated to migrate over the surface of the lens capsule, where subsequent adhesion between the epithelial cells occurs.

Q739
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
An area of peripheral retina demonstrates pathologic changes of inner retinal atrophy, retinal vascular sclerosis, and condensation and adherence of vitreous to the margins with an overlying pocket of liquefied vitreous. What is the diagnosis?
Correct answer: A. lattice degeneration
Rationale
Lattice peripheral retinal degeneration histopathologically demonstrates pathologic findings of a localized area of inner retinal atrophy with loss of the internal limiting membrane, adherent vitreous to the edges of the lesion with an overlying pocket of liquefied vitreous, and sclerosis of the remaining retinal vessels as shown (figures): Figure 1: Lattice degeneration may present as prominent sclerotic vessels (arrows) in a wicker or lattice pattern. The clinical presentation has many variations. Figure 2: The vitreous directly over lattice degeneration is liquefied (asterisk), but formed vitreous remains adherent at the margins (arrowheads) of the degenerated area. The internal limiting membrane is discontinuous, and the inner retinal layers are atrophic.
These pathologies give rise to the "lattice" of sclerotic vessels that cross the lesion. Lattice retinal degeneration is seen in approximately 10% of the population, but it rarely leads to rhegmatogenous retinal detachment. Lattice degeneration is, however, present in 20% to 40% of rhegmatogenous detachments. Traction from the adherent vitreous can lead to a flap retinal tear with persistent vitreoretinal traction. The liquefied vitreous can move to the subretinal space if a full-thickness retinal hole develops. Radial perivascular lattice degeneration is similar histopathologically; however, it is seen more posteriorly along the retinal vessels. It is more common in hereditary vitreoretinal degenerations, such as Stickler syndrome. In contrast, paving stone degeneration is due to outer retinal ischemia, presumably from occlusions of the choriocapillaris. A scalloped area of retinal atrophy (cobblestone, paving-stone) develops, with dense adhesions of the inner retina to Bruch membrane. Because of the dense adhesion, retinal detachments do not occur in these areas. Peripheral cystoid retinal degeneration and retinoschisis are early and advanced findings, with loss of the outer plexiform layer forming cystoid spaces that may coalesce.

Q740
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What histologic feature best explains the opaque appearance of the sclera?
Correct answer: A. variable collagen orientation
Rationale
In comparison to corneal stroma, scleral collagen fibers are thicker and more variable in thickness and orientation, resulting in the opaque appearance of the sclera. Loose fibrovascular tissue is present in episcleral and lamina fusca layers but does not contribute to the opacity of the sclera. Melanocytes are found in the lamina fusca. The scleral stroma has sparse vascularization.

Q741
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the most common clinical presentation of primary intraocular lymphoma?
Correct answer: A. vitritis
Rationale
Primary intraocular lymphoma (reticulum cell sarcoma, large cell lymphoma, or primary intraocular/central nervous system lymphoma) most commonly presents with posterior vitritis. Subretinal pigment epithelium (RPE) infiltrates are seen uncommonly. More than half of patients with primary intraocular lymphoma have or will develop central nervous system lymphoma, but vitritis is still the most common presentation. The disease usually presents in the sixth or seventh decade of life, with bilateral iritis, vitritis, retinal vasculitis, and occasional subretinal infiltrates. The vitreous infiltrate is heterogenous. The tumor cells are large lymphoid cells, often with an irregular nuclear membrane and multiple, conspicuous nucleoli, and are a monoclonal population of B cells. They are usually accompanied by small lymphocytes, which are reactive T cells. Ghost cells are common as well within the vitreous.
The subretinal/sub-RPE infiltrates seen less commonly are masses of atypical lymphoid cells, and may spontaneously involute, even without treatment. Optic nerve and retinal infiltrates may be present. The choroid is usually free of tumor cells in primary intraocular lymphoma. The 5-year survival rate is low despite chemotherapy and/or radiation therapy. Cytopathologic evaluation of the vitreous (third figure) is important in establishing the diagnosis and may include immunohistochemical studies, flow cytometry, and PCR analysis. Atypical cells (arrowheads) and cell ghosts (arrows) are indicated. Also see the figure that shows a clinical picture of sub-RPE infiltrates, and the figure that shows the corresponding pathology of tumor (arrow) with overlying retinal gliosis (asterisk) and choroidal inflammation.

Q742
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What are the typical histopathologic findings for adenoid cystic carcinoma (ACC) of the lacrimal gland?
Correct answer: B. basophilic cells in a cribriform pattern with nerve invasion
Rationale
ACC is composed of basophilic cells arranged in a variety of histologic patterns. The cribriform or "Swiss cheese" pattern is the most common. Other histologic patterns include basaloid (solid), comedo, sclerosing, and tubular. The presence of basaloid pattern is associated with a worse prognosis. This unencapsulated tumor has a tendency to erode bone and invade nerves, causing pain. The tumor does not contain prominent vascular elements, inflammatory cells, or myoepithelial islands. "Large, cavernous spaces containing red blood cells" refers to typical findings in a cavernous hemangioma of the choroid; "plump pericytes surrounding a rich capillary network" could describe a retinal capillary hemangioma; and "scattered patches of lymphocytes and myoepithelial islands" might be used to describe a lacrimal biopsy in Sjögren syndrome.

Q743
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
For 6 months, an 80-year-old man has had redness of both eyes. The left eye is shown in the figure. He has no previous history of eye redness, trauma, or surgery. What test would most likely confirm the ophthalmologist's working diagnosis of his conjunctival inflammation?
Correct answer: C. conjunctival biopsy with immunofluorescence analysis
Rationale
The figure depicts conjunctival fibrosis and fornix foreshortening. These findings are consistent with chronic cicatricial conjunctivitis (CCC). The differential of CCC is broad and includes immune blistering diseases (eg, mucous membrane pemphigoid), previous trauma/chemical injury, previous severe infection (eg, adenovirus, trachoma), and neoplasm. In an older patient, it is important to exclude mucous membrane pemphigoid by performing a conjunctival biopsy and sending the fresh specimen to a qualified pathologist for direct immunofluorescence studies. Immune deposition of immunoglobulins and complement in the basement membrane is the pathognomonic finding in these diseases. It is important to obtain a thorough patient history in CCC in order to rule out previous ocular trauma/infection and to identify other potential involved areas, including oral mucosa, skin, esophagus, and urethra.
A conjunctival swab can be sent for viral culture when an acute viral etiology is suspected or for Chlamydia testing. The patient's age, clinical history, and slit-lamp findings (lack of follicles) make Chlamydia a less likely cause for his chronic conjunctivitis. While atopic disease can be the cause of chronic conjunctivitis, the diagnosis is often made by history and physical findings alone and does not rely on serum IgE testing. Sarcoidosis can also present with a chronic conjunctivitis; however, the clinical finding is more commonly multiple conjunctival granulomas and not fibrosis. A chest x-ray can be used to look for pulmonary involvement in sarcoidosis.

Q744
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
Histologically, what defines the macula?
Correct answer: C. retinal region where the ganglion cell layer is greater than one cell thick
Rationale
Topographic organization of the retina varies, depending on the region. Histologically, the term macula refers to the area of the retina where the ganglion cell layer is thicker than a single cell. Clinically, this area corresponds with the area of the retina bounded by the inferior and superior temporal vascular arcades. The macula is further subdivided into the fovea and foveola. The central foveola contains only cone photoreceptor cells; ganglion cells, other nucleated cells (including Müller cells), and blood vessels are not present.

Rationale
Photo 1 shows optic disc drusen, which can be mistaken for papilledema. Evidence suggests that abnormal axonal metabolism leads to mitochondrial calcification and drusen formation. Q746
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A 3-year-old girl presents with a salmon-colored conjunctival lesion in her inferior fornix. What histopathologic finding would favor the diagnosis of reactive lymphoid conjunctival hyperplasia?
Correct answer: B. germinal centers
Rationale
Histologic features of benign lymphoid hyperplasia include normal-appearing lymphoid follicles with distinct germinal centers and small, mature coronal lymphocytes. Nuclear atypia, mitotic features, and sheet arrangement are histologic features of marginal zone lymphoma.

Q747
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What gene is associated with mutations occurring within ocular melanoma tissue that correlate with increased risk of metastasis?
Correct answer: C. BAP1
Rationale
BAP1

Frequent mutations have been described in the following 5 genes in uveal melanoma: BAP1, EIF1AX, GNA11, GNAQ, and SF3B1. Mutations in BAP1, SF3B1, and EIF1AX were almost mutually exclusive with each other, suggesting alternative downstream molecular events during tumor progression. BAP1 (BRCA1 associated protein-1 gene) mutations were associated with poor prognostic factors and high metastatic risk. In contrast, EIF1AX and SF3B1 mutations were associated with good prognostic factors. Meanwhile, GNAQ and GNA11 have been shown to occur early in tumor formation and are not associated with prognosis.

Q748
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the best management of patients with choroidal nevi?
Correct answer: A. Patients should return periodically for assessment of nevus dimensions to confirm the absence of growth.
Rationale
The recommended management of a choroidal nevus is photographic documentation of all lesions, optical coherence tomographic (OCT) measurement of lesions thinner than 1 mm, ultrasonographic measurement of lesions thicker than 1 mm, and regular, lifelong, periodic reassessment for signs of growth. Findings from fluorescein angiography are not diagnostic; choroidal nevi may either hypofluoresce or hyperfluoresce, depending on the associated findings.

The management of patients with choroidal nevi should include periodic assessment of dimensions to confirm the absence of growth. For typical choroidal nevi without observable elevation on ophthalmoscopy, A- and B-scan ultrasonography to document basal dimensions and thickness is not necessary. Likewise, fluorescein angiography is not needed for serial size comparisons, although baseline fundus photography can be useful for future comparison. Although optical coherence tomography (OCT) can be useful to measure the thickness of atypical nevi, it is not a substitute for ultrasonography, which generally provides more accurate thickness measurements along with the demonstration of internal reflectivity.

Q749
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the major cause of severe vision loss associated with choroidal osteoma?
Correct answer: B. choroidal neovascularization
Rationale
Choroidal osteomas are most often found in healthy, young women in the second or third decade of life. The majority of choroidal osteomas are unilateral and asymptomatic. Vision loss to the level of 20/200 or worse is most often associated with the presence of a choroidal neovascularization.
Choroidal osteomas have no association with vitreous hemorrhage, cystoid macular edema, or open-angle glaucoma.

Q750
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
During gross pathologic examination, what extraocular muscle is the most helpful in determining the laterality of a globe?
Correct answer: A. inferior oblique
Rationale
When trying to determine laterality of the globe, the inferior oblique muscle is a very helpful landmark. This muscle inserts temporally over the macula, with its fibers running inferiorly. Because of the posterior location of the inferior oblique insertion, the inferior oblique muscle is not typically cut flush with the sclera at the time of enucleation. The rectus muscles usually are cut flush with the sclera during enucleation to attach them to the prosthetic orbital implant, so the rectus muscles are not easy to see on the surface of an enucleated globe. The superior oblique is only present as a tendon at its insertion on the globe. This tendon, which is more anterior than the inferior oblique muscle, can be cut short surgically, making it less likely to be easily identified on an enucleated globe.

Q751
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the survival rate of patient with retinoblastoma confined to the retina if they receive appropriate treatment?
Correct answer: B. 90%
Rationale
When retinoblastoma is contained within the eye, survival rates exceed 90%, compared to less than 50% if extraocular spread has occurred. Treatment strategies must consider preservation of life over preservation of the eye or vision. Enucleation is therefore associated with the best survival rates if the retinoblastoma has not spread and is appropriate when more than 50% of the globe is involved, orbital or optic nerve involvement is suspected, or if the anterior segment is involved. Enucleation techniques must minimize the risk of inadvertent perforation of the globe, and yet should obtain the greatest possible length of optic nerve. Globe-sparing therapy includes external beam radiation, plaque therapy, and systemic and, more recently, intra-arterial chemotherapy. External radiation has been associated with delays in orbital development and an increased risk of secondary tumors in the radiation field, in addition to the increased general risk of secondary tumors associated with retinoblastoma.
Chemoreduction employs chemotherapy, followed by thermo- or cryotherapy as local consolidation, if necessary, and avoids external radiation. With chemoreduction, stages A (tumor less than or equal to 3 mm), B (greater than 3 mm without seeding), and C (subretinal and/or vitreous seeds limited to 3 mm from tumor) in the newer International Classification System for Retinoblastoma (ICSRB) have been shown to have success rates over 90%.

Q752
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
When evaluating an enucleated globe with retinoblastoma, what histologic findings suggest a higher risk of hematogenous spread?
Correct answer: D. massive choroidal invasion
Rationale
Optic nerve invasion, massive choroidal invasion, direct extraocular extension, and anterior chamber involvement are associated with higher risk of metastasis and poorer survival. Massive deep invasion of the choroid increases the risk of hematogenous spread. Invasion of the optic nerve is the most common route for retinoblastoma to extend out of the eye. Optic nerve invasion increases the risk of CNS metastasis, either by direct access in or along the nerve or by seeding of the subarachnoid space.

Q753
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A patient with a history of penetrating keratoplasty (PKP) and longstanding use of topical steroids presents with the findings shown in the figure. What is the most likely causative agent?
Correct answer: D. viridans streptococci
Rationale
Infectious pseudocrystalline keratopathy typically occurs in patients on long-term topical corticosteroid therapy, as following penetrating keratoplasty. The infection usually arises along a suture track or wound. The most common etiologic organism is viridans (alpha-hemolytic) streptococci, although other organisms have been reported.
No true crystals are present, but the bacterial growth results in a crystalline appearance clinically. This occurs because bacterial colonies aggregate in the interlamellar spaces of the stroma with little to no inflammatory response. It is thought that chronic immunosuppression from topical steroid, combined with properties of the organism's glycocalyx that sequester it from the immune system, allow the organisms to grow in this fashion.
Congenital syphilis is the classic cause of interstitial keratitis. Soft contact lens wear is associated with Acanthamoeba keratitis. Trauma with plant or vegetable matter is a risk factor for fungal keratitis.

Q754
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the histology of complexion-associated melanosis?
Correct answer: B. increased melanin production by melanocytes; no change in the number or morphology of melanocytes
Rationale
Intraepithelial melanosis of the conjunctiva can be classified into complexion-associated melanosis, primary acquired melanosis (PAM), and secondary acquired melanosis. Histologically, complexion-associated melanosis represents increased melanin production by melanocytes without a change in the number or morphology of melanocytes. Primary acquired melanosis is characterized by proliferation of melanocytes (hyperplasia) that can occur with or without atypia. Hyperchromatic nucleoli, cellular enlargement, and mitotic activity are some features that can be seen when atypia is present.

Q755
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
In which quadrant of the optic nerve head are colobomas most commonly observed?
Correct answer: C. inferonasal
Rationale
Typical colobomas of the optic nerve head result from defective closure of the embryonic fissure. They are generally observed inferonasally in the optic nerve head and are associated with colobomatous defects of the retina/choroid, ciliary body, and iris, which can occur at any point along the course of the embryonic fissure.

What morphologic feature is nanophthalmos associated with?
Correct answer: D. normal lens

Nanophthalmos is a rare disorder characterized by a short axial length (15–20 mm), a normal or slightly enlarged lens, and thickened sclera. Nanophthalmic eyes are predisposed to uveal effusion and glaucoma. Iris hypoplasia, scleral thinning, and optic atrophy are not associated with nanophthalmos.

What type of tissue adaptation occurs within orbicularis oculi and extraocular muscles in response to injury?
Correct answer: D. hypertrophy

The striate muscles of the orbicularis oculi and extraocular muscles are made of terminally differentiated cells that do not regenerate, but the viable cells may hypertrophy.

Q758
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the predominant type of collagen found in the scleral stroma?
Correct answer: A. type I
Rationale
The sclera is histologically divided into 3 layers (from outermost inward): episclera, stroma, and lamina fusca. The bulk of the sclera is made up of the stroma, a layer of sparsely vascularized, dense type I collagen fibers. Abnormalities that affect type I collagen, such as osteogenesis imperfecta, may impact the structural integrity of the sclera.

Q759
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What classification is given to a medulloepithelioma if both medullary epithelium and heteroplastic tissue, such as cartilage, is found on pathologic examination with extension into the anterior chamber?
Correct answer: A. malignant teratoid type
Rationale
The correct answer is a malignant teratoid type. Intraocular medulloepithelioma, a congenital tumor of the ciliary epithelium, generally occurs in the first decade of life as a fleshy, pink-to-tan ciliary body mass. Clear cysts are often present within the mass. The tumor has a tendency to cause secondary neovascular glaucoma, a characteristic lens notch and subluxation, a neoplastic cyclitic membrane, and a retinal detachment. The variety of clinical manifestations depends on the size and extent of the tumor at the time of diagnosis. In rare instances, a medulloepithelioma can be pigmented clinically and histopathologically. Medulloepithelioma can be classified histopathologically into nonteratoid and teratoid types, and both can be cytologically benign or malignant.
Medulloepitheliomas that contain solid masses of neuroblastic cells indistinguishable from retinoblastomas are more difficult to classify. Heteroplastic tissue, such as cartilage or smooth muscle, may be found in medulloepitheliomas. This variant of the tumor, composed of cells from 2 different embryonic germ layers, is referred to as teratoid medulloepithelioma. Medulloepitheliomas that have substantial numbers of undifferentiated cells with high mitotic rates and demonstrate tissue invasion are considered malignant. Recurrent medulloepithelioma tends to have more malignant histopathologic features. Although most medulloepitheliomas are cytologically malignant, distant metastasis is uncommon.

Q760
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the most commonly used fixative?
Correct answer: C. formalin
Rationale
The most commonly used fixative is 10% neutral-buffered formalin. Formalin is a 40% solution of formaldehyde that stabilizes proteins, lipids, and carbohydrates and prevents enzymatic destruction of the tissue (autolysis). Bouin solution is a fixative used in small biopsies such as conjunctival tissue. Glutaraldehyde is a fixative preferred for electron microscopy. Absolute ethanol is a fixative used for crystals such as corneal urate crystals.

Q761

What is the most common type of primary vitreoretinal lymphoma?
Correct answer: C. diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
Rationale
Primary vitreoretinal lymphoma is most commonly a high-grade diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and is often associated with central nervous system (CNS) lymphoma. Primary choroidal lymphoma is mostly a low-grade, B-cell lymphoma similar to extranodal marginal zone lymphoma. Chronic lymphocytic lymphoma and acute myeloid lymphoma are systemic lymphomas that in rare instances secondarily involve the eye.

Q762
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
Mutation in what gene has been reported to be associated with conjunctival melanoma?
Correct answer: D. proto-oncogene BRAF
Rationale
BRAF

Activating mutations in exon 15 of BRAF have been detected in a high proportion of cutaneous melanomas and conjunctival melanomas. According to Traboulsi and colleagues, pigmented ocular fundus lesions in the congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium category appear to be specific to Gardner syndrome among inherited diseases with gastrointestinal polyposis.
The RB tumor suppressor protein was first identified as responsible for the development of retinoblastoma. Recent evidence indicates a complex role for RB in cell proliferation, differentiation, and survival.
MAPK and p53 mutations are not as common as BRAF mutations in conjunctival melanoma.

Q764
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
Pathologic examination of a combined hamartoma of the retinal pigment epithelium and retina will show what finding?
Correct answer: C. dysplastic glia
Rationale
Combined hamartoma of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and retina was described by Gass (1973) in 7 patients demonstrating retinal lesions simulating choroidal melanoma or retinoblastoma. The tumors were slightly elevated, charcoal-gray masses involving the RPE retina and vitreous with fanlike peripheral extensions, covered by gray-white retinal and preretinal tissue with overlying contraction of the vitreous surface. The retinal vessels become tortuous from contraction of the glial elements in the tumor and the pre-retinal extensions. Combined hamartomas of the RPE and retina are rare tumors and are usually seen in children. There is an association in some cases with neurofibromatosis type 2, incontinentia pigmenti, X-linked retinoschisis, and facial hemangiomas. Pathologically there is a mass of proliferating RPE cells, dysplastic glia, and retinal blood vessels. Traction lines are produced in the retina with contraction of the glial elements and prominent intra- and epiretinal membranes. Orange pigmentation and spindle B cells are associated with choroidal melanoma. Cystic vascular spaces are associated with choroidal hemangiomas, but not combined hamartomas of the retina and RPE.
The photos show: A. Peripapillary combined hamartoma of the retina and RPE. Note the radiating traction lines through the fovea. B. Example of medium-sized combined hamartoma.

Q765
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
Excisional biopsy of an elevated, reddish, vascularized caruncular lesion in an adult is shown below. What is the diagnosis?
Correct answer: A. oncocytoma
Rationale
The figure demonstrates the histopathology of oncocytoma with a mass of benign small nuclei and copious eosinophilic cytoplasm. An oncocytoma is a benign epithelial tumor that is composed of cystadenomatous proliferation of columnar epithelium. It is found most commonly among elderly women. These cells have intensely eosinophilic cytoplasm (which is the result of an abundant amount of mitochondria in the cytoplasm). There is often a nesting (alveolar) or tubular growth pattern. Oncocytomas are found in the salivary gland, kidney, thyroid, and occasionally in the conjunctiva, where they are usually in the caruncle or fornix. They grow slowly in the conjunctiva as a cystic or red/blue/tan fleshy mass. Rare malignant transformation in the conjunctiva is described. Excisional biopsy is usually curative.

Q766
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What term describes increased thickness of the stratum malpighii, cellular layers of the epidermis in the eyelid?
Correct answer: D. acanthosis
Rationale
Acanthosis refers to thickening of squamous epithelium due to a proliferation of prickle cells or the stratum malpighii (consisting of strata basale, spinosum, and granulosum) of the epidermis. Acantholysis is a loss of cohesion between adjacent epithelial cells due to dissolution of intercellular bridges. It is a characteristic feature of inflammatory follicular keratosis.  Hyperkeratosis is increased thickening of the stratum corneum (surface keratinized layer) of the epidermis. The epidermal granular layer is present. In parakeratosis, there is retention of nuclei in the stratum corneum with absence of the granular layer. Dyskeratosis refers to premature individual cell keratinization within the stratum malpighii.

Q767
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the mechanism of bone formation in phthisis bulbi?
Correct answer: A. metaplasia of the retinal pigmented epithelium (RPE)
Rationale
Phthisis bulbi is defined as atrophy, shrinkage, and disorganization of the eye and intraocular contents. Not all eyes that are blinded secondary to trauma will become phthisical; however, blind eyes are at high risk for repeated trauma with cumulative destructive effects. In the end stage of this process, osseous metaplasia of the RPE with bone formation may be a prominent feature. The sclera becomes markedly thickened, particularly posteriorly. Extensive dystrophic calcification of Bowman layer, lens, retina, and drusen usually occurs.

Craniopharyngiomas form from odontogenic epithelial cells along the pituitary stalk, which is why these tumors often contain calcification. In patients with chronic lung disease from sarcoidosis or tuberculosis, longstanding granulomata may calcify.

Q768
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
Metastatic intraocular neoplasms most commonly arise from what primary origin?
Correct answer: A. lung in males
Rationale
Metastatic intraocular neoplasms most commonly arise from a pulmonary primary origin in males and from a breast primary origin in females. The incidence of intraocular pulmonary metastasis in females has increased in recent years. Metastasis from a gastrointestinal primary source is much less common in both males and females. In approximately 18% of cases a definite primary source is not identified.

Q769
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A 65-year-old man presents with a ulcerated nodule on the upper lid. The histopathology is shown. What is the diagnosis?
Correct answer: C. squamous cell carcinoma
Rationale
Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) can occur in the eyelids but is much less common than basal cell carcinoma (BCC). Most SCCs arise in sun-damaged skin and thus occur on the lower lid. However, there is a higher occurrence of SCC than BCC in the upper lid and outer canthus. Grossly, SCC has a varied appearance. Histopathology shows nests, strands, and cords of atypical squamous cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm. Tumor cells may be well differentiated (producing keratin), moderately differentiated, or poorly differentiated. The presence of intercellular bridges between tumor cells can help confirm diagnosis. Perineural and lymphatic invasion may be present. Regional lymph node metastasis is reported to occur in up to 20% of patients with SCC of the eyelid. Metastatic disease is particularly uncommon if SCC arose from actinic keratosis. Treatment includes the use of frozen section (conventional or Mohs microsurgery) or permanent section margin control.

Q770
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
Where are new lens cortical fibers produced?
Correct answer: D. equator
Rationale
The lens epithelium produces the crystalline proteins that become new lens cortical fibers. The outer edge of the epithelial layer at the lens equator, also known as the lens bow, is the active area of production of these new lens fibers. The nucleus is formed embryologically and grows throughout life as cortical fibers become compacted; the outer layers of the cortex represent the newest lens cortical fibers. The anterior capsule is lined by a monolayer of lens epithelial cells. Normally no epithelium is associated with the posterior capsule, so lens cortical fibers cannot be produced there.

Q771
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What type of choroidal melanoma cell type has the best prognosis?
Correct answer: A. spindle cell
Rationale
Cell type has one of the highest associations with survival from melanoma. Spindle cell melanoma has the best prognosis; epithelioid melanoma has the worst. Melanomas of mixed-cell type have an intermediate prognosis. In rare cases, a melanoma undergoes extensive necrosis, which precludes classification. The prognosis for completely necrotic melanomas is the same as that for mixed-cell melanomas.

Q772
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
Keratoacanthoma is a variant of what other eyelid malignancy?
Correct answer: B. squamous cell carcinoma
Rationale
Keratoacanthomas (KAs) occur most commonly on facial skin as single, large, elevated growth with a central crater. There is usually a history of rapid growth over 4 to 8 weeks, and often a history of spontaneous regression over several months. There is strong evidence that keratoacanthomas are a variant of a well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma. In fact, dermatopathologists and ophthalmic pathologists may refer to this lesion as well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma to emphasize the possibility of perineural invasion and metastasis.

Q773
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What represents the tertiary vitreous?
Correct answer: A. lens zonular fibers
Rationale
The embryologic development of the vitreous is divided into 3 phases:
  1. Primary vitreous, which consists of fibrillar material, mesenchymal cells, and vascular structures (including the hyaloid artery, vasa hyaloidea propria, and tunica vasculosa lentis
  2. Secondary vitreous, which is composed of collagen fibrils and hyaluronic acid
  3. Tertiary vitreous, which is composed of lens zonular fibers

Q774
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
For the pictured finding and associated pathology, what is the appropriate treatment?
Correct answer: B. systemic immunosuppression
Rationale
The clinical photograph shows extensive conjunctival nodules. The pathology demonstrates classic noncaseating (ie, without central necrosis) granulomas, characterized by multinucleated giant cells. This is pathognomonic for sarcoidosis and the preferred treatment is immunosuppression with steroids or immunomodulatory medication.
Systemic antibiotics would be indicated for adult inclusion cysts from trachoma. Systemic antihistamines are of benefit for severe allergic conjunctivitis. Radiation may be beneficial for localized conjunctival lymphoproliferative disorders.

Q775
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What clinical finding is most suggestive that a pigmented choroidal lesion is a choroidal nevus rather than a choroidal melanoma?
Correct answer: A. overlying drusen
Rationale
Although no single clinical factor is pathognomonic for benign versus malignant choroidal melanocytic lesions, 11%–58% of nevi have overlying drusen. This frequency increases with age of the patient. Thickness greater than 2 mm, subretinal fluid, symptoms, orange pigmentation, and peripapillary location are clinical risk factors for growth. Nevertheless, 6%–10% of nevi show orange pigment, and 9%–15% are associated with subretinal fluid.
