Q776
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is a clinical feature of a melanocytic choroidal lesion that is concerning for melanoma?
Correct answer: C. absence of drusen or degenerative retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) changes
Rationale
Using the mnemonic "To Find Small Ocular Melanoma Doing IMaging" (TFSOM-DIM) can assist in detecting factors that increase the risk of choroidal nevi transforming into small choroidal melanoma. The TFSOM-DIM acronym encapsulates the following risk factors:
  • Thickness >2 mm (on ultrasound)
  • Fluid subretinal (on OCT)
  • Symptoms of vision loss (by VA testing)
  • Orange pigment (on autofluorescence)
  • Melanoma hollow (on ultrasound)
  • DIaMeter >5mm (by photography)
Choroidal nevi may occur in up to 10% of the population. The typical nevus appears as a flat or minimally elevated gray-brown lesion with indistinct margins. According to the Collaborative Ocular Melanoma Study, a nevus (or freckle) is < 1 mm in thickness, < 5 mm in largest basal diameter. Tumors that are > 1 mm in thickness and > 5 mm in largest basal diameter are in the size range overlapping that of nevi and that of small melanomas.

Q777
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What degenerative lens change is caused by migration of lens epithelium along the posterior capsule, followed by enlargement or swelling of those epithelial cells?
Correct answer: C. posterior subcapsular cataract
Rationale
Posterior subcapsular cataract is a result of epithelial disarray at the lens equator, followed by posterior migration of the lens epithelial cells along the posterior capsule. As the cells migrate, they can enlarge to 5-6 times their normal size. These swollen cells are called bladder or Wedl cells. If they involve the center of the lens in the visual axis, they can cause significant decrease in vision.A duplication cataract occurs after injury to the lens epithelium. The lens epithelium undergoes metaplasia and forms anterior subcapsular fibrous plaques. Following the resolution of the inciting stimulus, the lens epithelium may produce another capsule that completely surrounds the fibrous plaque.The earliest sign of focal cortical degeneration is hydropic swelling of the lens fibers with decreased intensity of eosinophilic staining. Eosinophilic globules (morgagnian globules) accumulate in the slitlike spaces between the lens fibers. Ultimately, the entire cortex can become liquefied.Nuclear cataracts take on a subtle homogenous eosinophilic appearance and are difficult to assess histologically.

Q778
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the most likely location for metastasis from uveal melanoma?
Correct answer: A. liver
Rationale
The liver is the primary organ involved in metastatic uveal melanoma, and liver involvement is commonly the first manifestation of metastatic disease. After the liver, metastasis can affect the lungs, bones, and skin. All patients require metastatic evaluation prior to definitive treatment of intraocular melanoma.

Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
Macular corneal dystrophy nonsulfated glycosaminoglycan deposits stain best with what histopathology stain?
Correct answer: D. colloidal iron
Rationale
Colloidal iron and Alcian blue stains highlight the nonsulfated glycosaminoglycan deposits that accumulate intracellularly in stromal keratocytes and endothelium and extracellularly in the stroma in macular corneal dystrophy.
Macular dystrophy is autosomal recessive and caused by mutations in the carbohydrate sulfotransferase 6 gene (CHST6) on chromosome 16. The deposits in macular dystrophy are poorly defined, with hazy intervening stroma, and involve the cornea limbus to limbus.
Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) is a general tissue stain the stains the nucleus blue and the cytoplasm pink. Congo red stains amyloid and is useful in lattice corneal dystrophy. Masson trichome stains collagen blue and is useful for granular corneal dystrophy.

A conjunctival pigmented lesion is biopsied. What histologic feature indicates a risk of malignancy?
Correct answer: D. epithelioid melanocytes in the superficial epithelium
Rationale
Epithelioid morphology and migration into the superficial epithelium are consistent with atypical melanocytic proliferation and indicate a risk of malignancy. Epithelial cysts in the stroma are suggestive of a compound nevus. Increased pigmentation in the epithelial cells might be seen in complexion-­associated melanosis or conjunctival hypermelanosis/primary acquired melanosis without atypia. Intensely pigmented dendritic melanocytes in the episclera are a feature of oculodermal melanocytosis (nevus of Ota).

Q781
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A patient presents with an elevated lesion on dilated fundus exam. The B-scan is shown in Figure 1 and the A-scan is shown in Figure 2. What is the most likely lesion?
Correct answer: D. choroidal hemangioma
Rationale
This imaging is most consistent with a circumscribed choroidal hemangioma. These hemangiomas are usually orange, dome-shaped lesions that can be associated with exudative retinal detachments, which can affect vision if the fovea is involved. A-scan ultrasonography demonstrated high internal reflectivity, as illustrated in the photo. A choroidal detachment can sometimes be dome shaped but usually has low internal reflectivity. Choroidal melanoma demonstrates low internal reflectivity and can also demonstrate choroidal excavation. Choroidal osteomas often cause acoustic shadowing secondary to calcium.

Q782
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What histochemical stain would be useful in confirming a diagnosis of senile calcific plaque?
Correct answer: C. alizarin red
Rationale
Alizarin red stains calcium and is therefore useful in identifying lesions containing calcium, such as senile calcific plaques. Alcian blue, which stains mucopolysaccharides, is often used to identify the composition of corneal deposits in macular dystrophy. Calcofluor white and acridine orange can be employed for the identification of Acanthamoeba.

Q783
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A 34-year-old woman presents with a painless, eyelid bump that she first noticed several months ago. On examination, she has a nontender nodule near the eyelid margin. The pathology is shown. From what gland does this lesion arise?
Correct answer: D. meibomian glands, or less commonly glands of Zeis
Rationale
The lesion described in this question most likely indicates a chalazion, which should be differentiated from a hordeolum. A hordeolum or stye is an acute, inflammatory process typically involving the glands of Zeis and occasionally the meibomian glands of the eyelid. A focal collection of neutrophils and necrotic debris forms at the site of infection. The condition is usually self-limiting. A chalazion is a chronic lipogranulomatous reaction to lipid secretions from the meibomian glands or less often, the glands of Zeis. Sebum discharged to surrounding tissues thus causes an endogenous foreign body reaction. Because solvents in routine processing dissolve the dispersed lipid, histologic sections show histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells surrounding clear spaces. Lymphocytes, plasma cells, and neutrophils are also often present. Sebaceous carcinoma can mimic recurrent chalazion, and thus recurrent chalazia should be biopsied.
The glands of Moll are modified sweat glands that open into eyelash follicles. The glands of Wolfring are accessory lacrimal glands located in the eyelid.

Q784
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What imaging modality is most helpful in assessing an iris melanoma?
Correct answer: A. high-frequency ultrasonography
Rationale
High-frequency ultrasonography enables excellent characterization of iris tumor size and anatomical relationship to normal ocular structures. Anterior segment OCT may be helpful, but commercially available instrumentation often does not penetrate to the level of the posterior iris. Iris fluorescein angiography may show intrinsic vascularity, but this finding is of limited value. CT orbit is also of limited utility in assessing an iris tumor.

Q785
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What finding is demonstrated in this specimen?
Correct answer: C. photoreceptor loss
Rationale
Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is a clinically and genetically heterogeneous group of inherited retinal disorders characterized by diffuse progressive dysfunction of predominantly rod photoreceptors, with subsequent degeneration of cone photoreceptors and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). Histologically, marked photoreceptor cell loss and RPE migration into the retina in a perivascular distribution are apparent and correspond to the bone-spicule-like pattern seen clinically.
Drusen occur in age-related macular degeneration. Calcification occurs in retinoblastoma. Fibroglial membranes occur in combined hamartoma of the retina and RPE.

Q786
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A patient has bilateral stromal opacities that are fleck-like, with intervening stromal haze and extend from limbus to limbus. This is caused by mutation in what gene?
Correct answer: C. carbohydrate sulfotransferase 6 (CHST6)
Rationale
CHST6)


Macular corneal dystrophy (MCD), an autosomal recessive corneal stromal dystrophy, is caused by mutations in the carbohydrate sulfotransferase 6 gene (CHST6), located at 16q22. This dystrophy is characterized by diffuse stromal haze that extends from limbus to limbus and is associated with poorly demarcated focal opacities (macules).
Mutations in transforming growth factor beta-induced (TGFβI) (chromosome 5q31) result in abnormal keratoepithelin, an adhesion protein present in normal stroma. Reis-Bücklers dystrophy, lattice dystrophy types I and III, and granular dystrophy types I and II (Avellino dystrophy) are all caused by TGFβI mutations.
Mutations in UbiA prenyltransferase domain containing 1 (UBIAD1) cause Schnyder corneal dystrophy. The metabolic defect in stromal keratocytes leads to crystalline cholesterol deposition in the stroma.
The gelsolin gene (GSN) is responsible for an amyloid precursor protein. GSN mutation causes lattice dystrophy type II (Meretoja syndrome), a systemic amyloidosis.

Q787
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the approximate mortality rate for iris melanoma?
Correct answer: D. 4%
Rationale
Iris melanomas (figure) account for less than 10% of all uveal melanomas and are associated with a distinctly lower mortality rate (1% to 4%) than melanomas of the ciliary body and choroid. Most iris melanomas grow as elevated pigmented iris masses, but rarely they may be diffuse, producing heterochromia. The differential diagnosis includes iris nevus, cysts, foreign body, metastatic tumor, iridocorneal endothelial syndrome, juvenile xanthogranuloma, and other rare iris tumors or ciliary body tumors extending into the iris. Ultrasonic biomicroscopy is helpful in defining the extent and location of the iris mass and whether the ciliary body is involved. Growth involving the angle and trabecular meshwork up to 3 to 4 clock hours may be an indication for excision. Extrascleral extension, and seeding or secondary glaucoma require localized radiation therapy or enucleation. Risk factors for iris melanoma include fair skin color and light iris pigmentation. There is no relationship to ultraviolet exposure. The risk of uveal melanoma is increased in fairly pigmented patients with oculodermal melanocytosis. Iris melanomas are classified using the modified Callender classification. Most are spindle cell melanomas, compared to the mixed cell type, which is most common in choroidal melanomas. Biopsy may be helpful in difficult diagnostic situations.

Q788
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the most common histopathologic finding in pterygium?
Correct answer: B. basophilic degeneration
Rationale
The most common histopathologic finding in a pterygium is basophilic degeneration of collagen within the substantia propria, due to actinic damage. Squamous metaplasia, surface keratinization, and loss of goblet cells may be seen in a subset of pterygia, but it is not a universal finding. Nuclear hyperchromasia is a finding in ocular surface squamous neoplasia, which may occur in association with a pterygium, but is a neoplastic, not degenerative change. Eosinophilic deposits are characteristic histopathologic findings of amyloid deposits, not pterygium.

Hemangiopericytoma is considered a subtype of what kind of orbital mesenchymal tumor?
Correct answer: D. solitary fibrous tumor
Rationale
Solitary fibrous tumor (SFT) is the most common mesenchymal orbital tumor in adults. The superonasal orbit is a common site, and presentation can include proptosis, pain, diplopia, decreased vision, and epiphora.
Studies have shown that hemangiopericytoma, fibrous histiocytoma, and giant cell angiofibromas of the orbit share common histologic and immunophenotypic characteristics and may be classified as subtypes of orbital SFTs.
Varix is an abnormally enlarged thin-walled vein. An orbital cavernous hemangioma is a hamartoma, consisting of an encapsulated mass of mature venous channels. Meningiomas are central nervous system (CNS) tumors of meningothelial origin.

Pleomorphic adenoma (benign) and ACC (malignant) are lacrimal gland tumors that present with ptosis, proptosis, and orbital fullness. The major symptomatic distinction between these 2 tumors is the pain reported by patients with ACC, due to the tumor's tendency to erode adjacent bones and invade orbital nerves.

Image D

Q792
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
Mutation of what gene is associated with congenital aphakia?
Correct answer: B. FOXE3
Rationale
FOXE3

Mutations in the FOXE3 gene are associated with anterior segment mesenchymal dysgenesis. Homozygous mutations in this gene have been associated with a number of ocular diseases, including congenital aphakia, sclerocornea, microphthalmia, and optic disc coloboma. Reports of heterozygous mutations causing less severe ocular diseases such as anterior segment dysgenesis (sometimes referred to as anterior segment mesenchymal dysgenesis), and Peters anomaly have been published.
RB1 gene encodes the pRB protein, a tumor suppressor protein that is associated with retinoblastoma. One function of pRB is to prevent excessive cell growth by inhibiting cell cycle progression until a cell is ready to divide. When the cell is ready to divide, pRB is phosphorylated, becomes inactive, and allows cell cycle progression.
MYC is a family of regulator genes and proto-oncogenes that code for transcription factors. Mutation of MYCN has been associated with the development of retinoblastoma.
Alport syndrome is associated with bilateral anterior lenticonus. This syndrome is inherited in an X-linked manner and is caused by mutations in the COL4A5 gene in 80% of cases. In the remaining cases the condition is caused by mutations in the COL4A3 or COL4A4 genes; it may be autosomal recessive, or rarely autosomal dominant.

Diabetes mellitus, liver disease, and thyroid disease are less likely to be related to the presence of OSSN in this age group.

Q794

What clinical finding is more common in Chandler syndrome compared to the other variants of iridocorneal endothelial (ICE) syndrome?
Correct answer: B. corneal edema
Rationale
Chandler syndrome is the most common variant of iridocorneal endothelial (ICE) syndrome. It is characterized by minimal iris changes and predominantly corneal and angle changes. Microcystic corneal edema in the absence of elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) is more common in Chandler syndrome. Progressive iris atrophy, corectopia / polycoria, hole formation, and heterochromia are more common in essential iris atrophy. Iris nevi are seen in Cogan-Reese syndrome. Varying degrees of PAS formation occur in ICE syndrome, and these are usually present more anteriorly within the angle due to abnormal migration of endothelium over the angle.

Q796

What histopathologic description best characterizes a hamartoma?
Correct answer: A. abnormal amount of mature tissue at a normal location

Hamartomas are congenital anomalies formed by hypertrophy or hyperplasia of mature tissue in a normal location. An example of a hamartoma is a cavernous hemangioma. A choristoma consists of normal, mature tissue at an abnormal location and can contain 1 or 2 embryonic germ layers. A teratoma is a tumor consisting of abnormal tissue derived from all 3 embryonic germ cell layers. A stereotypic, monotonous new growth of a specific tissue phenotype represents neoplasia.

What is the normal timeframe after an eyelid skin injury for myofibroblasts to actively contract to decrease the size of the wound?

Approximately the third day after an injury to the eyelid skin, myofibroblasts derived from vascular pericytes migrate around the wound and actively contract, decreasing the size of the wound.

Q798
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the most prominent cell type found in the vitritis associated with bacterial endophthalmitis?
Correct answer: A. neutrophils
Rationale
The vitreous is acellular and avascular, so it is not often a primary site of inflammation. However, it commonly becomes secondarily involved in inflammation of adjacent tissues. Vitritis is the presence of white blood cells in the vitreous, either benign or malignant. Vitreous inflammation due to infectious agents is referred to as infectious endophthalmitis.
In bacterial endophthalmitis, the vitritis consists predominantly of an infiltrate of neutrophils (polymorphonuclear leukocytes), which are acute inflammatory cells.
Epithelioid histiocytes represent granulomatous inflammation. Infectious causes of granulomatous inflammation include fungal, viral, or atypical mycobacterial etiologies.
T and B lymphocytes are chronic inflammatory cells. The vitreous infiltrate in noninfectious uveitis is typically composed of chronic inflammation, including lymphocytes. Along with T and B lymphocytes, granulomatous inflammation may also be present in noninfectious causes of uveitis or vitritis.
Eosinophils are commonly found in allergic reactions, but may be present in some chronic inflammatory processes, such as sympathetic ophthalmia.

Q799
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What percentage of patients with intraocular lymphoma will develop central nervous system (CNS) involvement?
Correct answer: A. 60%
Rationale
Of patients who present with primary intraocular lymphoma (PIOL), 60% will develop CNS lymphoma.
PIOL is the most common and most aggressive type of lymphoma involving the eye. To differentiate it from primary uveal lymphoma, it is more accurately termed primary vitreoretinal lymphoma (PVRL). It is typically a large B-cell lymphoma with findings in the vitreous and retina. It usually presents as bilateral posterior uveitis in an older patient. Clinically, there are diffuse vitreous cells that may be associated with subretinal infiltrates, retinal vasculitis, or vascular occlusion, and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) clumping. PIOL is associated with primary CNS lymphoma. Ocular symptoms and signs may occur before the CNS findings.

Q800
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the best way to submit a pathologic specimen suspicious for conjunctival lymphoma?
Correct answer: C. submit fresh tissue for flow cytometry
Rationale
Both benign and malignant lymphoid lesions of the conjunctiva show a salmon pink appearance, with a flat, smooth surface and soft consistency.
In addition to histopathologic examination, the specimens can be evaluated by immunophenotypic analysis. This is achieved by either flow cytometry of the fresh, unfixed tissue or by immunoperoxidase staining. Molecular techniques to determine monoclonality by revealing either kappa or lambda light chain dominance may be employed.
Direct immunofluorescence microscopy is used to diagnose ocular pemphigoid; it demonstrates a linear deposition of immunoglobulin (Ig) G or IgA, or complement component 3 (C3), at the epithelial basement membrane.
Human papillomaviruses have been reported to cause conjunctival intraepithelial neoplasias.
Masson trichrome stain is used to stain the granular hyaline material in granular corneal dystrophy.

Q801
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
Glaukomflecken are seen on examination. What is the histology and patient history?
Correct answer: B. necrotic lens epithelial cells and degenerated subepithelial cortex following angle-closure glaucoma
Rationale
Glaukomflecken are composed of necrotic lens epithelial cells and degenerated subepithelial cortex that result from prolonged elevated intraocular pressure (IOP), as in acute angle-closure glaucoma.
Pseudoexfoliation syndrome is a systemic condition that is characterized by the production and progressive accumulation of a fibrillar material in tissues throughout the anterior segment and in the connective tissue of various visceral organs.
Iridocorneal endothelial syndromes, including Cogan-Reese, are acquired unilateral abnormalities of the corneal endothelium. All forms of ICE syndrome have epithelial-like metaplasia and abnormal proliferation of the corneal endothelium.
In phacolytic glaucoma, the trabecular meshwork becomes occluded by both the lens protein and macrophages that are engorged with phagocytosed proteinaceous, eosinophilic lens material.

Q802
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
For what clinical presentation would a biopsy, rather than excision, of a limbal mass presenting as an atypical pterygium be recommended?
Correct answer: B. focal leukoplakia
Rationale
Excisional biopsy rather than simple excision should be considered if the conjunctival lesion has features suspicious for ocular surface squamous neoplasia (OSSN).
One of these features is leukoplakia, a white, flaky appearance of the lesion surface. Leukoplakia is due to production of excess keratin (hyperkeratosis) by the conjunctiva. Normal conjunctiva consists of nonkeratinizing stratified squamous epithelium. Production of keratin by the conjunctiva suggests that these cells have become abnormal. This is not pathognomonic for OSSN, but it is worrisome for neoplastic change. Other concerning features include a gelatinous appearance of the lesion and presence of feeder vessels and/or tortuous vasculature. Size is generally not an indicator of potential malignant transformation. The development of pterygia is largely due to ultraviolet (UV) and wind exposure; it is not typically hereditary in nature.
If squamous neoplasia is suspected, excisional biopsy should be performed to confirm the diagnosis.

Q803
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the preferred treatment for the condition shown in the figure?
Correct answer: A. enucleation
Rationale
The image depicts a B-scan ultrasonogram of a choroidal melanoma. Enucleation is preferred because morbidity is greater following radiotherapy for a large choroidal melanoma (greater than 10 mm in thickness). The Collaborative Ocular Melanoma Study and other reports in the literature showed that pre-enucleation irradiation does not improve survival in patients with a medium or large choroidal melanoma.

Q804
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
According to the Collaborative Ocular Melanoma Study, how does eye-sparing plaque brachytherapy for well-selected patients affect melanoma-related mortality?
Correct answer: A. It does not adversely affect morbidity and mortality.
Rationale
The Collaborative Ocular Melanoma Study (COMS) confirmed several clinical features as being predictive of tumor growth (ie, orange pigment, larger tumor dimensions, lack of drusen, and lack of adjacent retinal pigment epithelium [RPE] changes). Most small choroidal tumors did not grow in 5 years. The study indicated a low risk of dying within 5 years from a small choroidal melanoma, even when not treated. COMS also demonstrated that enucleation and iodine brachytherapy are equally safe alternatives regarding life prognosis for management of patients with medium choroidal melanoma. The study also documented pre-enucleation irradiation does not improve survival in patients with a large choroidal melanoma.

Q805
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A 6-week-old child is brought to the clinic by his parents because of a 1 cm reddish mass on the left upper eyelid that prevents the eye from opening fully. It has grown rapidly since birth. What is the typical histopathologic appearance of this lesion?
Correct answer: A. well-developed capillary channels lined with plump endothelial cells in a lobular configuration
Rationale
This vignette describes a capillary hemangioma. These hemangiomas usually appear at or shortly after birth as bright red lesions, grow over weeks to months, and involute by the time a child reaches school age. Intervention is reserved for those lesions that affect vision because of ptosis or astigmatism and can cause amblyopia. The histologic appearance is well-developed capillary channels lined with plump endothelial cells in a lobular configuration.
Spindle cells arranged in a loose syncytium with occasional elongated cells demonstrating cytoplasmic cross-striations is a description of embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma. Although rhabdomyosarcoma could also present as a reddish, rapidly enlarging eyelid lesion, the average age of onset is 5-8 years, not at birth. Large, irregular cavernous spaces with thin, fibromuscular walls is the histologic description of a cavernous hemangioma, an encapsulated, orbital lesion found in adults. Thickened, tortuous nerves with proliferation of endoneurial fibroblasts and Schwann cells is a description of plexiform neurofibroma, which is pathognomonic for neurofibromatosis 1 (NF1).
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q806
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A 70-year-old woman presents with a left lower lid lesion. She has had multiple recurrent chalazia at the same location. Examination shows a yellowish lesion at the lid margin with loss of overlying eyelashes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: B. sebaceous gland carcinoma
Rationale
Sebaceous gland carcinomas are highly malignant tumors arising from sebaceous glands of the eyelid. These tumors may masquerade as recurrent chalazia or as chronic unilateral blepharoconjunctivitis. More than 50% of cases are initially misdiagnosed. Because these lesions typically demonstrate pagetoid spread, wide excisional biopsy and map biopsy of the conjunctiva are typically required.
Merkel cell carcinomas are typically violaceous-appearing lesions of the upper eyelid. These lesions are highly malignant and portend a poor prognosis.
Oncocytomas are slow-growing cystadenomas arising from the ductal and acinar cells of the accessory and main lacrimal glands, and may present as reddish-brown caruncular lesions.
Rosacea is characterized by excessive sebum secretion with frequently recalcitrant chronic blepharitis. It can progress, leading to chronic conjunctivitis, severe stromal keratitis, marginal keratitis, sterile ulceration, episcleritis, or iridocyclitis. If properly treated, these lesions can resolve with few sequelae.

Q807
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the major advantage of flow cytometry compared to immunohistochemistry in clinical practice?
Correct answer: C. It shows the percentages of particular cells in a specimen.
Rationale
Flow cytometry’s advantage is that it actually shows the percentages of particular cells in a specimen. Flow cytometry’s disadvantages are its failure to show the location and distribution of these cells in tissue and the possibility of sampling errors. Depending on the number of cells in the sample and on clinical information, the flow cytometrist chooses the panel of antibodies to be tested. Flow cytometric data should therefore not replace but be used as an adjunct to morphologic hematoxylin-eosin (H&E) staining and immunohistochemistry interpretation.

Q808
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A 65-year-old man notices progressive, painless visual loss in the left eye. Fundus examination reveals the lesion in the image. B-scan ultrasonography reveals diffuse, homogenous choroidal thickening with a crescent-shaped area of acoustically hollow extrascleral extension. What findings are expected on enhanced depth imaging optical coherence tomography (EDI-OCT)?
Correct answer: B. placoid lesions with thickening of the inner choroid
Rationale
Patients with uveal lymphoma typically notice painless, progressive vision loss. Ophthalmoscopically, the presence of multifocal creamy-yellow amelanotic choroidal lesions tends to be most helpful in establishing the diagnosis. Fluorescein angiography depicts variable findings in patients with uveal lymphoma involving the choroid; indocyanine green (ICG) angiography provides superior characterization. Classically, multiple scattered hypocyanescent lesions, which correspond to the area of choroidal infiltration by the lymphoma, are present. OCT, specifically EDI-OCT, reveals placoid or irregular lesions and thickening of the inner choroid, often associated with subretinal fluid. Biopsy confirmation should be targeted to the most accessible tissue. For isolated uveal involvement, fine-needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB) or pars plana vitrectomy with biopsy may be indicated. Dense lymphoid infiltrates are seen on histologic evaluation.
Although OCT findings are not diagnostic in primary vitreoretinal lymphoma, amorphous nodular lesions at the level of the RPE may be seen. In secondary metastasis to the uveal tract, OCT may demonstrate a lumpy, bumpy contour; choriocapillaris compression; and photoreceptor loss in the overlying retina. In choroidal melanoma, OCT may show shadowing of choroid, thinning of choriocapillaris, loss of photoreceptors, retinal edema, and loss of external limiting membrane.

Q809
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the most common intraocular tumor?
Correct answer: A. metastatic tumor
Rationale
While the most common primary intraocular tumor of adults is choroidal melanoma, the most common intraocular tumor overall is metastatic. Metastatic lesions are also the most common orbital tumor in adults.

Q810
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What optic nerve cells are phagocytes?
Correct answer: C. microglial cells
Rationale
Oligodendrocytes, astrocytes, and microglial cells are all types of glial cells, which support the function of the central nervous system. Oligodendrocytes produce and maintain the myelin sheath of the optic nerve; astrocytes are involved with support and nutrition; and microglial cells (central nervous system [CNS] histiocytes) have a phagocytic function. The axons of retinal ganglion cells are contained within the optic nerve.

Q811
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What secondary complications are common in patients with the lesion depicted in the figure below?
Correct answer: C. glaucoma and retinal detachment
Rationale
The "tomato ketchup fundus" in the figure shows the bright red color typical of diffuse choroidal hemangioma. Ultrasonography would reveal a diffusely thickened choroid with the thickest portion often in the central retina. Retinal detachment may occur secondary to disruption of the retinal pigment epithelium. Diffuse choroidal hemangioma frequently is located ipsilateral to a facial hemangioma, usually as a component of a variant of Sturge-Weber syndrome. The tumor is composed of well-formed choroidal vessels, which give the fundus a uniform deep-red color that has been compared to that of tomato ketchup. Sometimes only the posterior pole is involved; in other cases, the entire fundus is affected.
Choroidal hemangiomas are usually asymptomatic in childhood. During adolescence or adulthood, the choroid sometimes becomes markedly thickened. Degeneration or detachment of the overlying retina may follow. No treatment has been proven to prevent or reverse such deterioration, but scattered application of laser photocoagulation may help.
Glaucoma is the most common and most serious ocular complication. It has been reported to occur in up to approximately 70% of patients with SWS. Causes of elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) include elevated episcleral venous pressure, hyperemia of the ciliary body with hypersecretion of aqueous, and developmental anomaly of the anterior chamber angle. Involvement of the skin of the upper eyelid, choroidal hemangioma, iris heterochromia, and episcleral hemangioma increase the likelihood of glaucoma.
Onset of glaucoma can be at birth or later in childhood. SWS glaucoma is difficult to treat. Initial therapy with topical eyedrops can be effective, especially in cases of later onset. Surgery is indicated in early-onset cases and when medical treatment is inadequate. Adequate long-term control of IOP can frequently be achieved, but multiple operations are typically necessary. A particular risk of glaucoma surgery in SWS is intraoperative or postoperative exudation or hemorrhage from anomalous choroidal vessels; this complication is caused by rapid ocular decompression. The surgeon must exercise special care with implanted glaucoma drainage devices to prevent excessive early postoperative hypotony.

Q812
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A well-circumscribed, encapsulated, lobular orbital mass is excised from a 45-year-old woman with a 6-month history of painless proptosis and diplopia. What pathologic findings are most likely?
Correct answer: B. large vascular channels with intervening, delicate, fibrous tissue
Rationale
Cavernous hemangiomas of the orbit are encapsulated tumors composed of large vascular spaces with intervening fibrous stroma. Symptoms commonly include painless proptosis and diplopia.
Adenoid cystic carcinoma is composed of basophilic cells commonly in a cribriform pattern, although other patterns can be seen. Staghorn vascular pattern with densely packed oval- to spindle-shaped cells is seen in some solitary fibrous tumors formerly known as hemangiopericytomas. Spindle-cell tumor in a loose syncytium with occasional cells bearing cross-striations would be found in a rhabdomyosarcoma. Adenoid cystic carcinoma, solitary fibrous tumor (hemangiopericytoma), and rhabdomyosarcoma are unencapsulated tumors that frequently present with pain.

Q813
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What ultrasound finding is suggestive of melanoma?
Correct answer: C. low internal reflectivity
Rationale
Choroidal melanomas show characteristic low internal reflectivity that is homogeneous. Slow growth does not necessarily suggest or confirm malignancy. Acoustic shadowing occurs in choroidal osteomas.

Q814
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What ocular fundus finding identifies the carriers of Gardner syndrome?
Correct answer: D. hyperplasia of the RPE
Rationale
RPE lesions mimicking CHRPE may be present in Gardner syndrome, a subtype of familial adenomatous intestinal polyposis. Histologic study of the RPE changes in Gardner syndrome reveals that they are more consistent with hyperplasia (increase in the number of cells) of the RPE than with hypertrophy. The presence of 4 or more of these lesions in each eye of a patient with a family history of Gardner syndrome or the APC mutation identifies that patient as a carrier of the gene mutation. These patients have a significantly increased risk for the development of colon cancer. In combined hamartoma of the retina and RPE, the RPE is hyperplastic and frequently migrates into the retina in a perivascular location. Vitreous condensation and fibroglial proliferation can be present on the surface of the tumor. Neoplasia (adenoma and adenocarcinoma) of the RPE is very rare. Osseous metaplasia of the RPE with bone formation can be a prominent feature in phthisis bulbi.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q815
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
For what intraocular tumor is fine-needle aspiration biopsy typically avoided, due to concern for tumor seeding?
Correct answer: B. retinoblastoma
Rationale
Intraocular fine-needle aspiration biopsy may be used for evaluation of uveal tumors, specifically if the diagnosis is uncertain (based on less-invasive evaluation methods) or when genetic evaluation (to clarify prognosis, such as in the case of uveal melanoma) is desired.
Due to concerns for tumor seeding, fine-needle aspiration biopsy is avoided if retinoblastoma is suspected. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy is not thought to pose significant risk for seeding of the other tumors listed (uveal melanoma, melanocytoma of the ciliary body, adenocarcinoma of the retinal pigment epithelium).

Q816
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the normal depth of the anterior chamber?
Correct answer: A. 3.0–3.5 mm
Rationale
The anterior chamber is bound anteriorly by the corneal endothelium, posteriorly by the anterior surface of the iris-ciliary body and pupillary portion of the lens, and peripherally by the trabecular meshwork. The normal depth of the anterior chamber is approximately 3.0–3.5 mm.

Q817
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the most common initial therapy for ciliary body medulloepithelioma?
Correct answer: C. enucleation
Rationale
Medulloepithelioma often presents in an advanced state, with erosion into the anterior chamber and iris root, as well as neovascular glaucoma. In addition, these tumors can harbor malignant features, so management of medulloepithelioma usually consists of enucleation. Unlike its highly malignant counterpart in the CNS, as long as the tumor has not spread beyond the eye, intraocular medulloepithelioma has a good prognosis. Treatment options for ciliary body medulloepithelioma might also include cryotherapy, local resection, and plaque or external-­beam radiation therapy. The role of systemic or intravitreal chemotherapy in the treatment of ciliary body medulloepithelioma is not well established. Cryotherapy can be used for smaller or recurrent tumors. Local resection of medulloepithelioma is associated with tumor recurrence in 50%–100%. Standard-­dose external-­beam radiotherapy shows a mild response, but plaque radiation therapy is an alternative for smaller tumors. For larger tumors, enucleation is the preferred method of treatment.

Q818
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is a typical histologic feature of posterior subcapsular cataract?
Correct answer: B. posterior migration of lens epithelial cells
Rationale
Normally, lens epithelial cells are present along the inner surface of the anterior lens capsule and terminate at the lens equator. When the equatorial lens epithelial cells migrate posteriorly onto the posterior lens capsule, they swell 5–6 times their normal size and become bladder cells (also called Wedl cells), resulting in the clinical appearance of posterior subcapsular cataract.

Q819
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the treatment of choice for symptomatic circumscribed choroidal hemangiomas?
Correct answer: A. photodynamic therapy
Rationale
A circumscribed choroidal hemangioma typically occurs in patients sporadically, without any systemic association. In some cases, the tumors produce a secondary exudative retinal detachment that often extends into the foveal region, resulting in blurred vision and metamorphopsia. Asymptomatic choroidal hemangiomas require no treatment. The most common indication for treatment is exudative detachment of the retina with fluid tracking towards the fovea.
The primary treatment of choice for symptomatic circumscribed choroidal hemangioma is photodynamic therapy (PDT). Historically, laser photocoagulation was used but was often unsuccessful and created scars; moreover, recurrent detachments were common. External beam radiotherapy is used for treating diffuse choroidal hemangiomas. To date, there is little published evidence to support the use of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) inhibitors to treat choroidal hemangiomas.

Q820
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A 70-year-old woman with a recurrent chalazion is referred to an ophthalmologist. She has an erythematous, nodular lesion on her upper eyelid. On closer examination, the ophthalmologist notes associated eyelash loss. What is appropriate management of this lesion?
Correct answer: D. wide local excision with permanent margins
Rationale
Sebaceous cell carcinoma most often involves the upper eyelid of elderly patients (40+). It is more common in women and in people with Asian ancestry. It can arise from meibomian glands, Zeis glands, or sebaceous glands in the caruncle. The lesion can mimic a chalazion or chronic blepharoconjunctivitis, so misdiagnosis is common. Histology shows foamy, lipid-laden cytoplasm. Poorly differentiated tumors can be difficult to distinguish from other epithelial lesions, and lipid stains such as oil red O or Sudan black B can aid diagnosis. However, these stains must be performed on tissue prior to processing. For this reason, wet tissue should be saved if sebaceous cell carcinoma is a concern.
A characteristic feature of sebaceous cell carcinoma is pagetoid spread or dissemination of individual tumor cells and clusters of tumor cells within epidermis or conjunctival epithelium. Tumor cells can also completely replace conjunctival epithelium, and this growth pattern is referred to as sebaceous carcinoma in situ. Sebaceous cell carcinoma spreads by direct extension, but node and distant metastases are possible. Factors associated with poor prognosis are upper lid origin, large size (> 10 mm), meibomian gland involvement, late excision, infiltrative growth pattern, poor sebaceous differentiation, pagetoid invasion, and lymphatic, vascular, and orbital invasion. Treatment recommendations include wide local incision with permanent margins. Frozen sectioning or Mohs microsurgery is suboptimal because of difficulty in identifying intraepithelial spread. Large or deeply invasive tumors may require exenteration.

Q821
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the most common precursor of squamous cell carcinoma of the eyelid?
Correct answer: D. actinic keratosis
Rationale
Actinic keratosis is considered a precursor lesion to squamous cell carcinoma. Clinically, lesions appear as scaly, red macules or papules on sun-exposed skin in middle-aged to elderly individuals. Suspicious lesions should be biopsied and closely followed.
Keratoacanthoma is now thought to be a variant of well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma. It often spontaneously involutes. If there is invasion through the basement membrane, then the lesion should be considered invasive squamous cell carcinoma.
Seborrheic keratosis and papilloma are both benign lesions.

Q822
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A 7-year-old boy presents with rapid left-sided proptosis. Imaging reveals an orbital tumor with bony destruction. In what gene is translocation likely implicated in this tumor?
Correct answer: A. FOXO1
Rationale
FOXO1

In rhabdomyosarcoma, which is the most common orbital malignant tumor in childhood, proptosis is often sudden and progresses rapidly, requiring emergency treatment. Rhabdomyosarcomas arise from primitive mesenchymal cells that differentiate toward skeletal muscle. There are 3 recognized histologic types of orbital rhabdomyosarcoma: embryonal (most common), alveolar (worst prognosis), and pleomorphic (best prognosis). Histologically, spindle cells are arranged in a loose syncytium with occasional cells bearing ­cross-­striations. These cross-­striations are found in about 60% of embryonal rhabdomyosarcomas. Cytogenetic studies are important for identifying translocations such as FOXO1, which has prognostic implications. PITX1 mutations are associated with upper and lower limb deformities (club foot, Liebenberg syndrome). PAX6 mutations are associated with developmental ocular malformations (aniridia, Peters anomaly). GLC1 mutations are associated with primary ­open-­angle glaucoma.

Q823
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A 55-year-old man presents with a scaly, flat lesion on the eyelid. Biopsy and subsequent pathology of the lesion reveals thickened epidermis with atypia and solar elastosis of the underlying dermis. What is the risk of development of squamous cell carcinoma?
Correct answer: A. less than 15%
Rationale
Actinic keratosis is a precancerous squamous lesion appearing clinically as an erythematous or scaly macule or papule. Lesions most commonly occur in middle age on sun-exposed areas. Histologically, there are 5 subtypes that all display epidermal changes, such as acanthosis (epidermal thickening), hyperkeratosis (excess surface keratin layer), and parakeratosis (retained pyknotic nuclei with absence of granular layer). Epithelial dysplasia or partial thickness replacement by atypical cells is present and can range from mild to carcinoma in situ. Basal mitotic figures may be present. The underlying dermis displays solar elastosis similar to the elastotic degeneration seen in pinguecula or pterygium.
Squamous cell carcinoma may develop from underlying actinic keratosis (although most studies indicate the risk is less than 15%), and thus suspicious lesions should be biopsied. The base of the lesion must be examined to determine the presence of squamous cell carcinoma, and for this reason, shave biopsy is contraindicated. When squamous cell carcinoma does develop, however, there is a very low risk of metastasis compared to risk of metastasis from squamous cell carcinoma arising de novo.

Q824
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What type of cell proliferation is the most common clinical application for flow cytometry?
Correct answer: A. hematopoietic
Rationale
Flow cytometry is most commonly used in clinical pathology for immunophenotyping hematopoietic proliferations. It may be performed on vitreous, aqueous, or ocular adnexal tissue specimens. Cells analyzed by flow cytometry must be sent as fresh (unfixed) specimens.

Q825
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What conjunctival finding is shown in the figure?
Correct answer: D. papillae
Rationale
Conjunctivitis can be classified based on several features including chronicity (acute vs chronic); morphologic appearance (papillary vs follicular); and presence of membranes/pseudomembranes, cicatricial changes, or granulomatous inflammation.
The figure depicts (a) the clinical appearance of papillary conjunctivitis, along with (b) its histologic appearance, with closely packed, flat-topped papillae with central fibrovascular cores (arrows).
Follicular conjunctivitis is characterized clinically by small, pink, dome-shaped nodules without a clear central vessel. Granulomatous conjunctivitis may appear clinically similar to follicular conjunctivitis, and conjunctival biopsy may be used to confirm the diagnosis. Pyogenic granulomas on the conjunctiva appear clinically as red, elevated, pedunculated nodules and are formed by granulation tissue (not, in fact, granulomatous inflammation).

Q826
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What complication due to choroidal osteoma most commonly leads to visual loss?
Correct answer: C. subretinal neovascularization
Rationale
Choroidal osteomas are most common in the juxtapapillary location, and vision loss can occur due to development of subretinal neovascularization. Choroidal osteomas are benign tumors. Vitreous hemorrhage and retinal neovascularization are not associated with choroidal osteomas.

Q827
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What intraocular tumor frequently occurs in conjunction with central nervous system (CNS) involvement?
Correct answer: A. vitreoretinal lymphoma
Rationale
Primary vitreoretinal lymphoma (PVRL) or primary intraocular lymphoma (PIOL) is also referred as non-Hodgkin lymphoma of the CNS. More than half of patients presenting with ocular findings have or will develop involvement of the CNS.
Simultaneous brain and ocular metastasis may happen but are not thought to be directly related. A single case report is present in the literature describing such an event.
Uveal lymphoma is divided into primary and secondary categories based on the presence or absence of systemic lymphoma at the time of ocular presentation. The observed relationship between bilateral ocular involvement and systemic lymphoma is not limited to choroidal (uveal) lymphoma and has been reported for ocular adnexal and orbital lymphoproliferative tumors.
Retinoblastoma may invade the central nervous system. Trilateral retinoblastoma presents with bilateral tumors and pinealblastoma. The incidence of pinealblastoma among children with bilateral retinoblastoma is 6%.

Q828
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What type of lesion is an epibulbar dermoid an example of?
Correct answer: B. choristoma
Rationale
An epibulbar dermoid is an example of a choristoma, a lesion composed of normal mature tissue in an abnormal location. A hamartoma is an exaggerated hypertrophy and hyperplasia of mature tissue in a normal location; an example of a hamartoma is a cavernous hemangioma, an encapsulated mass of mature venous channels in the orbit. Neoplasia describes unregulated growth of cells that results in a tumor; neoplasia can be benign or malignant. Reactive lesions occur in response to a stimulus such as inflammation or trauma, for example, chronic inflammation can lead to reactive fibrosis.

Q829
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
An ophthalmologist performs an incisional biopsy of a pigmented eyelid lesion and suspects a melanoma. What histopathologic features would be consistent with this diagnosis?
Correct answer: D. radial intraepidermal growth pattern
Rationale
Cutaneous melanoma is rare in the eyelids, but concerning histologic features include cytologic atypia with nuclear enlargement and hyperchromasia, atypical mitotic figures, pagetoid intraepidermal spread, and lack of maturation. Additionally, invasive melanoma may be preceded by a vertical growth phase, resulting in an elevated mass. A bandlike lymphocytic host response along the base of a mass lesion is more common in melanoma. Superficial spreading melanoma displays a radial intraepidermal growth pattern beyond the invasive component.
Melanocytic nevi are benign proliferations of melanocytic cells. They may occur at birth (congenital) or develop later in life. Histologically, most nevi are composed of specialized melanocytic cells that are round in shape and cluster in nests. The cytoplasm contains variable amounts of melanin. These cells tend to grow within or around adnexal structures, vessel walls, and the perineurium. Nevi are classified as junctional, intradermal, or compound.
Junctional nevi are flat, pigmented lesions. Histology demonstrates nests of melanocytes confined to the epidermal–dermal junction. With age, nevus cells migrate into the underlying dermis. Intradermal nevi display nevus cells confined to the dermis. Compound nevi have components of both junctional and intradermal nevi. Intradermal nevus cells display polarity or an evolution in cytomorphology.
Superficial nevus cells (type A) are polygonal or epithelioid in shape. Type B cells in the mid dermis are smaller, have less cytoplasm, and resemble lymphocytes. Type C cells of the lower dermis are spindle shaped. This maturation is useful in classifying melanocytic neoplasms as benign.

Q830
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A 47-year-old woman comes in for a routine eye examination. She is found to have the lesion in the photograph. The intraocular pressure in the same eye is 36 mm Hg. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: D. iris melanoma
Rationale
The most likely diagnosis is iris melanoma. The majority of iris melanomas occur in the inferior sector and many are associated with glaucoma. This lesion is pigmented and imaging confirms significant thickening in the area of the lesion. Iris nevi cause minimal distortion of iris architecture and are less likely to be associated with unilateral glaucoma.
Juvenile xanthogranulomas are rare lesions that typically occur in children and are associated with spontaneous hyphema. Melanocytomas are jet-black lesions that can occur anywhere in the uveal tract, but most often are found in the peripapillary region.

Q831
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What ultrasonography finding is most likely with this clinical photo?
Correct answer: A. low internal reflectivity
Rationale
The lesion pictured is a choroidal melanoma. Standardized ultrasonography is the most important ancillary tool for evaluating ciliary body and choroidal melanomas. Standardized A-scan ultrasonography usually reveals a solid tumor pattern with high-amplitude initial echoes and low-amplitude internal reflections (low internal reflectivity). B-scan examination provides information about the size (thickness and basal diameter), general shape, and position of intraocular tumors. B-scan ultrasonography is also the best technique for detecting posterior extrascleral extension associated with intraocular malignancies.
Lesions that are less than 1 mm thick are more likely to be choroidal nevi. Calcifications occur in retinoblastoma. A lumpy, bumpy outline may occur in choroidal metastases.

Q832
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
For the past 4 months, a 60-year-old retired boat captain has had a lesion on his right eye, as shown. The lesion has been surgically removed. What virus has been identified as a risk factor for this lesion type?
Correct answer: C. human papillomavirus 18
Rationale
The patient has a conjunctival intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN). Pathologic examination confirms the diagnosis, as it shows full-thickness dysplasia of the epithelial layer. Human papillomavirus (HPV) 16 and 18 have been associated with CIN, as well as sessile papillomas, whereas HPV 6 and 11 have been associated with pedunculated papillomas. Human herpesvirus 8 is associated with Kaposi sarcoma. Human herpesvirus 4 (Epstein-Barr virus) has been associated with keratitis and uveitis.

Q833
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A patient presents for blurry vision and is noted to have a change in refraction. Slit lamp examination also reveals a large and engorged episcleral vessel, and gonioscopy shows a pigmented lesion in 1 clock hour of the iridocorneal angle. What is the most likely cause of the refractive change?
Correct answer: A. lenticular astigmatism
Rationale
Because of their location behind the iris, ciliary body melanomas often remain asymptomatic until they become rather large. Patients may note reduced vision from induced astigmatism when the tumor touches the lens (ie, lenticular astigmatism); this can also result in cataract formation. Additional signs and symptoms include episcleral sentinel vessels; photopsia and visual field alterations from associated retinal detachment; and, rarely, secondary glaucoma. Corneal astigmatism is unlikely to result from a ciliary body melanoma but may be caused by ocular surface neoplasia. Orbital tumors flattening the posterior surface of the globe may induce axial hyperopia. Axial myopia is unlikely to develop in an adult with neoplasm.

Q834
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the likely cause of increased intraocular pressure in the setting of chronic vitreous hemorrhage?
Correct answer: C. "ghost cell" degeneration of red blood cells
Rationale
Red blood cells (RBCs) in the vitreous cavity may undergo degenerative changes. Clots undergo fibrinolysis and RBCs may diffuse throughout the vitreous after 3 to 10 days, with the development of RBC degeneration. Hemoglobin leaks from the RBC change the normally biconcave pliable cells to spherical, hollow, khaki-colored, less-pliable "ghost" cells (figure). These may have small fragments of denatured hemoglobin adherent to the inner surface of the cytoplasmic membrane (Heinz bodies). These spherical ghost cells may remain in the vitreous cavity for months and may occlude the trabecular meshwork by passing into the anterior chamber, leading to ghost cell glaucoma. Aspiration of the anterior chamber can confirm the diagnosis with the demonstration of ghost cells with the Heinz bodies. Longer-term findings with the degeneration of vitreous RBCs include macrophage phagocytosis and cholesterol crystal formation from the lipids of the cell membranes, at times provoking areas of fibrous and foreign-body, giant-cell reaction. The cholesterol crystals are freely mobile within the vitreous, which is often degenerated and liquefied after a hemorrhage, leading to cholesterolosis bulbi.

Q835
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What retinal tumor occurs in patients with von Hippel-Lindau syndrome?
Correct answer: A. retinal hemangioblastoma
Rationale
Hemangioblastomas occur in the retina and other parts of the central nervous system (CNS) in patients who have von Hippel-Lindau syndrome. Diffuse choroidal hemangiomas occur in patients with Sturge-Weber syndrome, and astrocytic hamartomas occur in tuberous sclerosis complex. The nevus flammeus or port-wine mark (previously port-wine stain) also occurs in Sturge-Weber Syndrome.

Q836
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the most common finding on eye examination in patients with leukemia?
Correct answer: C. retinal hemorrhages
Rationale
Retinal hemorrhages, typically ­white-­centered hemorrhages, are the most common ocular manifestation of leukemia. Patients with leukemia and retinal hemorrhages typically have anemia and thrombocytopenia. The other findings listed are much less common.

Q837
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
An 8-year-old child presents with rapidly progressive unilateral proptosis. Biopsy shows spindle cells arranged in a loose syncytium with occasional elongated cells demonstrating cytoplasmic cross-striations, positive for desmin, vimentin, and myogenin on immunohistochemistry evaluation. What is the recommended primary treatment for this lesion?
Correct answer: D. chemotherapy and radiation
Rationale
Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common primary malignant orbital tumor of childhood (average age at onset is 5–8 years). The typical presentation is a child with rapid-onset, progressive unilateral proptosis. Due to the extremely rapid growth of the tumor, these patients require immediate attention, with urgent imaging and biopsy. There is often reddish discoloration of the eyelids that is not accompanied by local heat or systemic fever, as it is in orbital cellulitis. Orbital rhabdomyosarcoma has a better prognosis (overall 5-year survival rate of about 90%) than does rhabdomyosarcoma occurring in other body sites. Rhabdomyosarcoma arises from primitive mesenchymal cells that differentiate toward skeletal muscle. There are 3 recognized histologic types of orbital rhabdomyosarcoma: embryonal (most common), alveolar (worst prognosis), and pleomorphic (best prognosis, least common).
Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma may develop in the conjunctival stroma and may present as grapelike submucosal clusters (ie, botryoid variant). Histologically, spindle cells are arranged in a loose syncytium with occasional elongated cells demonstrating cytoplasmic cross-striations. These cross-striations are found in approximately 60% of embryonal rhabdomyosarcomas. Well-differentiated rhabdomyosarcomas feature numerous cells with well-defined cross-striations. Immunohistochemically, rhabdomyosarcoma typically is positive for desmin, muscle-specific actin, vimentin, and myogenin.
Before 1965, the standard treatment for orbital rhabdomyosarcoma was orbital exenteration, and the survival rate was poor. After 1965, radiation therapy and systemic chemotherapy became the mainstays of primary treatment, based on the guidelines set forth by the Intergroup Rhabdomyosarcoma Study Group. Exenteration is reserved for recurrent cases.

Q838
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What unique lens changes are possible after an episode of acute angle-closure glaucoma?
Correct answer: A. glaukomflecken
Rationale
Extremely elevated IOP may cause degeneration of lens epithelial cells, leading to irregular white patches just beneath the anterior lens capsule (glaukomflecken, first figure). The pathology of these changes is necrosis of the lens epithelial cells with adjacent degeneration of the anterior lens cortex (second figure: area of lens epithelial cell necrosis [arrow] beneath lens capsule [c] over lens cortex and nucleus [N], H&E). Glaukomflecken are helpful in demonstrating damage from previous episodes of acute angle-closure glaucoma.

Q839
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What immunohistochemical stain is helpful in identifying lesions that arise from cells with a neuroectodermal origin?
Correct answer: A. S-100
Rationale
Immunohistochemical stains are widely used in ophthalmic pathology. They take advantage of the specific antigens produced by specific types of cells. An antibody to a specific antigen is linked to a chromogen or color. When the stain is applied, the antibody binds to the cells that produce that specific antigen and the cell is stained by the chromogen.
Different antibodies can be used to identify different cell types and the lesions that arise from them. For example, epithelial cells produce cytokeratins. Therefore, a cytokeratin immunohistochemical stain can be used to identify adenomas or carcinomas which arise from epithelial cells.
S-100 is an antigen produced by cells that arise from neuroectoderm. The nervous system arises from neuroectoderm, including the retina and optic nerve. Neural tumors such as schwannomas or neurofibromas stain with S-100. Melanocytes also arise from neuroectoderm, so melanocytic lesions are positive with S-100 as well.
HMB-45 and Melan-A are more specific stains for melanocytes and melanocytic lesions. These stains are positive in nevi, primary acquired melanosis, and melanoma. But unlike S-100, they will not stain tumors of neural origin.
CD antigens are used to subtype white blood cells. T-cells stain with CD3 and B-cells with CD20. This is helpful in diagnosis of reactive lymphoid hyperplasia or lymphoma.
Actin, desmin, and myoglobin are used for lesions with smooth or skeletal muscle features, including leiomyoma or rhabdomyosarcoma.

Q840
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A patient undergoes conjunctival biopsy for a granulomatous conjunctivitis to determine whether the cause of the syndrome is sarcoidosis or infection. Histology shows aggregates of epithelioid histiocytes with multinucleated giant cells in the conjunctival stroma, with a cuff of lymphocytes and plasma cells, as well as central necrosis. What histologic feature present in the biopsy is most suggestive of an infectious etiology?
Correct answer: C. central necrosis
Rationale
The classic histologic finding in granulomatous conjunctivitis caused by sarcoidosis is noncaseating granulomatous nodules (round to oval aggregates of epithelioid histiocytes with or without multinucleated giant cells), which are present within the conjunctival stroma, typically with a cuff of lymphocytes and plasma cells. Central necrosis is not characteristic, and if present, suggests an infectious etiology.

Q841
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What mechanism best describes the pathophysiology of posterior subcapsular cataract (PSC)?
Correct answer: D. posterior migration of lens epithelial cells
Rationale
PSC may be the most common abnormality involving the lens epithelium. The pathophysiology of PSC consists of initial disarray of lens epithelium at the equator, followed by posterior migration of these epithelial cells that subsequently swell to 5-6 times their normal size and cause significant visual impairment. These enlarged cells are referred to as Wedl (or bladder) cells.
Anterior subcapsular fibrous plaques occur when inflammation, ischemia, or trauma results in injury to the lens epithelium, leading to a metaplastic transformation of epithelial cells into fibroblast-like cells.
A Soemmering ring secondary cataract is caused by sequestration of proliferating lens fibers in the equatorial region, causing a doughnut-shaped remnant.
Continual production of lens fibers subjecting the nucleus to the stress of mechanical compression causes hardening of the lens nucleus (nuclear cataract).

Q842
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What determines iris color?
Correct answer: C. melanin granules in anterior stromal melanocytes
Rationale
Iris color is determined by the size and number of melanin pigment granules in the anterior stromal melanocytes. Melanin granules in the posterior pigment epithelium, the thickness of posterior pigment epithelial layer, and the thickness of the anterior stromal layer do not determine iris color.

Q843
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the most common epithelial tumor of the lacrimal gland?
Correct answer: A. pleomorphic adenoma
Rationale
Pleomorphic adenoma (benign mixed tumor) is the most common epithelial lacrimal gland tumor, constituting approximately 50% of this category. This tumor grows slowly, excavating the lacrimal fossa and stimulating new bone growth without erosion. The slow growth causes gradual proptosis without pain. Although this is usually a benign tumor, recurrences are difficult to manage and can occur with incomplete excision or by seeding of the orbit from incisional biopsies. Surgical therapy is therefore directed at complete removal with an adequate margin, within the tumor pseudocapsule. The pathology is a combination of epithelial and stromal lacrimal gland elements, forming nests and tubules with the outer layer adjacent to stroma, which may be myxoid with occasional heterologous findings of cartilage or bone (figures).

Q844
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
If a patient is started on corticosteroids for presumed temporal arteritis, how soon should the confirmatory temporal artery biopsy be performed to avoid a false negative result?
Correct answer: D. within 14 days
Rationale
Corticosteroid treatment can alter histologic findings in cases of giant cell arteritis, by diminishing the inflammation. Biopsies performed within 14 days of the initiation of corticosteroid treatment are not likely to be affected.

Q845
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A 20-year-old man presents with a lump on his medial lower lid. He has a remote history of trauma to the area. The histologic specimen is shown below. Aside from excision, what further treatment is needed?
Correct answer: A. No further treatment is needed.
Rationale
Epidermoid cysts, also called epidermal inclusion cysts, are common in the eyelids and can arise spontaneously or as a result of traumatic laceration or surgical incision that entraps epidermis beneath the skin surface. These cysts are often round or oval and may be filled with a foul-smelling keratin debris. Histologic sections show that these are lined with stratified squamous keratinizing epithelium and contain keratin. Treatment involves complete excision of the lesion. There is no need for fungal cultures, cryotherapy, or Mohs technique, because the lesion is not malignant.

Q846
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What virus is most commonly associated with squamous papilloma of the conjunctiva?
Correct answer: D. human papilloma virus (HPV)
Rationale
Squamous papillomas occur more commonly in children and are associated with human papillomavirus (HPV) subtypes 6 and 11.
HIV is associated with ocular surface squamous neoplasia.
HSV may produce a conjunctival ulcer but has not been associated with squamous papilloma.
VZV may cause a follicular conjunctivitis but has not been associated with squamous papilloma.

Q847
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A 6-year-old child presents for evaluation of unilateral decreased vision and redness of the right eye. On exam, a 2 mm hypopyon and vitritis with large clumps of cells are visible, with no distinct retinal masses. The diagnosis of retinoblastoma is considered. What is the growth pattern most consistent with this clinical scenario?
Correct answer: D. diffuse infiltrating
Rationale
This child presents with a rare variant of retinoblastoma, diffuse infiltrating retinoblastoma, which is typically found in older children (>5), is unilateral, and is nonhereditary. Overall, retinoblastoma is typically diagnosed within the first year of life, with roughly 90% of cases being diagnosed before age 3 years.
Diffuse infiltrating retinoblastoma often presents with conjunctival injection, pseudohypopyon, and large clumps of vitreous cells. Notably, there is no distinct tumor mass; instead there is infiltration of the retina, which makes the diagnosis challenging. These cases are also difficult because the view to the fundus is limited, and the typical calcification on ultrasonography or computed tomography (CT) imaging can be absent. Frequently, this variant may be misdiagnosed as endophthalmitis or uveitis, and it represents a childhood masquerade syndrome. While it can also present with tumor seeding into the anterior chamber and vitreous cells, the endophytic growth pattern describes growth on the retinal surface into the vitreous cavity and would present with visible tumor mass. Exophytic growth describes growth underneath the retina, and often presents with serous retinal detachment. Suppurative is not a characterized growth pattern of retinoblastoma.

Q848
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the most important component of the systemic evaluation of a patient with choroidal melanoma?
Correct answer: B. imaging test of the liver
Rationale
Metastatic evaluation should include a comprehensive physical examination and imaging of the lungs and liver. Liver imaging is the most important component of the evaluation. Ultrasonography of the abdomen, triphasic computed tomography (CT), or MRI with gadolinium contrast is usually recommended in order to evaluate the extent of the disease. Chest imaging may be with CT scan or chest x-ray.
Liver function tests are usually performed; however, they have recently become less reliable in the evaluation of liver metastases because of increasingly common fatty liver disease and the widespread use of cholesterol-lowering statins, which may alter liver enzyme levels. Lung imaging is also usually performed at the time of diagnosis, although its yield is low. Possible novel blood markers for early detection of metastatic uveal melanoma are being explored.

Q849
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
An otherwise normal and healthy child presents with nonprogressive opacification and vascularization of the cornea probably caused by abnormal neural crest migration. What other finding is commonly associated with this presentation?
Correct answer: A. cornea plana
Rationale
Sclerocornea is a nonprogressive scleralization of the cornea probably caused by abnormal neural crest migration. It is usually bilateral, varying from mild and peripheral to diffuse. It can occur as an isolated abnormality but is more often associated with other ocular anomalies (eg, Peters), in which patients also have cornea plana. Band keratopathy, hypoplastic iris, and absence of Descemet membrane centrally are not associated with sclerocornea.

Q850
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
The abnormal endothelial cells in the iridocorneal endothelial (ICE) syndromes show what unusual characteristics?
Correct answer: D. epithelial characteristics
Rationale
The ICE syndromes were initially described as individual entities. Essential iris atrophy progresses from pupillary distortion to large iris defects and peripheral anterior synechiae. The iris nevus variant appears to have elevated iris nodules. Chandler syndrome shows guttata and corneal edema. All are unilateral and eventually may develop glaucoma from a Descemet-like membrane covering the iris and angle. The commonality to these is the growth of an abnormal Descemet membrane, probably from abnormal endothelial cells. These cells demonstrate epithelial cell immunocytochemical markers and may be phenotypically modified, metaplastic, corneal endothelial cells. The cells do not have vascular endothelial or melanocytic characteristics. Bowman layer is collagenous and is not composed of basement membrane components.

Q851
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the most common primary intraocular malignancy found in adults?
Correct answer: C. choroidal melanoma
Rationale
Choroidal melanoma is the most common primary intraocular malignancy found in adults. The most common secondary intraocular malignancy in adults is metastatic breast cancer in females and lung cancer in males. Retinoblastoma is the most common primary intraocular malignancy in children but is extraordinarily rare in adults. Adenocarcinoma is usually metastatic (lung or breast or other) but may be undifferentiated, making identification of origin difficult based upon cell type. Choroidal osteomas are choristomas and are not malignant.

Q852
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A previously healthy 6-year-old boy presents with rapid onset of unilateral painless proptosis. What is the most likely finding on microscopic examination of the orbital biopsy?
Correct answer: C. a few cells containing cross-striations
Rationale
The most likely diagnosis for a 6-year-old child with unilateral, sudden-onset painless proptosis is rhabdomyosarcoma. The embryonal subtype shows a few cells with cross-striations on pathologic examination. Small, round blue cells are typical of neuroblastoma, which presents at a younger age; the average age of onset is 5-8 years. Dermoids have tissue from all 3 germ layers, but are congenital and rarely present as sudden painless proptosis. Capillary endothelial cells are seen in orbital hemangiomas, which typically undergo a period of regression, not growth, after 1 year of life.

Q853
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
Amyloid deposition in the orbit typically occurs secondary to what underlying process?
Correct answer: B. primary systemic amyloidosis
Rationale
Amyloid deposition in the orbit typically occurs secondary to primary systemic amyloidosis and is usually benign.
Amyloid deposition in the conjunctiva is most commonly a localized idiopathic process, but it also can occur secondary to chronic inflammation, such as from trachoma, or (less commonly) in the setting of an underlying neoplasm, such as primary conjunctival lymphoma.

Q854
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What histopathological findings are seen on biopsy of an iris nevus?
Correct answer: C. dendritic, spindle, or epithelioid cells with indistinct nucleoli
Rationale
Histopathology of an iris nevus biopsy should have dendritic or spindle cells (or, less commonly, epithelioid cells) with bland nuclei and indistinct nucleoli.
Melanomas contain spindle and/or epithelioid cells with chromatin clumping and prominent nucleoli. Nevi do not have significant mitotic activity. Large, jet black, polygonal cells with bland nuclei on bleached sections would be found in the biopsy of a melanocytoma.

Q855
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A 39-year-old asymptomatic Hispanic female patient is referred for evaluation of a lesion noted (see image). What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: B. iris nevus
Rationale
Iris nevi typically appear as variably pigmented, small lesions of the iris stroma that produce little or no disruption of the iris architecture. They are more common than any of the other answer choices. The most important differential diagnosis is iris or ciliary body melanoma. The characteristics suggesting malignancy include large size, prominent ectropion uveae, vascularity, sectoral cataract, secondary glaucoma, seeding of peripheral angle structures, extrascleral extension, and documented progressive growth. Baseline/serial slit-lamp photography and/or high frequency ultrasound biomicroscopy may be indicated. Iris nevi usually require no treatment.

Q856
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the most common primary site of systemic cancer in men that causes intraocular metastasis?
Correct answer: D. lung
Rationale
The most common tumor occurring in the adult eye is a secondary metastatic tumor. This most frequently presents as a choroidal mass, disseminated from a carcinoma elsewhere in the body. In females, the breast is the most common primary tumor site; in males, the lung is the most common primary tumor site, accounting for 40% of solid tumors that metastasize to the uveal tract.

Q857
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
Patients with ocular or oculodermal melanocytosis may have an increased risk of what tumor?
Correct answer: C. choroidal melanoma
Rationale
Ocular melanocytosis (figures) is a congenital hyperpigmentation of the episclera and uvea. If there is associated cutaneous hyperpigmentation along the trigeminal nerve distribution, the condition is called oculodermal melanocytosis (nevus of Ota). These conditions may have associated melanocytosis of the meninges and orbit. Oculodermal melanocytosis is more common in Asian and African American populations, but uveal melanoma is rare in these groups and the incidence of melanoma is not increased with the presence of oculodermal melanocytosis. In white populations, however, the occurrence of ocular or oculodermal melanocytosis is associated with an increased risk of uveal melanoma. The pathology of the melanocytosis is increased dendritic melanocytes in the episclera, sclera, or dermal layers of the skin. Associated hyperpigmentation of the iris and choroid is another common finding. White patients with ocular or oculodermal melanocytosis should be followed carefully throughout life for the possible development of uveal melanoma. The lifetime risk of uveal melanoma in this group is about 1:400, much greater than the 1:13,000 incidence in the general white population. Recent studies have shown that nevi of Ota carry the same mutation in the G protein α-subunit genes (GNAQ and GNA11) that primary ciliochoroidal and central nervous system melanomas do.

Q858
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What genetic mutation causes retinoblastoma to develop?
Correct answer: D. mutations in both copies of the RB1 gene
Rationale
RB1 gene

Retinoblastoma develops when both copies of the retinoblastoma gene (RB1) become nonfunctional, either by a deletion error or by mutation. RB1 is located on the long arm of chromosome 13 and encodes for retinoblastoma protein, pRB, which functions as a tumor suppressor. Thus, loss of the gene does not actively cause tumorigenesis but rather leads to loss of tumor suppression, resulting in the development of retinoblastoma (and other tumors, such as osteosarcoma). A single normal gene copy is sufficient to suppress the development of retinoblastoma. However, when 1 abnormal gene is present, if a mutation in the remaining normal gene occurs during retinal differentiation, loss of tumor suppression occurs, and retinoblastoma is likely to develop.
A single-point mutation on chromosome 13 or even complete loss of 1 copy of the RB1 gene would not lead to retinoblastoma formation unless something were to happen to the second copy of the RB1 gene. Trisomy of the long arm of chromosome 13 is not associated with the development of retinoblastoma.
