Q859
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What management is recommended for a patient who has newly diagnosed melanocytoma (magnocellular nevus)?
Correct answer: B. observation
Rationale
Melanocytoma of the optic disc, a tumor that arises from melanocytes, is a rare tumor composed of characteristic large, polyhedron-shaped nevus cells that have small nuclei and abundant cytoplasm filled with large melanin granules. The pigmented lesions occur at the optic disc and often extend into the peripapillary retina and choroid. As they are generally benign lesions with an estimated 1% to 2% risk of transformation to malignant melanoma, observation is warranted in the absence of documented growth.

Q860
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
When monitoring a choroidal nevus, ultrasonographic measurements should be performed for lesions greater than what thickness?
Correct answer: A. 1 mm
Rationale
While the management of choroidal nevi should include photographic documentation of all lesions, lesions thicker than 1 mm should also be measured ultrasonographically. Fewer than 1% of lesions thinner than 1 mm are melanomas; however, more than 20% of choroidal melanocytic tumors thicker than 3 mm are melanomas. Tumors that are 1-3 mm in thickness are more difficult to classify; therefore, careful documentation of size and growth is important.

Q861
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the most frequent indication for frozen sections?
Correct answer: D. to determine neoplastic margins
Rationale
A frozen section, tissue that is snap-frozen and immediately sectioned in a cryostat, is indicated when the results of the study will affect intraoperative management of the patient. Permanent sections, tissue that is processed into paraffin prior to sectioning, are always preferred in ophthalmic pathology because of the inherent small size of the samples and the superior morphological preservation achieved with this technique. If the tissue sample is too small, it could be lost during frozen sectioning. The most frequent indication for a frozen section is to determine whether the resection margins are free of tumor, especially in eyelid carcinomas. When tissue is submitted for margin evaluation, appropriate orientation of the specimen, correlated with documentation (through drawings of the excision site, labeled margins, or margins of the excised tissue that are tagged with sutures or other markers), is crucial. Two techniques can be used for assessing the margins in eyelid carcinomas (eg, basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma): (1) routine frozen sections; and (2) Mohs micrographic surgery, which preserves normal tissue while obtaining clear margins. Eyelid lesions, especially those located in the canthal areas, require tissue conservation in order to maintain adequate cosmetic and functional results.

Q862
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A 70-year-old woman who is undergoing treatment for gastric adenocarcinoma presents with a complaint of a dark brown lesions around her right eye. On examination, there are multiple, well-circumscribed, pigmented lesions with a greasy appearance. She reports the lesions occurred suddenly several months before her cancer diagnosis. What will the histologic specimen show?
Correct answer: C. papillomatous proliferation of basal cells with pseudohorn cysts composed of concentric keratin layers
Rationale
Seborrheic keratosis is a benign epithelial proliferation that most commonly occurs in middle age. It appears as a well circumscribed, "stuck on" papule. Histologic sections show hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, and papillomatosis. Pseudohorn cysts are characteristic and are composed of concentric layers of surface keratin within the acanthotic epithelium. These lesions may be pigmented. Sudden onset of multiple seborrheic keratoses is known as the Leser-Trélat sign and is associated with systemic malignancy. Inverted follicular keratosis is irritated seborrheic keratosis. This appears as a cutaneous horn and histologically contains nonkeratinized squamous epithelial whirling or squamous eddies instead of pseudohorn cysts.
Papilloma refers to the growth pattern of fingerlike upward projections of epidermis surrounding fibrovascular cores. A squamous papilloma consists of keratinized epidermal fronds. A keratoacanthoma is a rapidly growing epithelial proliferation. Histologically, keratoacanthomas are composed of an invagination of squamous cells, often filled with keratin. The rapid proliferation of epithelial cells undermines adjacent skin.

Q863
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the main component of a dermolipoma?
Correct answer: B. adipose tissue
Rationale
Dermolipomas are choristomas containing a substantial amount of mature adipose tissue, which makes them softer and yellower than dermoids. They are an example of a choristoma, histologically normal tissue present in an abnormal location during embryogenesis.
Dermolipomas most commonly occur in the superotemporal quadrant, toward the fornix, and may extend posteriorly into the orbit. They also contain dermal adnexal structures, including hair follicles and sebaceous glands, although these are not the main component.
Clinically, complex choristomas are often indistinguishable from dermoids or dermolipomas. They may also be associated with linear nevus sebaceous syndrome. The histologic features of complex choristomas overlap with those of epibulbar dermoids or dermolipomas. However, complex choristomas contain other tissues such as bone, cartilage, lacrimal tissue, or neural tissue.

Q864
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What tumor may be associated with the scleral pigmentation shown in the figure?
Correct answer: A. uveal melanoma
Rationale
The slate-gray pigmentation involving the sclera and periorbital area is characteristic of oculodermal melanocytosis (nevus of Ota). Oculodermal melanocytosis is associated with an increased risk of pigmented tumors, such as uveal melanoma (1 in 400). Retinal cavernous angiomas, combined hamartomas of the retinal pigment epithelium, and choroidal hemangiomas are not associated with oculodermal melanosis. Choroidal hemangiomas may be isolated or associated with Sturge-Weber syndrome. Combined hamartoma of the retina and retinal pigment epithelium may be increased in frequency in neurofibromatosis type 2. Retinal cavernous hemangioma may be associated with cutaneous or other systemic angiomas.

Q865
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the most common etiologic cause of non-syphilitic interstitial keratitis?
Correct answer: D. herpes simplex virus
Rationale
The most common etiologic agent of non-syphilitic interstitial keratitis is the herpes simplex virus. Other organisms that can cause interstitial keratitis include Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Mycobacterium leprae, Borrelia burgdorferi (Lyme disease) and Epstein-Barr virus. Worldwide syphilis is the most common cause of IK. Treponema pallidum is, of course, the organism that causes syphilis. Interstitial keratitis can be caused by either congenital or acquired syphilis, although cases associated with congenital syphilis are more common.

Q866
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the peculiar pathologic feature exhibited by the tumor cells of an optic nerve melanocytoma?
Correct answer: D. plump polyhedral cells
Rationale
Melanocytoma is a darkly pigmented lesion, typically situated on or adjacent to the optic disc. It may extend into adjacent retina or posteriorly into the optic nerve. Melanocytomas are benign lesions and rarely have malignant transformation.
Histologically, melanocytoma is a magnocellular nevus with densely pigmented, plump, polyhedral melanocytes. The dense pigment obscures the cell detail, so bleach preparations are needed to see the cytologic features. The cells have small nuclei with small, regular nucleoli and abundant cytoplasm.
Spindle A, spindle B, and epithelioid cells are the different cell types of melanoma. A nevus consists entirely of spindle A cells, which are also called spindle nevus cells.

Q867
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What cells produce the collagen found in scar tissue?
Correct answer: A. fibroblasts
Rationale
Wound healing consists of an acute inflammatory phase, regeneration, repair, and contraction. Neutrophils and fluid enter the extravascular space in the acute inflammatory phase. Macrophages remove debris from the damaged tissue, new vessels form, and fibroblasts begin to produce collagen. Epithelial cells contribute to regeneration, which is the replacement of lost cells. Regeneration only occurs in tissues composed of cells capable of undergoing mitosis throughout life. Repair is the process of restructuring of tissues that leads to a fibrous scar. Contraction is the final phase that causes the reparative tissues to shrink so that the scar is smaller than the surrounding uninjured tissues.

Q868
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
An 85-year-old man presents with erythema and madarosis of the right eyelids. Incisional biopsy reveals foamy cells and pagetoid spread. A complete surgical excision is planned. What is the best histochemical stain to highlight these cells?
Correct answer: C. Sudan black B
Rationale
Histologically, ­well-­differentiated sebaceous carcinomas are readily identified by the microvesicular foamy nature of the tumor cell cytoplasm. Because they reveal lipid within the cytoplasm of tumor cells, special stains, such as oil red O or Sudan black B, can be used to diagnose sebaceous carcinomas. Tissue staining for lipids should be performed on frozen or cryostat sections because the lipid constituents are often removed during paraffin processing. Another common histologic feature of sebaceous carcinoma is pagetoid spread, which involves the dissemination of individual tumor cells and/or clusters of tumor cells within the epidermis or conjunctival epithelium. The PAS reagent, which stains glycogen and proteoglycans, is useful for identifying basement membranes (eg, Descemet membrane, lens capsule) and ­mucin producing cells (eg, conjunctival goblet cells) in ocular tissues. ­Hematoxylin-­eosin is a general tissue stain that stains the nucleus blue and the cytoplasm ­pink-­red. Calcium phosphate salts are stained black with the von Kossa stain, as in band keratopathy.

Q869
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the most important risk factor for metastatic disease on histopathology of an enucleated globe from a patient with retinoblastoma?
Correct answer: D. active tumor at cut end of optic nerve
Rationale
Children with intraocular retinoblastoma who have access to modern medical care have a very good prognosis for survival (over 95% in industrialized countries). The main risk factor associated with death is extraocular extension of the tumor, either directly through the sclera, or more commonly, by invasion of the optic nerve, especially to the surgically resected margin. Massive choroidal invasion, extrascleral extension, or postlaminar optic nerve disease increase the risk that metastatic disease could develop. The highest risk of developing metastatic disease is in the setting of active tumor at the cut end of the optic nerve; this clinical situation requires adjuvant chemotherapy and radiation therapy.

Q870
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A 45-year-old man presents with recent onset of unilateral diplopia, proptosis, and a palpable orbital mass. Biopsy of the mass shows a staghorn vascular pattern. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: C. hemangiopericytoma
Rationale
Hemangiopericytomas are rare orbital tumors with no sex predilection that most commonly present in the fifth decade (though the spectrum is wide) with proptosis, pain, and diplopia. They are considered part of the spectrum of solitary fibrous tumors. They are well-circumscribed lesions that demonstrate marked enhancement on CT imaging. The superonasal orbit is common. Histologically, the "staghorn" vascular pattern is present on 87% of fibrous tumors.
Lymphangiomas are congenital lesions that often present in childhood as fluctuating proptosis. Lymphangiomas are poorly circumscribed, diffusely infiltrating lesions.
Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common primary malignant orbital tumor of childhood. The average age of onset is 7-8 years, so it would be unlikely to be seen in a 45-year-old person.
Meningiomas are most often secondary lesions extending into the orbit from a primary intracranial lesion. Primary intraorbital meningiomas are usually intraconal, arising from the optic nerve sheath.

Q871
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What histopathologic corneal finding is present in cases of bullous keratopathy?
Correct answer: D. intracellular epithelial edema
Rationale
Bullous keratopathy is characterized by extensive loss of endothelial cells that leads to decompensation, triggering Descemet folds, stromal edema followed by intracellular epithelial edema, and, ultimately, separation of the epithelium from the Bowman layer. Descemet membrane may be thickened and folded but it is not atrophic.

Q872
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
Regarding the abnormality shown, what term applies to normal tissue present in an abnormal location?
Correct answer: B. choristoma
Rationale
A choristoma is a benign, congenital proliferation of histologically mature tissue that is abnormal for a given topographic location. Limbal dermoids (shown), a type of choristoma, are firm, dome-shaped, white-yellow nodules typically found at or straddling the limbus, most commonly in the inferotemporal quadrant.
Hamartomas are benign congenital proliferation, or abnormal overgrowth, of normally present tissue for a given location. For example, a capillary hemangioma of the eyelid is a hamartoma. A tumor that is made up of tissue derived from all 3 embryonic germ layers is called a teratoma (eg, an orbital teratoma). Sarcomas are malignant soft tissue tumors.

Q873
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What disorder is typically demonstrated by Langhans giant cells in histologic specimens?
Correct answer: B. sarcoidosis
Rationale
Multinucleated giant cells, including the Langhans giant cell, are characteristic of granulomatous inflammation and often observed in histologic specimens of sarcoid granulomas. Bacterial infections are characterized by acute inflammation and the presence of neutrophils. Lymphoma is a malignant lymphoproliferative process in which dense tissue infiltration of a monoclonal population of lymphocytes is typically present. The inflammatory infiltrate seen in orbital pseudotumor, also called nonspecific orbital inflammation, is composed of a mixture of acute and chronic inflammatory cells, including eosinophils, neutrophils, macrophages, lymphocytes, and plasma cells.

Q874
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What anatomic landmark marks the termination of Descemet membrane on gonioscopy?
Correct answer: B. Schwalbe line
Rationale
The termination of Descemet membrane is manifested gonioscopically as the Schwalbe line. The scleral spur, a triangular extension of the sclera, appears as a white band gonioscopically. The trabecular meshwork and the Schlemm canal are nested in the groove formed by the scleral spur and corneoscleral tissue. The iris root inserts posterior to the trabecular meshwork.

Q875
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the initial location of a ring melanoma?
Correct answer: C. ciliary body
Rationale
Ciliary body melanomas are not usually visible unless the pupil is widely dilated. Some erode through the iris root into the anterior chamber and become visible during gonioscopy or external examination. Eventually, the tumor extends through the sclera along aqueous drainage channels, producing an epibulbar nodule. Some ciliary body melanomas assume a diffuse growth pattern and extend up to 360 degrees around the eye; in this case, they are known as ring melanomas.

Q876
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
An otherwise healthy 57-year-old man had a circumscribed reddish-orange lesion in the superotemporal retina. Histology of the lesion is shown in the figure. What is the diagnosis?
Correct answer: A. choroidal hemangioma
Rationale
The figure shows a large number of thin-walled, variably sized vessels within the choroid, with overlying retinal detachment. Choroidal hemangiomas may appear as predominantly capillary hemangiomas, cavernous hemangiomas, or a mix of the 2. There may be compressed melanocytes, hyperplastic retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), and fibrous tissue proliferation in the adjacent and overlying choroid. Circumscribed choroidal hemangioma typically occurs in patients without systemic disorders.
Histologically, posterior uveal melanomas are composed of spindle cells and/or epithelioid melanoma cells. Choroidal osteomas are located in the peripapillary choroid and, histologically, are composed of compact bone. Histology of neurilemomas or schwannomas reveals choroid infiltrated by spindle-shaped cells with slender, wavy nuclei.

Q877
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A 45-year-old woman presents for a routine evaluation. The figure shows a slit-lamp photograph of her right eye. What extraocular manifestation of this disorder would be likely?
Correct answer: B. a deforming arthritis of the distal joints
Rationale
The figure demonstrates sclera thinning without inflammation. This presentation is most consistent with scleromalacia perforans, a condition typically seen in patients with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis. Manifestations of disease include a deforming arthritis of the distal joints. Episodes of shortness of breath can be seen in patients with sarcoidosis, another potential cause of scleritis, but not of scleromalacia perforans. Muscle spasms, weakness, tachycardia, and arrhythmias are not directly associated with this condition or rheumatoid arthritis.

Q878
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the critical finding in the diagnosis of phacoantigenic uveitis?
Correct answer: D. open lens capsule
Rationale
Phacoantigenic uveitis results from a compromise or violation (usually traumatic or surgical) of the lens capsule that causes the exposure of lens material, thereby inciting a granulomatous anterior uveitis. Hypopyon, granulomatous keratic precipitates, and elevated intraocular pressure (by virtue of lens material or macrophages that have ingested lens material that can obstruct the trabecular meshwork) can all occur in phacoantigenic uveitis, but lens violation must first happen. If lenticular capsule has not been breached in some way, then another cause of the inflammation should be sought out.

Q879
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What location of a periocular lymphoma is associated with the lowest risk of systemic lymphomas?
Correct answer: C. conjunctiva
Rationale
It is important to understand the risk of systemic lymphoma in a patient with periocular lymphoma. More than half of periocular lymphomas involve prior, concurrent, or future systemic spread (20%-30% have previous or concomitant systemic disease, 30% develop it over 5 years). This risk is somewhat predicted by the site of periocular origin: The risk is lowest for conjunctival lesions, greater for orbital lesions and highest for eyelid lesions. Lesions in the lacrimal fossa may carry a greater risk than those occurring elsewhere in the orbit. Bilateral periocular involvement greatly increases the risk of systemic disease, but it is not a definitive sign of systemic disease. The risk of systemic disease is increased for decades after the original lesion is diagnosed, regardless of the initial lesion’s location.
The prediction of biologic behavior of periorbital lymphoproliferative lesions is limited, despite clinical, histopathologic, and immunohistochemical studies. Pathologically, lymphoproliferative lesions with lymphoid follicles with germinal centers, a polymorphous mixture of plasma cells, and mature lymphocytes favor a diagnosis of reactive lymphoid hyperplasia. More monotonous, small, round lymphocytes are seen in low-grade malignant lymphomas, whereas high-grade lymphomas demonstrate more malignant nuclei and frequent mitoses. Immunohistochemistry demonstrating mono- or polyclonality is helpful on tissue sections or by flow cytometry.

Q880
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What systemic condition is associated with retinal pigment epithelial hamartoma?
Correct answer: D. colorectal carcinoma
Rationale
There is a strong association of hamartomas of the RPE (RPEH) and familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), an autosomal dominant condition with nearly universal development of colon cancer. Gardner syndrome is the association of FAP with extracolonic manifestations, including cutaneous cysts, osteomas, odontomas, and extracolonic cancers. Multifocal areas of RPEH have been described in family members of patients with FAP. These may differ from congenital hypertrophy of the RPE (CHRPE) in that RPEH lesions are bilateral, more haphazard, and have irregular and jagged borders. The RPE lesions are detectable before the development of polyposis and carcinomas. The pathology of the pigment epithelial lesions in RPEH is a monolayer or multilayered mound of RPE cells, representing a hamartoma (increased amount of normal tissue in its normal location). FAP is associated with a mutation on 5q21. In contrast to RPEH, CHRPE is usually a solitary well-demarcated, flat, darkly pigmented subretinal plaque from 1 to 19 mm, located in the midperiphery, which may be heavily pigmented.
The earliest CHRPE plaques are noted in patients in the second decade. CHRPE is usually nonhereditary and sporadic. Areas of depigmentation (lacunae) within the lesion may be noted. A depigmented ring may surround the lesion. Mild growth of CHRPE has been documented. Histologically CHRPE consists of taller than normal RPE cells, densely packed with large, spherical melanin pigment granules. There is both hyperplasia and hypertrophy of the RPE, with degeneration of the overlying retina. The figures depict selected clinical findings of CHRPE.

Q881
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What kind of feature is more commonly seen in adult conjunctival papillomas than in pediatric conjunctival papillomas?
Correct answer: D. limbal
Rationale
The most common ocular surface neoplasms are squamous in nature. Squamous papillomas may be divided into pedunculated and sessile types.
Pedunculated papillomas are exophytic, pink-red, strawberry-like fronds frequently localized to the caruncle, plica semilunaris, or forniceal conjunctiva. Pedunculated papilloma is associated with human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, subtypes 6 and 11. They may spontaneously involute over months or years. Pedunculated papillomas typically exhibit benign behavior and rarely undergo malignant transformation.
A sessile papilloma generally arises on the bulbar conjunctiva, especially at the limbus, and occurs more commonly in adults. This type of papilloma is also associated with HPV infection, subtypes 16 and 18—the same subtypes associated with squamous malignancies.

Q882
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the etiology of this skin lesion?
Correct answer: B. human papillomavirus
Rationale
Human papillomavirus may infect the skin of the eyelids, typically manifesting as verruca vulgaris, as seen in the photo. Clinically, verruca vulgaris is usually an elevated lesion with fine papillary projections. Histologically, the lesions exhibit a papillary growth pattern and demonstrate parakeratosis, hyperkeratosis, and acanthosis.
Molluscum contagiosum is caused by a member of the poxvirus family. Infections of the eyelid with the mite Demodex folliculorum is increasingly recognized as a cause of chronic eyelid and conjunctival inflammation. A hordeolum is typically caused by Staphylococcus aureus.

Q883
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A corneal scraping from a patient with keratitis demonstrates cysts and trophozoites. What is the etiology of the keratitis?
Correct answer: A. Acanthamoeba
Rationale
Acanthamoeba

Acanthamoeba protozoa have a cyst morphology, and these cysts are difficult to eradicate from the corneal stroma. Less commonly, trophozoite forms might also be identified. Epithelial cells infected with herpesvirus might display intranuclear inclusions; these are rarely seen histologically because corneal grafting is not generally performed during the acute phase of infection. Pseudomonas is a ­gram-­negative bacterium and is rod shaped (bacillus).

Q884
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What other organs should the ophthalmologist be most concerned about in a patient with a retinal capillary hemangioma?
Correct answer: A. brain and kidney
Rationale
Retinal capillary hemangiomas are a common disease manifestation of von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) syndrome, wherein cerebellar and/or spinal hemangioblastomas may develop in patients but are less common. The VHL gene, which is located on chromosome 3, is mutated in the syndrome. Mutations in VHL cause overproduction of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and other hypoxia-inducible factors, leading to the development of highly vascular tumors. A number of other tumors and cysts may develop in patients with this syndrome, the most serious of which are renal cell carcinoma and pheochromocytoma.

Q885
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
An 8-year-old girl presents with flat light-brown spots on the skin, benign skin growths, and encapsulated peripheral nerve tumors. Her father has similar findings. What feature would a biopsy of her optic nerve tumor most likely reveal?
Correct answer: C. Rosenthal fibers
Rationale
This girl and her father have neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1). Her peripheral nerve tumors are most likely representative of neurilemomas (also called schwannomas), which arise from Schwann cells. Neurilemomas have two histologic patterns. Antoni A spindle cells are arranged in interlacing cords, whorls, or palisades that may form Verocay bodies (collections of fibrils resembling sensory corpuscles). Antoni B pattern is made up of stellate cells that have a mucoid stroma. Optic nerve gliomas, which are frequently associated with neurofibromatosis 1 (NF1), most commonly present in the first decade of life and are ­low-­grade juvenile pilocytic astrocytomas. Enlarged, deeply eosinophilic filaments known as Rosenthal fibers, which represent degenerating cell processes, can be found in these ­low-­grade tumors. Psammoma bodies can be found in meningiomas. Staghorn vascular spaces are observed in hemangiopericytomas and related solitary fibrous tumors. Verocay bodies are collections of fibrils that resemble sensory corpuscles in the Antoni A spindle cell pattern observed in schwannomas (also called neurilemomas).

Q886
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What is the first-line treatment of choice for choroidal hemangioma-associated subfoveal detachment?
Correct answer: D. photodynamic therapy with verteporfin
Rationale
The current treatment of choice for symptomatic circumscribed choroidal hemangioma is photodynamic therapy (PDT). Most choroidal hemangiomas respond to PDT, with resolution of the subretinal fluid and partial regression of the lesion, often with associated improvement in vision. However, cystoid macular edema may persist, particularly if chronic, and any degenerative changes in the overlying retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) may limit visual recovery; PDT may need to be repeated. Choroidal hemangiomas were traditionally managed with laser photocoagulation, which created chorioretinal adhesions. However, photocoagulation was often unsuccessful and created scars. Recurrent detachments were common. Low-dose radiation (via brachytherapy or external radiotherapy methods such as charged-particle, stereotactic, or external beam) has been successfully used to treat choroidal hemangiomas, including those unresponsive to PDT. For diffuse choroidal hemangioma, because of the diffuse nature of the tumor, external beam radiotherapy techniques, rather than plaque brachytherapy, are used. There is little published evidence to support the use of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) inhibitors to treat choroidal hemangioma.

Q887
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What inflammatory cells, when found aggregated together, are indicative of granulomatous inflammation?
Correct answer: A. epithelioid histiocyte
Rationale
Inflammatory cells characteristic of chronic inflammatory processes include monocytes and lymphocytes. Monocytes are classified as histiocytes or macrophages when they migrate from the intravascular space into tissue. Histiocytes have eccentric nuclei and abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm. Some histiocytes are referred to as epithelioid histiocytes because of their resemblance to epithelial cells, with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and sharp cell borders. Epithelioid histiocytes may form a ball-like aggregate known as a granuloma, the hallmark of granulomatous inflammation.

Basophils contain basophilic intracytoplasmic granules; when found in tissues rather than in the blood, they are referred to as mast cells.

Neutrophils typify acute inflammatory cells and can be recognized by their multisegmented nucleus and intracytoplasmic granules. They are usually associated with bacterial infections and may be found in blood vessel walls in some forms of vasculitis.

Lymphocytes are cells characteristic of chronic inflammation. They are small with round, hyperchromatic nuclei and scant cytoplasm. They either mature in the thymus (T cells) or bone marrow (B cells). B cells may produce immunoglobulin and differentiate into plasma cells that are characterized by eccentric "cartwheel" or "clockface" nuclei and a perinuclear halo corresponding to the Golgi apparatus. These cells may become completely distended with immunoglobulin and form Russell bodies.

Q888
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What growth pattern of retinoblastoma is most likely to cause an exudative retinal detachment?
Correct answer: A. exophytic
Rationale
The 3 growth patterns of retinoblastoma are endophytic, exophytic, and diffuse infiltrative. In the endophytic growth pattern, the tumor appears as a white or cream-colored mass that breaks through the internal limiting membrane. Endophytic retinoblastoma can be associated with vitreous seeding. Exophytic tumors are yellow-white and occur in the subretinal space. Exophytic retinoblastoma is often associated with subretinal fluid; the exudative retinal detachment can mimic the appearance of Coats disease.
Diffuse infiltrating retinoblastoma is usually unilateral and nonhereditary. It is found in children older than 5 years. The tumor presents with conjunctival injection, anterior chamber seeds, pseudohypopyon, large clumps of vitreous cells, and retinal infiltration of the tumor. There is no nodular growth pattern for retinoblastoma; however, uveal melanoma metastatic to the liver may exhibit a nodular or infiltrative pattern.

Q889
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A 5-year-old boy is found to have unilateral telangiectatic retinal vessels with an exudative retinal detachment. What histologic findings are characteristic of the likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: C. foamy histiocytes and cholesterol crystals
Rationale
Coats disease is clinically evident within the first decade of life and is more common in boys. It is characterized by a unilateral retinal telangiectasia with mild to severe leakage and possible exudative retinal detachment. Foamy histiocytes and cholesterol crystals in the subretinal space are common histologic findings.
Loss of capillary pericytes and thickening of the retinal capillary basement membrane can be seen in diabetic retinopathy. Dilated, thin-walled vascular channels between the RPE and the outer aspect of Bruch membrane are found in polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy. Focal sclerosis of retinal vessels with an overlying pocket of liquefied vitreous is found in lattice degeneration.

Q890
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A 68-year-old non-diabetic woman develops cystoid macular edema 6 weeks after cataract surgery. In what retinal layer will cysts most likely be present?
Correct answer: C. outer plexiform layer
Rationale
Postoperative cystoid macular edema classically involves the outer plexiform layer (OPL). In the OPL of the fovea (Henle fiber layer), nerve fibers run obliquely. This results in the petaloid appearance of postoperative cystoid macular edema on fluorescein angiography.

Q891
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
What structure is indicated by the arrow (figure)?
Correct answer: D. anteriorly displaced Schwalbe line
Rationale
The photograph depicts a posterior embryotoxon, which appears as a thin, gray-white, arcuate line on the inner surface of the cornea. Anatomically, it signifies an anteriorly displaced Schwalbe line, which is the junction between the Descemet membrane and the trabecular meshwork. A posterior embryotoxon may occur as an isolated finding, or it may be seen in conjunction with ocular anomalies like Axenfeld-Rieger and Alagille syndromes. When the posterior embryotoxon is observed, it is important to look for other ocular abnormalities including fine peripheral iris strands to Schwalbe line (seen in the photograph), iris stromal hypoplasia, and glaucoma. Multilayered endothelial cells can be seen in posterior polymorphous corneal dystrophy and in iridocorneal endothelial syndrome and can be demonstrated histologically or via confocal microscopy. Thinning of the corneal stroma with lipid exudation would be seen in Terrien marginal degeneration. A linear pattern of inflammatory cells on the endothelium (Khodadoust line) can be seen during episodes of corneal graft rejection.

Q892
Ophthalmic Pathology & Intraocular Tumors
A 9-year-old child with a history of recurrent bacterial infections develops an intractable respiratory infection that proves fatal. The ocular and histopathologic findings of the patient are shown in the figure below. What is the most likely underlying disease in this patient?
Correct answer: D. Chédiak-Higashi syndrome
Rationale
The ocular findings as shown in the above figure, iris transillumination defects, fundus hypopigmentation, and decreased melanin distribution in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and choroidal tissue are consistent with ocular albinism. Two notable syndromes associated with ocular-cutaneous albinism are Chédiak-Higashi syndrome and Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome.
Chédiak-Higashi syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder with a mutation in a lysosomal trafficking regulator protein that renders inadequate phagocytosis. This results in recurrent pyogenic infections, often involving the respiratory and cutaneous systems. Patients with Chédiak-Higashi syndrome rarely survive past 10 years of age and often succumb to infection. Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by ocular-cutaneous albinism and bleeding problems from a platelet abnormality. Gaucher disease is an autosomal recessive inherited disorder of metabolism involving glucocerebroside. Gaucher disease is not associated with albinism. Niemann-Pick disease type C (NPC) is a rare progressive genetic disorder characterized by an inability of the body to transport cholesterol and other fatty substances (lipids) inside of cells.
